Sant Darshan (Vision of the Saint)

_Sant darshankun Jivana. Ash kare Vaikunth. Vaikunth bapareki kaha chali. Jo vanchhe Kamala kanth. ||1||_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: even Vaikunth longs for the darshan of a saint. What good, poor thing, is Vaikunth itself to one who truly desires the Lord of Kamala [Vishnu, consort of Lakshmi]?)

_Ram bhakti sab ko kare. Brahma Shankar Shesh. Sant sangat bin Jivana. Dularbh Harika desh. ||2||_ (Everyone -- Brahma, Shankar, and Shesh -- performs devotion to Ram. Jivandasji Maharaj says: without the company of saints, the abode of Hari is very hard to attain.)

_Sarvar taruvar santajan. Chautha barasai meh. Parmarath ke karanai. Charo dhari deh. ||3||_ (The lake, the tree, the saintly person, and, fourth, the rain cloud -- these four have taken on bodily form only for the sake of others' good.)

The Sadguru's Balgopal (child devotee):

_Pruthvi pralay jaat thi. Jo aise na hote das. Naam dhun kari Jivana. Ta aadhar aakash._ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: the earth would have gone to ruin, had there not been such devotees. By the constant chanting of the divine Name, that alone becomes the support of the very sky.)

In the whirl of maya (illusion), all souls -- from human beings to gods and goddesses -- are trapped in the ocean of worldly existence (bhavsagar). Therefore, because of unrighteousness (adharma), great destruction was about to befall this earth; but by performing devotion to God, one is saved from the world's threefold afflictions (tritap). Thus, saints who take the Name of God rescue deserving souls. God sends such saints into the world, and thereby the welfare of humankind is accomplished. Even the wise (jnani), the meditative (dhyani), yogis, silent ascetics (mauni), or those who practice austerities (tapasvis) cannot be saved without the Name of God. Therefore only saints can save us through the path of devotion (bhakti).

In this world, the sadhus, bavas, sannyasis, vairagis, and those wearing the garb of holy men that we see all begin to appear to us as saints, but for devotion to God such outward observances are useless; therefore it is not possible to know who the true saint really is. Sadhus, bavas, sannyasis, vairagis, renunciants, those in holy garb, and hypocrites wander about the world driven by the desire to become gurus by making disciples of their own. True saintly beings of the highest order -- Sadguru Kabirji, Lord Padmanabh, Jivandasji, and others -- save us from such fake gurus. A saint like Jivanji Maharaj manifests and leads us into loving devotion (prem bhakti), saving us from the ritualism carried on in the name of religion.

Jivanji Maharaj has shown the true path of devotion; this will become clear from the deeds of his life. Loving devotion is not attained through rites such as yajnas (sacrificial rites), japa (repetition of the Name), tapa (austerity), pilgrimage, or vows and fasts; therefore Jivanji Maharaj gave us the true understanding of devotion. One must beware of the path of ritual action that deceives under the pretext of devotion, and one must be saved from self-interested "saints" who lead people down such a path in the name of sainthood.

Jivanji Maharaj and Sadguru Kabirji made people give up the worship of anadev (gods other than Hari) -- anadev being whatever is turned away from Hari. All these gods and goddesses lead one only into their own respective self-interests. The words Sakat and Salil refer to worshippers of such gods and goddesses. The loving devotion that Jivanji Maharaj has given us will become clear -- its vision (darshan) -- through the deeds of his life.

In this world, those who practice devotion are of three kinds: (1) Sakat -- worshippers of anadev, that is, those who worship deities other than Hari, such as the Shaktas and the like. (2) Salil -- such devotees sometimes worship their chosen deity (ishtadev) and sometimes worship anadev. (3) Anin, meaning ananya (exclusive, undivided devotion) -- such a devotee worships no god or goddess besides their chosen deity, Hari.

This book gives us a vision (darshan) of the God-devoted deeds of Jivanji Maharaj, Jnaniji Maharaj Kabirji, Padmanabhji, and others. May it be our prayer that all of us, understanding Jivanji Maharaj and the devotion he has shown us, join in devotion, and, going into his refuge, be granted such devotion that brings about our own welfare.

With respectful Ram Kabir greetings -- Swami Jagdishchandra Chadunath.

Ramkabir

_Gurjar khandmein pragate, Gnani Gorakhnath; Das Kabire jeevna, mastak dino hath._ ||129|| — Prabodh
(In the land of Gujarat appeared Gorakhnath as the Knower [Gnani]; Das Kabir gave him spiritual life, placing his hand upon his head.)

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj says that in the region of Gujarat, Gorakhnath appeared as Gnaniji. Das Kabir placed his hand on his head, graced him, and bestowed devotion upon him — there is another couplet [sakhi] like this:

_Gujaratmein gnani bhaye, jaanat hai sab koy; Das Kabira aayke, darshan deena soy._
(Everyone knows that a knower [gnani] such as this appeared in Gujarat; Das Kabira came and gave him his darshan.)

Everyone knows the fact that a devotee like Gnaniji appeared in Gujarat. Das Kabirji came and gave him darshan, making him fulfilled. In his previous birth, Gnaniji had been Gorakhnath. He had wasted his life in yogic practice and attained eighty-four siddhis [supernatural powers], and out of the pride these gave him he went to defeat Kabir — sitting upon a trident, he asked Kabirji to debate him. Kabirji took one end of a ball of thread used for weaving cloth, kept it on the ground, threw the thread up into the sky, and, sitting on its far end, asked Gorakhnath to come and sit facing him. Seeing this, Gorakhnath admitted defeat, gave up the five emblems of the Gorakh sect [Gorakhpanthi], and begged devotion from Kabirji — this is recounted in the Gorakh-Kabir Dialogue.

_Topi kopi koobadi jholi jhanda haath, kripa bhai Kabirki; Paancho maatra sompi deenhi Gorakhnath._
(The cap, loincloth, crutch, satchel, and flag in hand — when Kabir's grace fell upon him, Gorakhnath surrendered all five of these emblems.)

When Kabir's grace fell upon Gorakh, he handed over to Kabirji the cap, loincloth, crutch [under-arm staff], satchel, and flag — all five emblems.

The account of how Kabir told Gorakh — who had squandered his life in yogic practice — that he would grant him devotion when he took his second birth, is found in a text called the Garbhavali.

Gorakh said:

_Suno swami garabh bandhana, kaise hansa hoy chhootana; Kaise mite jathar-ki traasa, so saheb kaho hum paasa._
(Listen, O Master: how may the soul [hansa] bound in the womb be freed, and how may the torment of the womb-fire be ended? Tell me this, O Lord.)

Gorakh said, "O Swami! Listen — how may the soul [jivatma] bound in the womb be freed, and how may the torment of the digestive fire [jatharagni] in the womb end? Tell me this, Master."

Sadguru Kabir said:

_Ab main tumkun bhed bataai, desh Murdharmein janamo jaai; Jesalmer Murdhar mojhara, Bhathi ke ghar lyo avatara. Gnani hoye jo naam tumhara, khoji guruko lev vichara; Fir aavo Gujarat mojhara, Kanam mandal seedh bhom bandhana. Jahan hoy tumaro asthana, in dehise tohe samujhaai; Tumharo panth bichal sab jaai, tumaro bhekh chale sansara. Main tumhare jivka karo ubara, tum to boond sadhna keenha; Bhag dekhi tum boho daraana, taate garabhvasmein aai. Tumharo panth gaman hi paai, Gorakh manmein aisi aai. Deh dharun Sindhmein jaai, chhatri ghar leu avatara; Jugat jugatse karu ubara._
(Now I tell you the secret: go and take birth in the land of Murdhar [Marwar]. In Jaisalmer, within Murdhar, take incarnation in the house of the Bhati [Rajput clan]. Your name shall be Gnani [the Knower]; seek out the guru Khojiji and take his teaching. Then come again to Gujarat, and dwell in the plain, level land of the Kanam region — that shall be your abode. Through this very body I shall make you understand. Your entire [Gorakh] path will waver and be led astray, and the practice [bhekh] you adopt there will spread through the world. I shall deliver your soul, but right now you are engaged in the practice of retaining the seed [celibate discipline], and you are greatly afraid at the sight of the female organ — that is why you must enter the womb. The thought came into Gorakh's mind to follow the path Kabirji had shown — that he would take a body by going to Sindh, taking incarnation in a Kshatriya house, and through various means bring about his own deliverance.)

— Sakhi —

_Kahe Gorakh sadguru suno, main leu avatar; Fir tum hamkun kaise milo, so guru kaho vichar. Kar jodi Gorakh kahe, sunho swami sujaan; Sharan tumhari mohi rakh ho, dyo apna nijgyan._
(Gorakh says: "Sadguru, listen — I shall take incarnation, but then tell me, by what reasoning, how will you meet me again?" Folding his hands, Gorakh says: "Listen, O all-knowing Master, keep me in your refuge and grant me your own true knowledge.")

Kabir's word — Kabir says:

_Khoji mootat hans oothe, tum hi haso apaar; Tab khoji man sanse pare, tumse boojh deedar. Khojika saansa mite, sahje hoy ubaar. Batak beejki maandmein, dekh bhaya man dheer; Jan Gnanika sanse mita, sadguru mile Kabir. Kahe Kabir suno Gorakha, maano vachan hamaar; Nizh gyan samjhaavahu, doosar janam tumhaar. So Jesalmer (vaahitare) janamiya, Bhathi kul rajput; Gurjar dhar (desh) paavan kiyo, so gnani gun avadhoot._
(Kabir says: "When Khojiji laughs while relieving himself, you too shall laugh without measure. Then Khojiji will fall into doubt — 'I laughed, but why did you laugh?' — and to find out why, he will come searching for you. Then I shall grant you darshan, and Khojiji's doubt will be resolved; thus your deliverance shall come about with ease. Seeing the fig-fruit swept along in the stream, his mind grew steady." "The devotee Gnani's doubt was resolved when he met the Sadguru Kabir." Kabir says: "Listen, Gorakh, heed my word — I shall explain true knowledge to you in your next birth. So [Gorakh] was born in Jaisalmer, in the Bhati Rajput clan, and sanctified the land of Gujarat — that knower, endowed with the qualities of a true renunciate [avadhoot].")

Sadguru Kabir said, "Now I shall show you the way: go and take birth in the land of Murdhar. Having arrived in Jaisalmer, within Murdhar, take incarnation in the house of a Bhati [Rajput]. Your name will be Gnani, and you shall receive the teaching of Guru Khojiji. Then come to Gujarat and dwell in the plain, level land of the Kanam region — wherever your dwelling shall be. And I, through this very body of Kabir, shall make you understand; your entire Gorakh path will be led astray and abandoned, and the practice of devotion [bhekh-achar] that you adopt there will spread through the world. I shall bring about the deliverance of your soul, but right now you are engaged in the practice of preserving the seed [celibate discipline] and are greatly afraid at the sight of the female organ, and so you shall now enter the womb [take birth]." The thought arose in Gorakh's mind that he should follow the path Kabirji had shown him, and that he should go to Sindh and take incarnation as a Kshatriya, and through various stratagems bring about his own deliverance.

Sakhi — Gorakh began to say, "Sadguru, listen: I shall indeed take incarnation, but then explain to me how you will meet me again." Folding his hands, Gorakh said, "O all-knowing Master, listen: keep me in your refuge, and teach me your own knowledge." Kabir's word — Kabir says, "When Khojiji laughs while urinating, you too will laugh uncontrollably. Then Khojiji will suspect: 'I laughed, but why did you laugh?' — tell me the reason for my laughter. As you search for this reason, you will come looking for me, and then I shall give you darshan, and the doubt Khojiji had raised will be resolved — thus your deliverance shall come about with ease." Seeing the fig-fruit of the banyan tree being carried away in the urine, Khojiji's mind was struck with wonder, and the question this raised for Gnaniji was resolved when he later met Sadguru Kabir — that as long as the seed remained attached to the tree it was safe, but once separated from the tree it is carried away in filth and urine. In the same way, as long as the soul remains attached to the feet of the Lord it stays safe, but turning away from God it keeps drifting in the filth and urine of the womb of this ocean of worldly existence [bhavsagar]. The seed contains the tree within it, and the tree contains the seed within it — in this way the world is contained within God, and God within the world; the two are interwoven. Kabir went on to say, "O Gorakh, heed what I say — I shall explain my own true knowledge to you in your second incarnation." Thus this Gorakh was born in the dwelling of Jaisalmer, in the Bhatiya Rajput clan, and this Knower, possessing the qualities of a true renunciate, sanctified the land of Gujarat. Dayaldas has written about Gnaniji:

_Dayaala aise sadguru Kabir hai, jine Gorakhku chetaaye; Jaaki doormat metke, bandhan diye chhodaaye._ ||13||
(Dayal[das says]: such is the merciful Sadguru Kabir, who awakened Gorakh; erasing his ill understanding, he freed him from bondage.)

Dayaldas says that such is the merciful Sadguru Kabirji, who awakened Gorakh, and having removed the evil intellect [durmat] that was in him, freed him from the bonds of worldly existence.

_Dayaala sadguru das Kabirji, jine Gorakhkun diyo gyan; Gorakh ko saanso mityo, tabahi laagyo nishchal dhyan._ ||14||
(Dayal[das]: Sadguru Das Kabirji is such that he gave knowledge to Gorakh; when Gorakh's doubt was dispelled, he then fixed himself in unwavering meditation.)

Dayal[das says] — Sadguru Das Kabirji is such that he gave teaching to Gorakh, and when he dispelled Gorakh's doubts, Gorakh then engaged in unwavering devotion.

_Dayaala tab Gorakh man vicharke, mudra dhari utaar; He samrath kripa karo, mohe utaaro paar._ ||15||
(Dayal[das]: then Gorakh, reflecting in his mind, removed the yogic emblems [mudras] he wore, and said, "O capable one, be gracious and carry me across.")

Dayal[das] — then Gorakh, reflecting in his mind, removed the emblematic postures [mudras] of the yogic path and said to Kabir, "O capable Kabirji, now be gracious to me and deliver me across the ocean of existence."

_Dayaala tab sadguru boliya, janam dharo avataar; Fer paachhe janam dharo, tab hi utaru paar._ ||16||
(Dayal[das]: then the Sadguru said, "Take incarnation [now]; when you take your next birth after this, then I shall carry you across.")

Dayal[das] — then Sadguru Kabir said, "You must take a[nother] incarnation, and it is when you take that [next] birth that I shall carry you across."

_Dayaala Gorakh man vicharke, chaalyo Murdhar desh; Jesalmermein upanyo, naam dharyo naresh._ ||17||
(Dayal[das]: Gorakh, reflecting in his mind, set out for the land of Murdhar; he was born in Jaisalmer and was known there as a prince [naresh].)

Dayal[das] — Gorakh reflected and set out toward the land of Murdhar, and appeared [was born] in Jaisalmer, where he became known as a prince.

_Dayaala agiyaar varaski umare, tiko rajko hoy; Tab chatursinghe vichariyo, fand paduugo soy._ ||18||
(Dayal[das]: at the age of eleven, when the crowning of the kingdom was to take place, Chatursinh reflected: "I shall thereby fall into a trap.")

Dayal[das] — when the prince reached the age of eleven, the royal coronation [rajtilak] began to take place; then Chatursinh thought, "In this way I shall fall back into the snare of maya."

_Dayaala tab manmein chinta bhai, main bhakti kaaj dhari deh; Jo rajko sukh lahu, to kaal pakad mohe leh._ ||19||
(Dayal[das]: then anxiety arose in his mind — "I took this body for the sake of devotion; if I accept the pleasures of kingship, death shall seize me.")

Dayal[das] — [then] anxiety arose in his mind that, "I took this body in order to attain devotion; so if I accept the pleasure of the splendour of the kingdom, then ruin [kaal] will seize me."

_Dayaala — chatur sanghe vichariyo, neekasu aadhi raat; Chalte-chalte tahan jaau, jahan desh Gujarat._ ||20||
(Dayal[das]: Chatursinh reflected, "I shall leave at midnight, and journeying on, go there, to the land of Gujarat.")

Dayal[das] — Chatursinh thought that he would leave at midnight, and travelling on and on, go to where the land of Gujarat is.

_Dayaala Gurjar dharmein aaiya, jahan Sokhado gaam; Chatusinghe vichariyo, ihaan karu visraam._ ||21||
(Dayal[das]: [Jnaniji — Chatursinh] came into the land of Gujarat, to where the village of Sokhda is; Chatusinh thought, "I shall rest here.")

Dayal[das] — Jnaniji [Chatursinh] came to the land of Gujarat, to where the village of Sokhda is, and there Chatusinh thought that he would take rest.

_Dayaala sarovarki paale rahyo, tapsi bhekh samaar; Bhojan denkun nit hi, aave dvijki naar._ ||22||
(Dayal[das]: he stayed on the bank of a lake, wearing the garb of an ascetic; a Brahmin's wife would come every day to bring him food.)

Dayal[das] — wearing the garb of an ascetic [tapasvi], he stayed on the bank of the lake; a Brahmin woman would come every day to give him food.

_Dayaala taakun ek putra tho, maran paamiyo soye; Chatusinghe kripa kari, tabahi sajivan hoy._ ||23||
(Dayal[das]: that woman had one son, who died; Chatusinh showed his grace, and he thereupon came back to life.)

Dayal[das] — that woman had one son, and he died; Chatusinh showed grace, and he then came back to life.

_Dayaala tabahi Chatusinh oothe chale, gaye Sanjhake dwaar; Taahaan Dwarakadasji bhetiya, bohot kari manuhaar._ ||24||
(Dayal[das]: then Chatusinh got up and set out, and came to the gate of Sanjha; there he met Dwarkadasji, who welcomed him with great warmth.)

Dayal[das] — after that, Chatusinh got up from there and set out, and, travelling on, arrived at Sanjha, where he met Dwarkadasji, who received him with great warmth and respect.

_Dayaala Chatusingh charane namya, mohe sunaavo naam; Tab Dwarka dase kripa kari, naam bataayo Ram._ ||25||
(Dayal[das]: Chatusinh bowed at his feet [and said], "Recite the Name to me"; then Dwarkadas, in his grace, gave him the name of Ram.)

Dayal[das] — Chatusinh fell at his feet and said, "Recite God's name for me"; then Dwarkadas graciously gave him the name of Ram, and showed him the devotional practice of remembering [japa of] the name of Ram.

_Dayaala ek same aisi bhai, hase he Dwarakadas; Tab Chatusingh paachhe hasya, tab gure kahyo parkaas._ ||26||
(Dayal[das]: once it so happened that Dwarkadas laughed; then Chatusinh laughed afterward too; then the guru told [him] to reveal [the reason].)

Dayal[das] — once it happened that Dwarkadas began to laugh; then Chatusinh also laughed after him; then the guru asked him to tell the reason why he [the guru] had laughed.

_Dayaala hame hasiya kon khojmein, sohi khoj le aavo; Chatusingh khojan chale, manmein dhari eh bhaavo._ ||27||
(Dayal[das]: "Find out why I laughed and bring that reason to me"; Chatusinh set out to search, holding this thought in his mind.)

Dayal[das] — "Go and find out the reason why I laughed, and bring it [to me]." For this reason, holding this intention in mind, Chatusinh set out to discover the reason.

_Dayaala dhyaan dharyu Revake betmein, mohe male Bhagvan; Sanso mero metke, ohi bataave gnaan._ ||28||
(Dayal[das]: he took up meditation on an island of the Reva [Narmada], thinking, "May God meet me and, dispelling my doubt, reveal the knowledge.")

Dayal[das] — thinking, "If God meets me [there], he will dispel my doubt and reveal the explanation to me," he began meditating on an island of the Narmada [Reva].

_Dayaala saat din tapasya kari, manmein aani dheer; Tab sadguru dayaa kari, jan-ki jaani peer._ ||29||
(Dayal[das]: he practised austerity for seven days, keeping patience in his mind; then the Sadguru, knowing his devotee's suffering, showed grace.)

Dayal[das] — he practised austerities for seven days, keeping patience in his mind; then the Sadguru, knowing the suffering of his devotee, showed grace.

_Dayaala din ugat sadguru mile, daatan keeno aay; Taaki chiran ropke, vatahi kiyo banaay._ ||30||
(Dayal[das]: at daybreak the Sadguru came and met him, having used a tooth-twig; planting the splinters of it, he made [them grow into] a banyan tree.)

Dayal[das] — as the day dawned, Kabirji came and met him, having cleaned his teeth [with a twig]; he then planted the pieces of that twig and made them grow into a banyan tree.

_Dayaala Chatusingh charane namya, chhaandi apno dhyaan; Tum daata ho mugatke, mohe bataavo gnaan._ ||31||
(Dayal[das]: Chatusinh, leaving his meditation, bowed at his feet [and said], "You are the giver of liberation — grant me your knowledge.")

Dayal[das] — leaving his meditation, Chatusinh bowed at his feet and said, "You are the giver of liberation, the deliverer — teach me your knowledge."

_Dayaala tab sadguru-e dayaa kari, bhed bataayo ek; Chatusingh samjhaaiya, kahe jo vaat vivek._ ||32||
(Dayal[das]: then the Sadguru, in his grace, revealed one secret, and explained it to Chatusinh, telling him this discerning matter.)

Dayal[das] — then the Sadguru, in his grace, explained the reason for the doubt to Chatusinh, and told him to tell his guru the secret [of why he had laughed].

_Dayaala tabahi Chatusinh jaayke, guruku sheesh namaay; je sadguru-e samjhaaiya, so guruku kahi samjhaay._ ||33||
(Dayal[das]: then Chatusinh went and, bowing his head to his guru, told and explained to the guru what the Sadguru had explained [to him].)

Dayal[das] — then Chatusinh went to his guru, bowed his head to him, and told and explained to him what the Sadguru had explained to him:

_Dayaala vaari utaarat behe gayo, vatko beej chanik; Tab gurudev yon boliya, vaat kahi ten neek._ ||34||
(Dayal[das]: "While relieving myself, a fig-seed was in an instant swept away — [that is why I laughed]"; then the guru said, "You have spoken the matter well.")

Dayal[das] — [Chatusinh said]: "While I was urinating, the fig-fruit of the banyan tree was swept away in an instant, and seeing that, I laughed." Hearing this, the guru [Dwarkadas] said, "You have told the truth exactly."

_Dayaala tab gurudev yon boliya, ke anbhe upji tohe; Ke sadguru tohe malya, sohi bataavo mohe._ ||35||
(Dayal[das]: then the guru said, "Has fearlessness [true realization] arisen in you? Or has some sadguru met you? Tell me this too.")

Dayal[das] — then the guru went on to say, "Has fearlessness [true realization] now come to you? Or has some such sadguru met you? Tell me that too."

_Dayaala mohe to sadguru malya, sab bhed diya bataay; So tumkun main aaye kahya, mokun sadguru bhaye sahaay._ ||1||
(Dayal[das]: "I did meet a sadguru, who revealed every secret to me; I have come and told you this — the Sadguru became my helper.")

Dayal[das] — [Chatusinh said]: "I did meet a Sadguru [Kabirji], who revealed every secret to me; that is what I have come and told you — thus the Sadguru became my helper."

_Dayaala guru sevak donu gaye, jahan baithe das Kabir; Tab guru-e gnani kahya, sevak bada sudhir._ ||36||
(Dayal[das]: the guru and the disciple both went to where Das Kabir was seated; then the guru called him "Gnani," [saying] "the disciple is of great steadfastness.")

Dayal[das] — the guru [Khojiji — Dwarkadas] and the disciple Chatusinh both went to where Das Kabirji was seated. There the guru addressed Chatusinh by the name "Gnani" and said, "O devotee, you are of great patience and steadfastness."

_Dayaala sadguru saaheb Kabirji, leela agam apaar; Aage bohot vistaar hai, so harde dharo vichaar._ ||38||
(Dayal[das]: the deeds of Sadguru Saheb Kabirji are unfathomable and boundless; there is much more that unfolds further — keep this thought in your heart.)

Dayal[das] — the deeds and character of Sadguru Kabir Saheb are so profound that they cannot be fully fathomed. There is much more of this story yet to come — keep this understanding in your heart.

The prince Chatusinh of the Bhati clan of Jaisalmer, who came to have darshan of Kabirji at Kabirvad [the banyan of Kabir], was gripped by the doubt of whether the seed lies within the tree or the tree within the seed — that doubt in his mind, Kabirji resolved. One who seeks God by roaming through pilgrimage places, temples, and other such shrines of the divine does not find God in this way; likewise, one who merely performs worship, vows, and rituals cannot attain God. Though the Lord Ram pervades all moving and unmoving creation, he is not seen. When Gnaniji, who was searching for that very Ram, had the darshan of Ram in Kabir, Gnaniji asked, "Baba, are you Ram, or are you Kabir?" Kabirji said, "What do you see?" Gnani said, "Outwardly you appear as Kabir, and yet Ram, who dwells within you, appears clearly to me. Why do we not see this in ourselves?" Kabir said, "When can the essence be seen clearly in a vessel of unclean glass? Only when the vessel is clean does the essence appear clear. In the same way, when the mind becomes pure, and your vessel remains clean, the Ram who dwells within you will become visible." It is evident from this episode of Gnaniji, who had the vision of the united form of Ram and Kabir, that —

_Bahar Kabira dekhke, bharam pado jan kaay; Kabir bhitar Ram dhani, Ram Kabir bhinn na hoye. Kabira man nirmal bhaya, Ram hirde raha samaay; Nirmal bartan ras jyu, Kabir antar Ram darshaay._
(Seeing Kabir outwardly, let no devotee fall into delusion; within Kabir dwells the Lord Ram — Ram and Kabir are not separate. Kabir's mind became pure, and Ram came to dwell in his heart; just as the essence shows clear in a clean vessel, so within Kabir, Ram is revealed.)

Let no one — no devotee — fall into delusion upon seeing Kabir outwardly. Within Kabir dwells the Master, Ram; that Ram and Kabir cannot be separate. Kabir's mind became pure, and Ram came to dwell within his heart. Just as the essence appears clear in a clean vessel, so too Ram is clearly seen within Kabir's heart.

Gnaniji, who had this vision of the united form of Ram and Kabir, awakened the Ramkabir tradition. At Kabirvad, he entrusted the seat [gaadi] to Nirdas. There is a memorial inscription at Kabirvad from the time Kabirji came there. Kabirji regarded temples and idols as obstacles to the worship of God and opposed them. Chatusinh, a prince of the Bhatiya clan of Jaisalmer in Rajasthan, was — in a former birth — the yoga-fallen soul Gorakhnath. Since Chatusinh remained detached from worldly life, his royal family arranged his marriage to the princess Pranakunvarba of Jaipur, and the wedding rites were performed; but during the circling [of the sacred fire], upon hearing the word "sāvadhāna" [be alert], he became alert and fled from the wedding rites. He then took initiation from Khojiji, but the matter of the fig-fruit incident remained unresolved; [to resolve it] he went into meditation [samadhi] at Shulpaneshwar and attained mastery of raja-yoga, but even so his doubt was not resolved. Then he came to Kabirji at Kabirvad, who had given Tattvajiva true recognition of a true saint, and he attained discipleship. Gnaniji's bodyguard and Pranakunvarba too came to Kabirvad. Kabirji explained to Gnaniji that devotion to Hari can be practised even while remaining in householder life; non-attachment is more important than renunciation. Remaining unattached, and through understanding of the mind, one can attain God even while living in the world. Through loving devotion, rather than through renunciation, God can be attained more readily. Gnaniji spent his householder life with Pranakunvar in the great village of Sanja. A religious assembly was held at this place, in which the pandit Sarvajit, defeated in debate, became a disciple of Kabirji.

Anantdas has said, in Kabir's Parachai [hagiography]:

_Ramkabir ekhimeka, jin koi karo apni teka; Jan te thakor te jan hoi, aisi jugat bani hai doi. Pala re jal ten upajya, funi pala jal maanhi samaaya; Bhakt bhagvant aadya hai doi, jhoothe bharam pado mat koi._ ||9-10||
(Ram and Kabir are one and the same — let none rely on doubt regarding them; the devotee becomes the Lord, and the Lord becomes the devotee — such is the way the two are joined. Frost arises from water, and again dissolves back into water; the devotee and God have both existed from the beginning — let none fall into false delusion.)

Ram and Kabir are interwoven with each other, so, by mistake, let no one harbour any doubt about them. The devotee — the Harijan — is God himself, and God is the Harijan himself; such is the mystery contained within these two. Ice is born from water and again dissolves back into water; in the same way, the devotee — the Harijan — and God are, from time immemorial, inseparable from each other. So do not fall into any false delusion.

Brahmalin Muni writes: history says that Gnani had the direct darshan of Guru Kabir Saheb. By Kabirji's grace he had the darshan of Ram; therefore he united Ram and Kabir and uttered the word "Ramkabir."

Sadguru Jivanji says: "Kabir is the form of the Primal Being [Adi Purush]. He showed grace upon Gnaniji, and Gnaniji understood Kabirji to be none other than Ram himself. He did not regard the Sadguru and God as separate. He united Sadguru Kabir and Ram as one, and established the term Ramkabir."

Gnaniji's manifestation [birth] was in Samvat 1451, Posh Sud 11. Gnaniji's living samadhi [conscious departure from the body] took place in Samvat 1559, Posh Sud 11. In Mota Sanja there is a Tulsi platform marking Gnaniji's samadhi. The neem tree under which Gnaniji used to sit was once split into two by a lightning strike, but it sprouted again and has grown fresh leaves once more; the leaves of this neem carry no bitterness. Mota Sanja can be reached from Zaghadia. Kabirji came to Gujarat from Kashi, and visited Patan Padmavadi, the courtyard of Narsinh Mehta in Junagadh, Pipaji's place in Gangrod fort, and Tattvajiva's place in Mangaleshwar (at Kabirvad).

Haridas Nadiada and Vaishnav Shyamdasji Maharaj, who have narrated the life-story and philosophical teachings of Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj, have made no mention at all of certain episodes of his life. Either Jivanji Maharaj himself did not inform anyone of certain events in his life, or he simply paid no attention to recording them. One such matter is that of his birth, his birthplace, and information about his parents — regarding this, we have not been able to obtain any definite information.

Vaishnav Haridas Nadiada, the earliest editor of the Samagam [the collection of teachings], writes about Jivanji Maharaj's manifestation that he appeared at Gahej Goriyad on Shravan Sud Eighth of Samvat 1660, at the age of eleven. But interpreting this sentence in light of his couplets [sakhis] and the references found within the Samagam, it appears that on this day he renounced his home and adopted the life of a mendicant. Since he had already crossed eleven years of age in Samvat 1660, his birth must have taken place in Samvat 1649. Furthermore, the genealogist's records state that he was originally born into a Leva Patidar family of Karamsad, and that he lost the shelter of his parents in his childhood. It was therefore in this condition that he renounced his home and took initiation at Gahej Goriyad. However, this record makes no mention at all of the names of his parents.

Whatever the truth may be, he must certainly have been born somewhere, and for some reason he must have renounced his home and begun his wanderings. And at the age of thirty-four, in Samvat 1683, he bowed to Gopaldas, addressing him as Ramkabir, and accepted him as his Sadguru. Thus, on this day, he accepted the Ramkabir tradition. But where he stayed and what he did during all these intervening years, he himself never mentioned to anyone, nor have Haridas Nadiada or Shyamdasji made any mention of it.

sections.title_en: Vaishnav Gopaldas Is Accepted as the True Guru
sections.translation:
On the eighth day of the bright half of Shravan in Samvat 1660, the Vaishnav Jivandasji manifested at the age of eleven in Gahej Goriyad. There the true dharma revealed itself to him. But he always cherished the wish that wherever a Vaishnav was to be found, he might have the good fortune of asking about sakhi (devotional couplets) and see love for God deepen. When he turned sixteen, at Keslubaa (present-day Kesaru, near Palej) he had his very first meeting with Gopaldasji, the Barot (bard-poet) of Chorenda. Jivandasji greeted Gopaldasji with "Ram Ram." Gopaldasji was returning from another village where he had performed someone's last rites. Jivandasji then invited Gopaldasji to his own temple-home, brought him there, and they sang hari-kirtan (devotional hymns); on that occasion satsang and holy company continued for a full day and night. From there Gopaldasji returned to his own temple-abode.

In Samvat 1683, on the thirteenth day of the dark half of Aso, Jivandasji went to Chorenda. There satsang and holy company happened again, and a very long discussion took place on whether God has form or is formless. Citing evidence from the nitya-akshari (word-for-word) exposition of Namdev, Kabirji, Adhyaruji, the Bhagavad Gita, the Bhagavat, the Shiv Mahimna Stotra, Hariram Vyas (disciple of Hit Harivansh), Rankavanka, Govinddas's Sarvang Leela, the verses of Jaydevji's Geet Govind, the words of Vidurji in the Mahabharat, the sayings of Premanand, the sayings of Jaswantji, and the couplets in the sahasranama (thousand-name hymns) of Seni, Dhana, Peepa, Rohidas, Mirabai, Surdas and others, they arrived at a conclusion on whether God is sagun-sakar (with attributes and form) or nirgun-nirakar (without attributes, formless). The final conclusion reached was this: the true Supreme Being is the enchanting Flute-Player (Moral Manohar) sung of in the Vedas, spoken of in the Bhagavad Gita, described in the Bhagavat and in the sahasranama — He is the true Lord of Namdev and Kabirji. This entire universe has lost its way on this point. Just as the Lord of the clouds is the ocean, and the Kshirsagar's waves are His waves, so too the divine plays (leela) and incarnations — Ram, Krishna, and the rest — are like the waves of that same ocean; among all these incarnations, Ram and Krishna are the principal ones bearing His name and form. All the other incarnations, however, are merely the names given to the forms that God assumed. Those incarnations, therefore, were like the sixteen ornaments (adornments) worn by the sakhis (companions) of the Rasa circle — in their adornment one could see only Krishna's reflection, not the original Krishna. The original Krishna was the one on whose shoulder Radhaji placed her hand while dancing the Rasa — He alone was the true Krishna. Thus these incarnations were like waves of the ocean; they were but one form of that original God. So the conclusion reached was this: the true Supreme Being is the enchanting Flute-Player who resided in Radha's hand — the one bearing the Name upon whom the form rested. As for the rest — the various forms of the incarnations that bore that form's name — they are but one glimpse (a partial reflection) of God, and cannot be counted as the complete Parabrahm (Supreme Absolute). Thus the Deity who is Name-and-then-Form is the true one, but the deity who is Form-and-then-Name is not the complete Supreme Being. Having resolved every doubt about God's form and formlessness in this way, Jivandasji Maharaj accepted Sadguru Gopaldasji as his own true Guru — this took place when he went to Chorenda on the thirteenth day of the bright half of Aso in Samvat 1683, on the day of the Sharad Purnima festival. _Paani peena chhaanke, guru karna jaanke_ (Water should be drunk only after straining it, and a guru should be made only after knowing him well) — meaning that just as water must be filtered before drinking, one must be certain of a guru's worthiness before accepting him. It was on this occasion that Jivanji Maharaj spoke these words:

_Kaamika guru kaamini, lobhika guru daam._
_Kabirka guru bhagat hai, bhagatanke guru Ram._
_Guru kije vicharke, jehi bataave Ram._
_Sarju teere Jeevana, nagar Ayodhya gaam._
(The lustful man's guru is the woman he desires; the greedy man's guru is money. Kabir's guru is the true devotee, and the devotee's guru is Ram Himself. Choose a guru only after due thought — one who can truly reveal Ram to you. — Thus speaks Jivan[a], on the banks of the Sarayu, in the town of Ayodhya, [of the Ram who dwells there].)

Men driven by lust fall into the snare of women; being under the sway of a woman or wife, they must live as she dictates. A greedy man, on the other hand, holds money dear, and so falls into the trap of whoever dangles wealth before him. But a truly worthy guru is one like Kabir — a real saint, for true saints are devoted only to the worship of Ram. Hence it is said: before making anyone one's guru, one must think carefully whether he can give true conviction of Ram — the guru chosen should be one who can grant true realization of Ram of Ayodhya, of what He truly is. Jivandasji, in his quest for truth, resolved to make a saint his guru, but the question was how to recognize a true saint. Renunciants and ascetics can be found in plenty, but how does one know a true saint, and by what test can he be recognized? So he planted a dry, dead stump of a banyan tree in his courtyard, resolving that he would accept as his guru whichever saint's charanamrit (water that has washed a saint's feet) made that dry stump turn green. Saints passing on their pilgrimage-circuit (parikrama) of the river Reva-Narmada were served by him; he would wash their feet and water the dead stump with that charanamrit. As word of this vow (tek) spread, people began to think Jivandasji had gone mad. Some said that no saint should be tested in such a manner, and that this had corrupted the intellect of these Brahmins. Yet an inner voice assured him that a saint like Kabir would indeed be found this way. Jivanji Maharaj wandered and struggled a great deal; he had even, for a time, taken sannyasis (renunciate ascetics) as his guru. But finally, to secure a true guru, he tested Gopaldasji thoroughly and, once he had understood the real truth, accepted him as his guru. From childhood he had wandered and struggled; the true dharma had revealed itself to him from the age of eleven, and by the time he reached maturity he had also grown wise. It was for this reason that he made such an untiring, deep effort to be certain of Gopaldasji's worthiness. And Gopaldasji proved that his own view and path were indeed the ones that lead to true bhakti (devotion).

sections.title_translit: Harma Ba Par Jivanji Maharajni Krupa
sections.title_en: Jivanji Maharaj's Grace upon Harma Ba
sections.translation:
While traveling to Chorenda with a company of saints, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj rested beneath a dry peepal tree on the bank of the pond in the village of Dhanora. Men sent by order of the village headman to cut down the peepal tree saw that it had turned green, and carried the news back to the village. The villagers and the headman, filled with reverence, came to have darshan of the saints and of Jivanji Maharaj, and made their request. This event is recorded in handwritten manuscript no. 28, pages 95 to 97, as follows: Jivandasji Maharaj came to Dhanora on his way from Chanderi to Chorenda. Jivandasji arrived at Dhanora. While travelling to Chorenda for the Sharad-night festival, the village of Dhanora came on the way. There, Jivandasji and the other Vaishnavs were seated together by the pond, beneath a peepal tree, and hari-kirtan was being sung. Now that peepal tree was dry. Because it had dried up, the village headman sent men to cut it down. At that, Jivandasji said that the peepal was in fact green and should not be cut; moreover, the Gitaji itself says that a peepal tree should not be cut — this is stated in the Gita, chapter 9, verse 10. The men then went back and reported that the peepal had indeed turned green.

On hearing this, all the villagers came at once to have darshan of the saints, and the moment they did, everyone's mind grew clear and pure. They asked, "This peepal was dry — how did it turn green?" Jivandasji replied that this peepal had dried up because of the bones of an ungrateful man, and that, likewise, water no longer remained in the pond either. He then spoke this sakhi (couplet) on the matter:

_Kritaghnike haadsu peepal sooko jaay,_
_so Jeevan leelo kiyo Sadguru tane pasaay. ||1||_
(Because of the bones of an ungrateful man this peepal had dried up; that same tree Jivan[a] made green again, by the grace granted by the Sadguru.)

Then they understood that some great soul had come to their village, and with this understanding they made a request: "This young woman is disabled from birth, and belongs to our own family." They brought the girl and placed her at his feet, whereupon Jivanji Maharaj showed his grace.

He told one attendant, "Go and bring water from the pond." The attendant took the kamandal (water vessel) and went to fetch water, but found no water at all in the pond, and returned. He told the Maharaj that there was no water in the pond. Jivandasji then said, "Brothers, in this world, just as the peepal dried up because of the bones of an ungrateful man, so too there is no water in the pond — but by the glory of the saints, water shall appear." He sent the attendant a second time, telling him to go and bring water from the pond. By the glory of the saints, water appeared there.

_Adhik badhaavat aapate, jan mahima Raghuveer,_
_Savari pad raj prasartaan, shuddh bhayo sarita neer. ||2||_
(Lord Raghuveer magnifies the glory of His devotee even more than His own; just as when the dust of Shabari's feet touched the river, its water became pure.)

In this way the water appeared, and the attendant brought it and gave it to the Maharaj. He took that water, sprinkled it upon the young woman's body, and also gave her some to drink; by this her disability left her body and she became whole, and moreover the light of true knowledge dawned in her.

Harmabai's Words

_Harmaanbai harkhiyaan, Jeevan darshan paay,_
_Shareere saanso mitiyo, bhayo gnaan prakaash. ||3||_
(Harmabai rejoiced on receiving the darshan of Jivan[a]; the affliction in her body was removed, and the light of true knowledge dawned.)

Harmabai's Words

_Gnaan prakaashi guru milyaa, so kem visaryo jaay,_
_Jo Govind kripa kare, to guru milenge aay. ||4||_
(The Guru who met me and lit the lamp of knowledge — how could he ever be forgotten? If Govind bestows His grace, that Guru will surely come and meet again.)

sections.title_en: A Trance of Devotion (Bhava-Samadhi) in Jagannath Puri
sections.translation:
On hearing this sakhi, Jivanji Maharaj felt great joy, and understanding that this was some meritorious soul, he placed his hand upon her head — and at once her disability left her. Seeing this, Harmaba's father, Ratansinh, said, "I offer my daughter to you." Hearing this, Jivanji Maharaj said that they were wanderers who roamed from land to land, and that this would not befit a life of renunciation. The other devotees of the Guru who were present then persuaded Jivandasji.

Word of this also reached Gopaldasji in Chorenda, and he too said that this was indeed the wish of the Gracious Lord — that he should enter into worldly life (grihasth ashram). Jivandasji then agreed. Harmaba, moreover, said:

_Tumkun chhod avar kahaan jaau, nishadin tumhaari sang rahaavun._
(Leaving You, where else could I go? Day and night I shall remain in Your company.)

Hearing these words of Harmaba, he accepted her — just as Jagannath Swami had once given Padmavati to Jaydevji. In this way, by Hari's will, he accepted Harmaba, and himself stayed on for one month, singing hari-kirtan. He gave everyone knowledge (upadesh/teaching) and dispelled their ignorance. He then told Harmaba, "I shall travel with Gopaldasji through Malwa, Jagannathji, Naimisharanya, Kashi, Ayodhya, Mathura, and Badrikashram, and when I return I shall take care of you" — and having said this, he himself departed for Chorenda.

Bhava-Samadhi in Jagannath Puri

By the command of Guru Gopaldasji, Jivanji Maharaj set out with him from Chorenda toward Malwa on the tenth day of the bright half of Aso, in Vikram Samvat 1687. But in Malwa, since the financial condition of Gopaldasji's friend was not sufficient to support both guru and disciple, Jivanji Maharaj sought leave from Guru Gopaldas and travelled on ahead alone. On the way, afflicted by hunger, Jivanji Maharaj ate the fruit of the beheda tree. Having eaten too much of the fruit,

he became intoxicated by it and fell unconscious, remaining so for some time beneath that very tree. At this time, a company of saints happened to be passing on their way to pilgrimage at Jagannath Puri; they saw Jivanji Maharaj lying unconscious, and this company of saints then brought him along with them to Jagannath Puri. He remained there for some days. One evening, in the presence of Lord Jagannath, Jivanji Maharaj slipped into bhava-samadhi (a trance of devotional absorption), losing all awareness of time. In this state he remained seated, leaning against a pillar. As night fell, the temple's attendants and priests closed the temple doors and went home.

Jivanji Maharaj lay absorbed in bhava-samadhi, with no awareness of time at all. At midnight, hearing the sound of someone moving about on every side, he awoke from his trance and began looking around, only to realize that he was shut inside the temple. He could see no one, yet he heard the sound of someone's footsteps. This episode in the life of Jivanji Maharaj —

— describing this episode in the life of Jivanji Maharaj, Shyamdasji writes:

_Sandhya same aarti bhai, mandirmen baithe sukhamai._
_Aarti kari sab uthike chale, sej sanvaarine paande mile. ||9||_
_Sej sanvaari prabhu podhai, sabai chale charan sir naai._
_Sadguru Jeevan rahe lukaai, taaki kaahu khabar na paai. ||10||_
(At evening time the aarti was performed, and the deity sat there in bliss within the temple. After the aarti, all rose and departed; the priests arranged the resting-couch and then took their leave. ||9|| Having arranged the couch and settled the Lord to rest, all bowed their heads at His feet and departed. Sadguru Jivan[a] remained hidden there, and no one came to know of it. ||10||)

According to a popular belief, no one may spend the night inside the Puri temple; it is said that anyone who stays there overnight will either die or lose his sanity. But Jivanji Maharaj disproved this belief — nothing of the kind happened to him; he neither died nor went mad.

A Dialogue with Lord Jagannath

In writing the parchari (hagiographic account) of Jivanji Maharaj, Shyamdasji Maharaj has drawn our attention to several events. Jivanji Maharaj's coming into the world had a definite purpose — it is well known that he appeared for the welfare of his own devotees (nij-jans). Haridas Nadiyada, too, stated this at the very outset of the satsang gathering. In the course of the gathering he merely mentioned that Jivanji Maharaj had spent a night inside the world-famous temple of Jagannath. But Shyamdasji, in his parchari of Jivandasji, has also described the conversation that took place between Jivanji Maharaj and Lord Jagannath.

_Tum kaho ihaan kahaan te aaye, aras paras mili kanth lagaaye._
_Kehi kaaran tum bhaye prakaashaa, tabahi bole Shri Jeevandaasaa._
("Tell me, from where have you come here?" — saying this, the two embraced each other, neck to neck. "For what reason have you appeared here?" — then Shri Jivandasji spoke in reply.)

At evening time, while having darshan of Jagannathji in the temple, Jivanji Maharaj had entered into bhava-samadhi. Meanwhile, as the hour grew late, the priests closed the temple and departed. Then, at midnight, Lord Jagannath

woke Jivandasji and asked him, "O Saint! From where have you come here?" So saying, the two embraced each other, neck to neck, and He asked the reason for his coming. Jivanji Maharaj replied, "I have received the command of the supremely gracious Ram; therefore I have come for the welfare of His own devotees." Lord Jagannath said, "O supreme saint! The Lord's divine play (kreeda) is infinite — no one can fathom its limit. I too am but one small portion (ansh) of Him, and day and night I sing His praises."

Hearing this, Jivanji Maharaj said, "O Lord! You alone are capable of knowing how much love I bear toward the Supreme Being. But I have a longing (bhaav) to witness Your rasa-leela (the divine circle-dance). Please grant me its darshan." On hearing this, Lord Jagannath performed the rasa-leela that very night, together with all the gopis. Instruments began to play, and with deep devotional feeling He created an atmosphere steeped in loving bhakti.

sections.title_en: A Vision of India Seen from the Himalayas
sections.translation: Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, travelling on from Naimisharanya, visited the holy sites of Dantanagar in Aryavrat and then went on to Badri. From Badrinath he reached the peak of Kailash in the Himalayas. On the way, in Aryavrat, there dwelt a people called the Paag. He journeyed among them for four days, and on the fifth day was able to pass beyond them, arriving amid the sava-lakh (a hundred and twenty-five thousand) peaks. There he climbed Mount Kailash and sat leaning against a stone slab. As he turned his mind over the four directions of Bharat (India), he saw that every human being in the world was suffering in the fire of self-interested striving — through various forms of worship, ritual observance, fear, superstition, blind faith, the path of the Vedas, and the like. Troubled at heart, he cried out, "O Maharaj — no one truly goes [to You]!" — that is, "O God, in this world, who is it that truly performs loving devotion toward You...

No one like that can be found. In the Kali Yuga many ascetics wearing the garb of renunciation will be found, but true saints of Shri Hari will not be found however much one searches. From atop Kailash, flames are seen rising in all four directions — flames of lust, anger, greed, hypocrisy, and the like. In sacrificial rites (yajnas), the flames of violence are seen blazing. At places of pilgrimage, the flames of craving for charity and offerings are seen. Looking toward Gujarat, however, a little greenness appears that brings peace to the mind — his own devotees are seen waiting eagerly for him. Vaishnav Jivandasji, like the kunj bird that hides its eggs in the sand at the seashore and goes off to graze as far as Lake Mansarovar yet never forgets its young or the way back, set out for Gujarat in that same spirit, to meet the devotees who kept him in remembrance.

In Aryavrat he passed through the region of Shiva's Ekpad Ganas. While making the panchakoshi (five-stage) circumambulation of Kashi, the site for the darshan of the Ekpad Ganas comes midway. Kashi may only be a place that commemorates these Ganas, but Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj actually went to the true, original land of these Ganas and had a direct experience of them there — such was his capability. For the sake of his own devotees he made this journey all the way to the Himalayas of Bharatvarsha (India), for the sake of true devotion. He gained knowledge about every branch and sub-branch of the tradition. Having left his own people at places such as Chanderiya and Ujjain, Jivanji Maharaj now turns back for the welfare of those kinsmen. The longing awakens in him to accomplish the task he had come to do, and so he began the tradition of Uda Dharma and spread pure, unblemished devotion.

When Jivanji Maharaj was preparing to come from Malwa to Gujarat, nine devotees from there also got ready to leave their homeland and come along with him. After they had gone halfway, Jivanji Maharaj felt like testing whether the love of these devotees was genuine. So, saying "I can walk no further now," Jivanji Maharaj sat himself down. The devotees thereupon left their belongings lying right there, seated Jivanji Maharaj in a palanquin, and carried him a distance of five kos (about ten miles). Because they passed Jivanji Maharaj's test, by his own power he had their bundles brought to that very spot; and once the bundles arrived, he had rice and other provisions taken out from them and ordered a meal to be prepared. These loving devotees had not become so infatuated as to be unwilling to accompany Jivanji Maharaj — rather, Jivanji Maharaj himself had said:

_Pendama pad Jivana | jahan nikse harike das ||_
_Sang rahe ke le chale | pure mankee aas ||1||_
("Take your stand on the path, Jivan, wherever the servants of Hari pass by. Either they will stay with you, or they will take you along — either way your heart's longing will be fulfilled.")

If we wait patiently upon the very path along which God's devotees are known to pass, holding fast to that spot, then someday, whenever a true saint happens to come that way, he will either remain with you and remove all the desires of your mind and the sufferings of the disease of worldly existence, or he will take you along with him. Such feelings were firmly fixed in the minds of these devotees. That is why true Sadgurus would take such people along with them. Whoever passes through the guru's test may attain their welfare, but this test must be endured — and so Kabir says:

_Kabir khari kasoti Ramki | khota take na koy ||_
_Ram kasoti te sahe | je jivat mratak hoy ||2||_
("Kabir says: the true test is Ram's own test — no false one can withstand it. Only one who is dead while yet alive can endure the test of Ram.")

When a true examination is made of who is genuine and who is a mere hypocrite in the practice of devotion to Ram, those who are weak, soft, and hypocritical fail it. So the true test of devotion to Ram can be borne only by those devotees who, having given up their own ego, worship him free of desire.

These devotees passed the test of Ram. Those devotees who were prepared to follow the Uda Dharma tradition that Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj set going had to face a situation as hard as, or even harder than, that of the devotees from Malwa. Because Jivanji Maharaj made them give up the company of their own kinsfolk, it is hard even to imagine today how difficult it must have been for those who accepted this faith to observe the prohibition against eating with their own kin, parents, or relatives, and against giving and taking daughters in marriage outside the fold. Moreover, they had to boycott the Vedic path of ritual observance, keep strict abstinence from all vices, wholly reject the degrading custom of sutak (birth/death ritual pollution) and the taboo of menstrual impurity, and put a complete stop to practices such as beating the chest in mourning (chhajiya) and the buying and selling of brides and grooms — one has only to consider how much hardship this must have caused in everyday worldly dealings. For us, in our present circumstances, thanks to the merit and grace of our forefathers and elders, we face not the slightest difficulty in observing these customs. Before any new practice can be established, it is always very hard to clear away the old rubbish. Thus our whole community of devotees today does not have to undergo even a trace of the testing of worldly custom and Vedic ritual that they went through. To that extent we are fortunate indeed. Blessed is such a Sadguru, and blessed are such brave and valiant devotees.

sections.title_translit: Shahpurama Ananya Vaishnav Uda Dharmano Marg Drudhavyo
sections.title_en: In Shahpura, the Path of Uda Dharma Was Firmly Established for the Exclusively Devoted Vaishnavs
sections.translation:
Indian society was caught in blind faith, distrust, and corrupted customs and traditions. It was burning in the flames of false scriptural doctrine, brahmin-priestcraft, and empty ritualism. Padmanabh of Patan had spread the Ramkabir tradition of Gnaniji Maharaj widely. The Ramkabir tradition had begun in Kabirji's own time, but it had not yet taken shape as a distinct sect — it was only the influence of Kabirji and the spread of his knowledge and devotion. So Jivanji Maharaj established the Uda sect in Gujarat. He revealed such a path for these singularly devoted Vaishnavs that it required no austerity (tap), no pilgrimage (tirth), no yoga, no yajna, no votive offerings (manata), no ritual water-offering (arghya/anjali), no formal Vedic study (adhyayan), no fire-oblation (hom), and no ritual observance (karmakand) — only devotion was to be practiced. He gathered together the four essentials — tilak, tulsi, the name of Ram, and the company of saints — as the substance of the essence, and there was no place for the six schools of philosophy or the six branches of scripture. In marriage, without needing an auspicious hour fixed by astrology, bride and groom were wed in the manner of Sita's svayamvar in King Janak's court. Thus he practiced devotion to Vishnu.

_Uda kudya Jivana, jap tap tirath dan ||_
_Ved marag pichhe rahyu, jai malya Hari naam ||1||_
("Jivan, the Uda devotees have leapt clear of japa, austerity, pilgrimage, and charity; leaving the Vedic path behind, they have gone straight and merged into the name of Hari.")

The Uda devotees crossed over the practices of japa, tap, pilgrimage, charity, and the like, set aside the ritual observance of the Vedic path, and merged directly into the worship of God's name.

In the tradition of Uda Dharma, none of the following are accepted: lineage, ritual action, formal religious deeds, pilgrimage, vows, worldly custom, Vedic custom, the Vedic path, the worship of minor deities, or the abodes of heaven, Vaikuntha, and the like. Apart from single-minded, exclusive devotion to Ram and Krishna, there is no worship of any other god or goddess. Moreover, there is no idol worship and no brahminism. They hold no faith in sacred threads, amulets, vows, or votive bindings. The practice of the Uda devotees' Vaishnavism differs from the way ordinary Vaishnavs practice devotion. Ordinary Vaishnav people practice idol worship, ritual observance, and the worship of minor deities. But the Vaishnavs of the Uda devotees do not worship minor deities, Ganpati, or other gods and goddesses the way they do.

In this way, the Uda devotees practice pure devotion to Vishnu. Ordinary Vaishnav people worship minor deities by performing yajnas and other rites, but the Vaishnavs of the Uda devotees do not accept yajnas and such rites. They do not revere the Shaligram stone, do not perform shraddha (ancestral rites), do not honor renunciate garb (bhekh), and do not worship goddesses such as Gayatri.

sections.title_en: Holy Company with the Saint at Shahpura
sections.translation:
Nana Gopaldas and other devotees came from Malwa together with Jivanji Maharaj and settled at the station of Shahpura. This Nana Gopaldas was from Chanderiya. He was inquisitive by nature, and so he used to hold very extensive discussions on dharma with Jivanji Maharaj. And whatever Jivanji Maharaj told him, Haridas would write down — these words and teachings of Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj. That writing exists with us to this day. We call it the Samagam (the Holy Discourse) of Jivanji Maharaj.

(Based on the couplets of Jivanji Maharaj!)

When Jivanji Maharaj went from near Vadsar to an ochhav (festive gathering) at Samiyala, he took Gopaldas Haribhai from Dhanyavi along with him. Haribhai was so overcome with longing for the darshan of the Guru that, while walking along the road, he began reciting a couplet, saying:

_Kabir nadiya jal koyla bhai, samudra laagi aag ||_
_Machhi ja tarvar chadhi, uth Kabira jaag ||1||_
("Kabir says: the water of the rivers has turned to charcoal, and fire has broken out in the ocean; the fish has climbed up into a tree — arise, O Kabir, awake!" — "The river of my hope and craving has burned to ashes, and a fire has broken out in the ocean of my worldly desire. So the fish of my own mind, to escape the fire of illusion (maya), taking refuge in me, has climbed up onto the tree that is the guru who can ferry me across the ocean of birth and death. That is to say, I have become frantic to meet the Guru.")

Seeing Haribhai in such a state, the merciful Lord Jivanji Maharaj at once spoke this couplet:

_Kabir muj virahankun piu muyu, dagh diyo nav jaay ||_
_Maans gali gali bhuy pade, aur kanak rahi galelaay ||2||_
("Just as a widow, scorched by the unbearable fire of separation from her husband, has her flesh fall away in charred lumps upon the ground, and yet lives on by the barest support of the little that clings on like a fleck of gold — such was my own anguish too, for meeting a lover like you.")

So Jivanji Maharaj, granting this loving Haridas the garland and the tilak, took him into his refuge.

There are, in this way, four Gopaldas: Nana Gopaldas of Chanderiya, Mota Gopaldas of Khediya, Sant Gopaldas of Shahpura, and Guru Gopaldas (according to the Samagam). Of these, Mota Gopaldas of Khediya arranged the darshan of Jivanji Maharaj for the Gopaldas of Chanderiya. Nana Gopaldas had been eager for a guru, and had told Mota Gopaldas of Khediya, "If any saint should come, do arrange a meeting for me." So Mota Gopaldas brought that Nana Gopaldas of Chanderiya along to have darshan of Jivanji Maharaj. This Nana Gopaldas was extremely inquisitive, and having had darshan of Jivanji Maharaj he was deeply moved, and in a couplet of offering he says:

_Chanderie vaase vasu, Jivan pragate aay_
_Sitapati Raghunathko, dino naam bataay_
("I dwell residing in Chanderiya; there Jivanji Maharaj appeared and came, and he gave and showed me the name of Raghunath, the Lord of Sita.")

This inquisitive devotee used to have many discussions with Jivanji Maharaj, and Haridas of Nadiad wrote down those discussions, along with the couplets that Jivanji Maharaj must have spoken, in the book of the Samagam. Thus this Haridas of Nadiad has done our community a very great service. Had he not written anything at all, we would have been left deprived of the Guru's own words.

sections.title_en: Aritha - The Field of Val Papadi (Flat Beans)
sections.translation: It is said that once Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj came to the home of the devotee Shri Haridas of Nadiad, in a village named Aritha. At that time the summer season was in progress. In the height of summer all the farmers' crops had dried up. At that time Jivanji Maharaj made the devotee Vaishnav Haridasji's field of val papadi (flat beans) turn green and showed it so. This brought great joy to all the devotees. Even today this field lies at the edge of the village.

Bhoja Gurjarno Uddhar

_dvapare atha yuge prapte, bhojo pretatvam apsyati ||_
_lilaganena krishnasya, pretamuktir bhavishyati ||1||_
(When the Dvapar age arrives, Bhojo will attain the state of a ghost (pret); and through the singing — kirtan — of Krishna's leela, he will be freed from that ghost-state.)

In Vraj bhoomi there lived an Ahir (cowherd) named Bhoj Gurjar, who had a daughter named Dhanbai. Once, while going to Mathura to sell curd, as the child Krishna was looting the curd, she kept saying no, no — yet he embraced her and kissed her. In this pulling and tugging her garment tore, and a tooth-mark was left on her lower lip. Seeing this, Bhoj Gurjar perceived a fault in it; therefore Shri Krishna, seeing that Bhoj Gurjar had found this fault, cursed him to go into pretyoni (ghost-existence). Having attained the ghost-state in the Dvapar age, Bhoja's ghost entered the body of Rambai, wife of the goldsmith Keshavdas Zadeshwariya of Mangaleshwar. To free this Bhoja from the ghost-existence, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj — the very form of Shri Krishna — came to Mangaleshwar together with a company of saints on the 2nd day of the bright fortnight of Magsar, Samvat 1716. The account of this event, as a noteworthy record taken down by a Ram Sanehi saint, appears on a page of handwritten manuscript no. 98, and it reads as follows.

In the Dvapar age, Krishna's avatar took place in Gokul; in that, all are devotees (bhakt). Vaishnav Jivandasji too belongs to that same leela (divine play). In the year Samvat 1716, on the 2nd day of the bright fortnight of Magsar, Vaishnav Jivandasji came to the village of Mangaleshwar on the bank of the Narmada; on the way he recited this couplet (sakhi):

_dasho dish bandhu jivana | deu raghupatiki aan ||_
_vaat ghaat raksha kare | chhodve chare khaan ||2||_
(Jivana binds the ten directions, swearing by the name of Raghupati [Ram]; he guards the pathways and river-crossings, and frees [beings] from the four wombs of birth.)

Returning, he came to the village of Mangaleshwar and for many days gave joy to the Vaishnavs. On the 2nd day of the bright fortnight of Jeth, Samvat 1716, Bhoja Gurjar came before Vaishnav Jivandasji and made his plea (a petition) there. He tells of the leela that took place at the time of Krishna's avatar in the Dvapar age. Vaishnav Jivandasji, in the form of a devotee, had been present in Gokul at the time of the raas-leela — it is that event that Bhoja Gurjar describes. Bhoja Gurjar's daughter, named Dhanbai, was at one time attending upon Vaishnav Jivandasji in service; seeing this, her father Bhoja Gurjar took it amiss, and an evil eye/suspicion arose in him. Therefore Krishna cursed Bhoja Gurjar, saying his after-death state would be wretched. Thereafter, when his life ended — that is, when he died — Bhoja Gurjar's wretched state (avagati) came upon him. Afflicted by the suffering of that wretched state, Bhoja Gurjar pleaded with Shri Krishna: "O Maharaj! Why such a thing? I am indeed your servant." Then Shri Krishna said: "You saw fault in My own devotee — that is why this state has befallen you." Then Bhoja Gurjar pleaded for grace. Vaishnav Jivandasji asked him to prove his identity, saying, "How can this be believed?" Then Bhoja Gurjar told of the matter of Brahma — that Brahma had once come to receive prasad but had not received it. He further told another private matter, of the circle of childhood cowherd-friends, saying he would name the cowherds: Arjan, Bhoj, Vishal, Sajal, Gang — and he told their private affairs as well. "Among these, I am Bhoja Gurjar — that is my name" — this is the leela of Gokul that he related. Hearing this, Vaishnav Jivandasji was pleased. He then asked Bhoja whether he would take prasad. Bhoja Gurjar said, "Yes, Maharaj, I will take prasad." Then Vaishnav Jivandasji gave the order that prasad be given to Bhoja. At this time,

Raghukahanji's mother, Bahenjibai, sang a kirtan composed by Narsinh Mehtaji, which has been recorded as follows.
Raag Kolero (Kedaro)

_mathurama mahi vechavane gayan tan, kahanaji'e palav zalyo re ||_
_ma ma karatan alingan didhun, chumban lidhun banh vali re || tek ||_
_aa joni adhar dank lagyo, aa su kidhun anyai re ||_
_bhoja gujar tani re hun beti, marun naam dhanai re ||1||_
_ughadi jaat ahir hamari, bol kuhuna nav sankhu re ||_
_patine gamtan vaar na laage, laaj tamari rakhu re ||2||_
_dahiyan mahiyan vechine jivun, dithade maarag jaau re ||_
_bese kar te kansne aapu, javaab kaho ne na deu re ||3||_
_mara kulmaan kaaval nahotun, mari ratansi dehahi vansai re ||_
_narasaiya chaa swaamini sange ramtaan, sansaar vaat jaanavi re ||4||_
(We had gone to Mathura to sell curd; on the way, Shri Krishna caught hold of the end of my sari-hem. I said no, no, and still he embraced me, held me tight in his arms, and kissed me. But from this a tooth-mark was left on my lower lip — ah, what an improper thing you have done! I am the daughter of Bhoja Gurjar; my name is Dhanbai. We of the cowherd caste are of such a shameless, brazen nature that we heed no one's disgrace; I never tolerate anyone's ill jest or ill word. Though it takes no time to become displeasing to one's husband, still I guard your honor. I walk only my own familiar path, and I make my living selling curd and butter; whatever toll falls due I pay to Kansa, and to no one besides him do I give anything. There was not the least stain of misconduct in my family, but in this way you have defiled my pure body. In sporting with Shri Krishna, whom Narsinh Mehta worships, this matter of mine has become known to the whole world.)

Then Vaishnav Jivandasji said: "Are you that Bhoja? And is this Dhanbai?" Bhoja Gurjar replied: "Yes, Maharaj, I am that Bhoja, and this is Dhanbai." Then Vaishnavji accepted the matter as true. Vaishnav Jivandasji then said: "Bhoja, what fault has Dhanbai committed?" He then asked Bhoja: "Which prasad will you take?" Bhoja Gurjar answered: "O Maharaj! In the way we used to play the chhakleeli (curd-sport) in Gokul, give me the prasad of curd in that same manner." Then Vaishnav Jivandasji told Harmabai to bring the gauras (curds). Harmaba brought the curds. At that time Gopaldas told Naranadas and Vasantdas to fetch a padiyo (leaf-cup). As Vasantdas rose to fetch the leaf-cup, Vaishnav Jivandasji asked: "O Bhoja! In what will you take the prasad?" Bhoja Gurjar said: "O Maharaj! In the way we used to take it there in Gokul, I will take it cupped in the hollow of my palm." So Vasantdas, who was going to fetch the leaf-cup, turned back. Then the curd prasad was given to Bhoja, and Bhoja received it in his palm. After that Bhoja Gurjar said, "Now I am satisfied." Bhoja Gurjar then asked leave to depart, pleading: "O Maharaj! Remove all my faults." Vaishnav Jivandasji then said: "O Bhoja, whatever faults you have had, past and present, up to this day — the Gracious Lord (Kripanath) has removed them all." Bhoja Gurjar then bowed in reverence, and as soon as he bowed, Bhoja Gurjar's deliverance (uddhar) took place, and he reached the presence of Kripanath. This account has become known from a handwritten manuscript, written by the Ram Sanehi sadhu Bilasi Ram — disciple of Guru Duleramji — on Chaitra Vad 10, Vikram Samvat 1872, and obtained from Vaishnav Dasalad Prabhu Mangalji.

Bhoja Gurjar, cupping his palms as a leaf-bowl, expressed the wish to drink in the very manner he had once drunk curd-milk among the company of cowherds in Vrindavan. Having lived a span as long as five thousand years, from the Dvapar age down to this day in Kaliyug, his deliverance came about; regarding this, the devotee Dayaldas has written a pad (hymn):

_bhoja gujarne odhaariyo, mangaleshwar mozhaar |_
_paanch sahasra varsha rahyo pret jonaman, paayo dukh apaar ||_
(Bhoja Gurjar was delivered, in the midst of Mangaleshwar; he remained five thousand years in the ghost-existence, and endured boundless suffering.)

To deliver Bhoja Gurjar, who had endured the ghost-existence for five thousand years, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj had to come — because when Shri Krishna cursed him, he had said: "The very one whose faults you have seen — that same one shall deliver you."

Among Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj's most exalted devotees, in the women's line, were Bhagat Raghubhai of Kandari and Bahenjibai, mother of Kahandas. The pad composed by Narsinh Mehta relating to Bhoja Gurjar — "We had gone to Mathura to sell curd" — this she sang. Now, Narsinh Mehta lived before Jivanji Maharaj's time, so the doubt may arise that this pad could not be Narsinh Mehta's own; but Narsinh Mehta also composed a pad relating to Jivanji Maharaj, one that mentions Dhanbai by name, in his own collected Harmala (garland of hymns) — there is another such pad. This pad appears, in this form, in Bhagat Bapu Vrindavan Patrawala's book no. 1, page 48, and in Bhagat Ranchhod Haribhai Vayada Polwala's book, page 240.

_vahalo gokulman raheto, tahan navneet chori leto ||_
_gurjari dhanai gher jaato, tahan taadho toomro khaato ||1||_
_dhanai baandhati gaanthe taani, tahan mukaavta saarangpaani ||_
_tamo te vela sambhalo, ehavun jaanine ugaaro ||2||_
_maaho maahe motaai na aano, mune potaano kari jaano ||_
_maahari pat jaataan taahaari jaase, tyaare vaikunthaman nahin rahevaas ||3||_
_am sanghaate vaad na kije, mune haar taantano dije ||_
_lok varvaan bole maaharaan, dhaank maaharaan udhaadis taaharaan ||4||_
_hala maahara roode taaharun roodun, maahare bhoonde taaharun bhoondun ||_
_naagar batka bola kahiye, tun to kaain na aane haiye ||5||_
_ha tun kohona roodeman betho, valti maahaari mite nahin ditho ||_
_tune vrukhabhaan suta rahi raakhi, tene aanandthi joto zhaankhi, ehavi ved vade chhe saakhi ||6||_
_shukdev naarde chhupaayo, parikshitne shravane samaao ||_
_pretne mukti to param vallabh, hetuna jiv te hetu trute ||7||_
_taare narasaiyo rise bharaay, muj vina jash kon gaay ||_
_taahara varvaan pooraan na thaae, pad ek narasaiyo gaay ||8||_
(The Beloved of the people of Braj, Shri Krishna, when he dwelt in Vraj, used to steal butter there. He would go always to the house of Dhanbai, the Gurjar cowherd-woman, and eat there the cold, coarse millet-porridge she offered. When Dhanbai bound it up and tied it away in her provision-bundle, the Lord would break it free from her by force — so remember that leela of that time, and knowing that you were once such a one, deliver us from illusion (maya). Do not, between us, keep any difference or discrimination; make me truly your own — your maidservant, your servant. If my honor is lost, your own honor will be lost too; then in Vaikunth you will grow restless to save me, and you will come running from there to my rescue, unable to remain at rest in Vaikunth. So rather than that, you ought not to bandy words or delay with us; give me some slight help, like a slender thread's worth, for people speak ill of me. If you do not protect my honor, I will not sing your praises, but will instead make your weakness known... Ah, in my well-being is your own well-being; in my misfortune, your honor too will be lost. A person as plain-speaking as I will surely say that in your heart you hold no true feeling for us. Ah — in whose heart have you settled, that even my keen eye has failed to catch sight of you again? Surely Vrishabhanu's daughter Radha keeps you bound in some illicit relation, and you too, they say — those who know the Vedas — secretly watch her with sweet, loving glances. Such leela of yours with Radha, Shukdev and Narad kept concealed, and told Parikshit other things instead. For a ghost (pret), to hear even harsh things said, if it brings about deliverance, is welcomed gladly — for such deliverance is most dear to it. Self-interested souls become content the moment their own purpose is served. That is why, whenever such concealment happens, Narsinh Mehta grows displeased with you. Yet without me, who will sing your praise and glory? Your faults cannot fully be told, but this Narsinh sings this one hymn of yours.)

In this pad, the ghost-turned character of the Bhagavat, Gokarna, had only the self-interest that his own deliverance would come about through hearing the Bhagavat recited. But the ghost-turned Bhoja has the aspiration of being freed from the ghost-existence and reaching the abode of Kripanath.

That Narsinh Mehta composed this poem with reference to Dhanbai proves that Narsinh Mehta had full knowledge of such matters of Krishna's leela. Furthermore, in the 94th pad of the Harmala too, there is mention of Dhanbai.

Raag – Prabhati

_mahare mandalik su padi chhe hod re, mune tahara charan joyana kod re |_
_mune bhav bandhanthi chhod re, tamo zakh maarso mune haar aapso || tek ||_
_mune tamo vecho tahan vechau re, kaache taantane bandhai jaau re |_
_hun govindana gun gaau re ... ... ... ... ||1||_
_tune gurjar dhanai bandhati ghaado tani re, taare hun mukaavto saarangpani re |_
_men to pothanmata tahaari jaani re, tento maahari poorav preet na jaani re ||2||_
_lok varvan bole chhe maharan re, dhaankya maharan ke ughades tahaaran re |_
_tahaaran manda haju nathi hariyaan re, ... ... ... ... ||3||_
_tune vrushabhaan suta rahi chhe raakhi re, te to maahara manman rahyo chhun saankhi re |_
_men karuna tahari bhaakhi re, ... ... ... ... ||4||_
_amo naagar batak bola kahiye, kahyaan kathan na aaniye haiye re |_
_tam vina sharane amo kohone rahiye re, ... ... ... ||5||_
_tahaaro narasaiyo rose bharaay re, muj vina jas tahara kon gaay re |_
_tun van vaahare maahaari kon dhaay re, ... ... ... ... ||6||_
(I have made a wager for victory or defeat with King Mandalik; I long only to behold your feet. Free me from the bondage of worldly existence, and — even reluctantly, only when there is no other way — come to that place and grant me victory. If you were to sell me, I would let myself be sold — whatever wretched state you put me in, I would accept it, and rather than act willfully toward you, I shall remain faithful to you; and I shall sing the praises of the Lord. The Gurjar woman Dhanai used to hold you bound by force; then I would free you from her. I knew of your calamity, but you did not value my

[continued from the previous page] loving devotion from my previous birth. People speak ill of me, so if you do not guard my honor, I will make these doings of yours public. For your heart is still not softened — has not yet become compassionate. That Vrishabhanu's daughter Radha keeps an illicit bond with you — this I am enduring within my own heart. Such is the grace [I have described] of yours. We Nagars are reckoned truly plain-spoken people, and whatever we happen to say, good or ill, we give no thought to it. Without you, at whose feet shall we take refuge? Therefore your devotee Narsinh Mehta has become angry. He says: without me, who will sing your praises? Without you, who else will come to my aid?)

Thus, the pad "We had gone to Mathura to sell curd," sung by Narsinh Mehta, was sung by Narsinh Mehta even before Jivanji Maharaj's own arrival, in anticipation of Jivanji Maharaj's manifestation itself. Thus Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj had appeared in order to deliver Bhoja Gurjar.

Krishna Darshan

Shyamdasji, who set down in words the life-story of Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj, has described many aspects of his life. He has given a beautiful account of just such an incident. Once, among Jivanji Maharaj's own devotees (nij jan), there was an exceedingly pure, love-drenched, singularly devoted, unique woman devotee, all on her own; a certain thought kept coming to her mind again and again. Many thoughts about her own Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj kept arising in this very innocent (bhali) woman devotee's mind. Having found so great a philosopher-sage, so singular a Sadguru, this woman devotee had become deeply moved. Moreover, seeing so beautiful a social order and arrangement, thoughts would arise in this sister's mind: who could such a great saintly person really be? Who could this Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj really be, who has spread so beautiful and so lofty a stream of thought throughout Gujarat? On this question, many thoughts kept arising. Once, sinking deep into such thoughts, this innocent woman devotee entered a state of loving trance (bhaav samadhi) and had a beautiful vision. Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj told her in that dream: "O innocent sister! When I lie down to sleep, come then to see me."

As soon as she had this beautiful experience, this innocent woman awoke from her loving trance, and at once went to the room where Jivanji Maharaj lay sleeping. She lifted the cloth covering that lay over the face and head of the sleeping Jivanji Maharaj to look, and was struck with wonder. She beheld the form of the Complete Brahman (Purna Brahman) — the Supreme Being, wearing a peacock crown and yellow silk garments (pitambar). Beholding the flute-bearing Lord, radiant as a crore of suns, this sister began to feel most blessed. She fixed this form firmly in her heart, and all her doubts and misgivings were dispelled, and she began to worship with ever-increasing love and devotion.

sections.title_en: He Gave the Vaishnavs Water to Drink
sections.translation:
