_Kunvarbai jab kahi nishani, kyari manse tum paayo paani_ (Kunvarbai then gave the sign, saying: "You gave water within the furrow-bed.") (from Gnan Mahima)

Once there was a festival (ochhav) in another village (Ori Gaudi - Kasampur). Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj was travelling in a bullock-cart together with the child-devotees (bal gopal), singing bhajans and kirtans along the way. On the road the sants and children became extremely thirsty, and the small children began to cry loudly. Then one sant ran ahead and had all the carts (the covered bullock-carts, damaniyan velo) halted. Seeing some shade, everyone stopped there and gathered together. Jivanji Maharaj welcomed them lovingly. Then Kunvarbai said, "Antaryami (indwelling knower of every heart) Sadguru, listen: everyone is very thirsty, water is not to be found anywhere, so please find some way." Jivanji Maharaj got down from the cart. Kunvarbai then said, "When you took the Krishna-avatar and were sporting as a cowherd grazing cattle on Govardhan hill, the gopis and cowherds had all gathered there, and at that time they had become extremely thirsty. Then you lifted up a clod of earth (dhekun) and gave everyone water to drink. Since you are capable of such things, give us water to drink now too, by whatever means." Then, going to a low-lying spot where the ground had dried and cracked open, Jivanji Maharaj lifted up a mound of earth; at once water welled up and filled the place. He told everyone to quickly drink water from that pit. Everyone first gave Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj water to drink, then they drank themselves, and everyone also filled their own vessels with water. Then Jivanji Maharaj covered the mound back over, and the ground became as dry as it had been before. All the sants bowed at Jivanji Maharaj's feet. Then they reached the village of Ori.

From the village all the sants came out to meet him, playing the kansi, taal and mridang (cymbals and drum), and bowed in prostration before Jivanji Maharaj. Then, just as when Ramchandra, having brought Sitaji back from Lanka, returned to Ayodhya, and Bharatji together with the people of Ayodhya went out with music and celebration to welcome Ram, Lakshman, Bharat and Hanuman, Bhandas composed a hymn (pad) describing that occasion.

Singing that very hymn, they brought Jivanji Maharaj into the village with music and festivity, ceremonially welcoming him (padharamani). We still sing that hymn today on the occasion of a guru's ceremonial arrival. This hymn was probably being sung even in Jivanji Maharaj's own lifetime, because it is mentioned in the parcharee (the traditional account of his life and wonders) of Jivanji Maharaj, and that proves it. So this hymn has been in use in our community since ancient times, and its importance is all the greater for that reason.

_Aavu rudu ne rasalu re, aavya ayodhyaman ramji re || Praja te lei bharat parharya re, harina vadan nihalu re || Aavya ||_ (How lovely and delightful — Ramji has come to Ayodhya! Taking the people with him, Bharat went out to receive him, saying, "Let me behold the Lord's face." — He has come.)

In our community, the greatest special quality compared to other communities is that on every occasion our devotees send for their guru and welcome him ceremonially with due honor. This is not seen anywhere in any community but our own; rarely, only once in a while, do people elsewhere send for their guru, whereas we always send for the guru first, welcome him ceremonially, and only then begin to celebrate any occasion at all. Moreover, the meal-offering (bhojan prasad) too is served in the row of diners (pangat) only after the guru has offered the rosary (mala) to it, in a disciplined manner; and while it is being served, everyone together calls out "Aad," and only when Jivanji Maharaj's jai (victory-cry) is raised does everyone eat the meal-prasad, saying "Ramkabir." Such a disciplined practice is not found anywhere else. In this way Jivanji Maharaj has made our community fully virtuous and disciplined in every respect.

Offering the rosary to the food before it is eaten is also our distinctive practice, and even at ordinary festivals, the meal-prasad is given only after a tulsi leaf has been offered near the devotee of the household shrine (parthara). Another feature that is astonishing about our community is this: on any occasion — whether we gather for bhajan-kirtan and bhakti at Ram-Janma or Krishna-Janma or any other festival, where devotional hymns being sung is only natural — even at a wedding, a death, a farewell occasion (aana-tanaa), a house-warming, or any other kind of occasion, we sing nothing but devotional bhajan-kirtans. So for us a wedding is not merely a wedding but an occasion for bhajan-kirtan, and we treat every such occasion purely as an occasion for bhajan. Hence even at our weddings, wedding songs are sung, but among them nothing but devotional songs to Ram or Krishna are sung, never other wedding ditties or ordinary wedding songs. This is why it is no failing at all that the devotee community records its surname as "Bhagat" (devotee). We truly are practicers of devotion, so it is not out of place that our surname should be Bhagat; we are not devotees in name only but true practicers of devotion, and so we fully deserve, in the truest sense, the surname of Bhagat. The sad thing is that when our community sees other, worldly communities and, drawn toward them, imitates their ways, that tarnishes our worthiness. We have never considered even the occasion of death inauspicious; so although it is a sorrowful occasion, we do not create an atmosphere heavy with excessive grief, but only do bhajan-kirtan. Just as we make a sukhadi meal-offering at birth and at the thread-initiation (kanthi diksha), so too at a death we distribute sukhadi as prasad. This is because we say that death is not death but hari-sharan, having taken refuge in the Lord. Furthermore, even in everyday speech we use these cultural terms: jal instead of paani (water), prasad instead of khavu (eating), hari-sharan instead of maran (death), and so on. In no community but ours is it ever possible to sing devotional wedding-songs at a wedding, whereas for us it is never possible to sing anything at a wedding but devotional songs. So if someone in another community were to sing our wedding song, which is a devotional hymn, at their wedding the way we do, it would not seem fitting to that community, and they would feel in their minds, "We have gathered for a wedding now, we have not come for a bhajan program." But when we sing these very hymns on a wedding occasion, no such hesitation whatsoever arises in anyone's mind. That is precisely why, though we are devotees, we are truly exceptional, unparalleled Vaishnavs.

A true Vaishnav is not a hypocrite or a fraud, so we do not put on false show. Jivanji Maharaj never expressed any sense of pride in being a guru. He was the founder of the Uda path (the true devotees' path) and the giver of true devotion, so he never engaged in outward pomp or showy display. Yet today we have fallen into the error of hypocrisy and false conduct. People may well have bowed at Jivanji Maharaj's feet, but it is never written or heard anywhere that anyone, at any place, washed his feet and took that foot-water (charanamrut) with special honor. This excess of outward show is shameful. Moreover, cloth is considered valuable, and yet to spread it in dusty roads and lanes in order to welcome the guru with special honor is entirely improper. To welcome the guru ceremonially while playing kansi, taal and mridang and singing kirtan is fitting, but to hold up an umbrella and spread out cloths even when there is no sun is a false display and is laughable. Looking through the Illustrated Life-Episodes of Jivanji Maharaj, Part 3, it is clear that compassionate Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj showered nothing but grace for the love and devotion of his devotees. On the way to Ori village, Kasampur, past Ganpatpura, between there and Kurali, there is a small pond, which still exists today. There, we too have often given water to thirsty bullocks. So it must have been right at this very pond that Sadguru Jivanji gave water to these thirsty child-gopal-sants. And so this pond, even today, is a place that recalls Jivanji Maharaj to memory.

_Mala doshi Jivana, khai anadevki jutha || Jiv jatan bohotek kare, pan swami dini pootha ||1||_ (O Jivan, guilty of neglecting the mala — you ate the leftover food offered to Anadev, a folk deity. However much the soul may strive and take care of itself, still the Master has turned His back on it. ||1||)

Instead of offering the tulsi rosary (mala), one who disregards it and eats such leavings offered to a folk deity (jutho, food already offered and left over, considered polluted) — even if such a person is ready to eat that leftover food most lovingly and carefully — God does not show love or grace toward him, and turns His love away from him.

The very first disciples to accept Jivanji Maharaj as their guru were the devotees of Malwa. They did not adopt Jivanji Maharaj without thinking it through; rather, they asked Jivanji Maharaj to clear up the doubts and misgivings arising in their own minds. Among these doubts was one: whether God actually partakes of the food when devotees offer the rosary to it — they had asked Jivanji Maharaj to clarify this. These devotees wrote down, in hand-copied manuscripts, the bhajans and kirtans concerning the love and devotion they had received from Jivanji Maharaj. Some of those manuscripts have come to be seen by us. In one of them, Malwa manuscript no. 220, on the back of page 254, the above sakhi is written. On the back of page 146 of this same manuscript there is a passage, given below, about whether God partakes of the food when the rosary is offered. Along with it there is also a clarification of whether Khojiji's guru had indeed departed for his heavenly abode. It reads as follows: Khojiji asked his guru, "How will we know that you have gone to the supreme abode?" The guru replied, "Tie a bell; when it rings, know that I have reached the supreme abode." The guru then passed away, but the bell did not ring. Khojiji grew doubtful, thinking some unfulfilled desire must have remained with the guru, and that he had therefore not attained liberation. He pondered a great deal; finally, near the place where the last rites had been performed, his eye fell on a ripe mango on a mango tree. A doubt arose in his mind; he cut the mango open, and a worm fell out from inside it and died — and at that very instant the bell rang.

_Pharasa vani sarasa, sakal shiromani shyam dhani || Soch vichar kahat haridasi, khojo kahetan vaat ghani ||2||_ (Meaning: Farsuram says — understanding and reflecting that Shyam Krishna is the greatest and most excellent master of all, the devotee who serves the Lord in devotion says, "Search and see whether what I have said is correct — you will find that what I have said is indeed exactly true.")

A Vaishnav asked Jivandasji, "O Maharaj! How are we to know that God accepts the prasad?" Jivanji replied, "When the time comes, I will tell you." Later, on a certain occasion, all the Vaishnavs brought their meal-plates and all the plates were gathered together, except that one Vaishnav's plate was kept apart, because that plate had been prepared with money earned by improper, worldly means. When the rosary was placed upon that plate, a bead of the rosary broke; then all the devotees understood that God does indeed accept the devotees' prasad.

_Saat paanch sangi male, surabhi lei uthaye | Jivan man atakyo shamsu, nek naan it ut jaye ||1||_ (Meaning: Jivanji Maharaj says — just as five or seven people together lift up a weak cow that has sunk into mud and mire, five or seven sant-like devotees, like Harijans, in this same way rescued me from eating such polluted leftover food offered to Anadev. And so now my mind has become firmly fixed on accepting only devotion to Lord Krishna, and only the meal-prasad offered to Him; without devotion to Him, my mind will not waver even the slightest bit toward devotion to anyone else.)

From this passage in the Malwa hand-copied manuscript, we see that the Malwa devotees had two questions clarified by Jivanji Maharaj. One was this: Khojiji's guru, at the time of his death, had tied a bell and said, "If that bell rings, know that I have attained liberation." But Khojiji was not present when the guru passed away, and the bell had not rung. So Khojiji went and lay down at the very spot where the guru had lain at his last moment, and there he noticed a ripe mango. He cut it open, and a worm came out of it and vanished, and at that very instant the bell rang. In this way he sought out and found his guru's fate, and so he came to be known by the name Khojiji [the seeker/finder]. He also had his own disciple Gnaniji go in search of a sadguru like Kabirji, and for this reason too he was called Khojiji. So, after this clarification about Khojiji, the second question was asked: when we offer the rosary to Thakorji, is there proof that He actually accepts that food as prasad? Jivanji Maharaj said, "I will give you that proof." So, on one occasion, all the devotees, following the custom of our community, brought meal-prasad from their own homes, and when they came, all the plates were gathered together and the rosary was offered over them, but one plate was kept separate. When the rosary was offered upon that one, a bead of the rosary broke, and so everyone became certain that Thakorji does accept the prasad.

Then, by way of a sakhi, he explains that one whose mind is truly and sincerely devoted to God's bhakti comes to understand for himself whether meal-prasad is pure or impure. Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, answering this, said that this plate had not been prepared from the fruit of one's own honest labor, but had been made with someone else's money, and that is why God did not accept that plate.

In this way, the beads of Jivanji Maharaj's rosary that broke [in this manner] have been kept, together with his original rosary, preserved separately in a small bottle. And besides these, whenever other beads of this rosary broke in the same way — offered upon impure meal-prasad — during the time of any of the Maharajs who came after him, all those broken beads too have been collected and kept in this same bottle. Now, out of fear that, because of today's corruption, all the beads of this rosary would break, the revered Yadunath placed this original rosary on the gadi (seat) for worship, and began using a different rosary instead. Therefore we no longer offer this original rosary over the meal-prasad. But we sincerely pray to Jivanji Maharaj, with true hearts, that he may once again make our community one of pure conduct and thought, so that we may become fortunate enough to partake of prasad offered with his original rosary.

I too had a deep longing to eat meal-prasad offered with this rosary, and, observing very strict purity, I took the supreme good fortune of eating meal-prasad offered with this rosary for just 15 days. But then, fearing that some fault might inadvertently occur, I placed the rosary back in worship again. Still, I hope that Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj will make every one of the child-devotees of his Uda-devotee community worthy of receiving, even once, the excellent good fortune of eating meal-prasad offered with this very rosary.

sections.title_en: Grace Shown to the Jambu Tree
sections.translation:
Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj, together with his own devoted household devotees, set out for Dwarka on Bhadarva Sud 11 (the eleventh day of the bright half of the month of Bhadarva) in Vikram Samvat 1726. At this time his second son, Shyamdasji, made an earnest, insistent request: "Take me along with you, to serve you." Yielding to his insistence, Jivanji Maharaj took Shyamdasji along too. This company of sants proceeded onward on the road to Dwarka; on the way, in the village named Patdi in what is now Surendranagar district, this company halted for the night. Everyone had gone to sleep. Shyamdasji, in order to serve, was pressing Jivanji Maharaj's feet. As the night passed and morning came, everyone rose and got ready. On this desolate, wilderness spot stood the trunk of a dried-up jambu (black-plum) tree. Describing this episode in poetic form, Shyamdas says:

_Bohotek dinko gayo sukaai, chhal ukhari pari hai tahi. Take dhig jab thade rahe, sunmukh dekhi vachan tab kahai. Hamahi Dwarika jaay aru aavahi, nav pallav hoy rahiyo bhai. Aiso vachan kahi aap padhare, je Shrishyam doo sang sidhare._ (Meaning: It had been dried up for many days; its bark too had peeled off and fallen away. Going up to this utterly withered tree, [Jivanji Maharaj] spoke to it lovingly: "We are going to Dwarka; when we return, O brother, may you have become green again, full of fresh new shoots.")

In this way, having given his blessing to a tree, he set out toward Dwarka. He stayed at Dwarka for many days and visited numerous sites, including the original site of Dwarka, which has sunk into the sea. Jivanji Maharaj was, in fact, originally a native of this very region; he has said in a doha:

_Kathiyavad kutumb bhayo, Mathura hamaro desh. Santo tane melavade, aavyo gurjar desh ||1||_ (Meaning: We are, at root, from Mathura, descendants of the Yadav lineage, and our family came to live in Kathiyawad. But now, for the sake of meeting with sants and for the welfare of all, I have come to the land of Gujarat.)

In this way, seeing his own original homeland, he felt immense joy. Describing the various sites he visited in Dwarka, the original editor of Samagam, Shri Haridas Nadiyada, writes that he had darshan of the following places: 1) Swarga Dwar (Gate of Heaven), 2) Kabirji's platform, 3) Mirabai's platform, 4) went to Rohidas's platform, 5) went to Pipaji's temple, 6) Ramanandji's cave, 7) Krupanath's in-laws' home, 8) Sevantri stepwell, 9) Damodarkund, 10) Kel-Kailas — Kukalashkund.

Thus, going about to these various sites and having their darshan, he spoke of their glory. In this way the pilgrimage to Dwarka was made. There, a certain devotee of God, a Thakor named Gangaram, hosted him, and he stayed at his house. In front of that house there was a well, and water from it was used for cooking. Having stayed here for nine days in this way, on returning he told his own devotees that this is a holy land. "One should come here bringing five or ten Vaishnavs along, and take the benefit of hari-kirtan and satsang (holy gathering)." And he said further that it would be very good if, at this place where he had stayed for so many days, a permanent tulsi-plant bed were built.

Today we have no information about the original hometown of Thakor Gangaram — only his name has come down to us.

At the outskirts of Patdi-Bajanu village, Jivandasji lay down to rest at night. Shyamdasji was in attendance, serving his feet. The other sants and devotees had also gone to sleep. At midnight, Jivanji Maharaj instructed Shyamdasji, who was serving his feet, that it had grown very late, midnight was near, and so he should go to sleep. Shyamdasji went to sleep. At this time Jivanji Maharaj lay in a state of loving trance (bhava samadhi); Krupanath himself had come in person to attend to him.

Jivandasji welcomed him with great honor, and then asked: "O Krupanath! What fruit will you give to those who come to us? The crippled, the lame, the disabled, the blind, the old, the young, children — all kinds of people come. What fruit will you give to one who comes to us with true devotion?"

Krupanath said to Jivandasji: "O Jivandas! Hear my word. If one comes here holding one-pointed attention, he will not have to wander through the eighty-four lakh species (the cycle of 8.4 million forms of birth). But so that he may complete his bonds of karma, I will grant one human birth to whoever holds loving devotion (prem-bhakti) toward me. This is my promise."

_Tab bole Ranchhod pyare, Jivandas suno vachan hamare. Ek chitvrutt dhari aave yahi, ek ber chorasi nahi. Dehu mankha tan avatara, je kou rakhat bhav hamara. Puni jeti sant sangahi kare, mero dhyan sada ur dhare._ (Meaning: Then the beloved Ranchhod spoke: "Jivandas, listen to my words. Whoever comes here holding one-pointed attention need not go even once through the eighty-four lakh births. I shall grant a human birth to whoever holds love for me — and further to whoever keeps the company of sants and holds my remembrance always in his heart.")

In this way the Lord gave his fearless promise. If, in that human body received a second time, the soul becomes alert and fixes its attention on the company of Krupanath, it will become liberated while living (jivan-mukta). But if it falls into indulgence and pleasure, it will again certainly come under the bondage of karma and go on wandering. This beautiful conversation continued, and many other things were spoken of. Shyamdasji, who was sleeping beside Jivandasji, did not hear any of this conversation. In the morning, on rising, he requested Jivandasji to relate the night's event to everyone in detail.

Hearing this, Jivandasji was filled with great joy and described the whole event in detail. Hearing it, all those present were filled with great joy, and after finishing their morning rituals, they set about preparing, with much joy, for the darshan (sacred viewing) of Krupanath.

After hearing this event, everyone's disposition toward going to Dwarka changed, and the love they already held for their own true guru increased further. An extraordinary joy began to rise in everyone, and with the feeling of "when will we reach Dwarka and meet Krupanath," the fatigue of everyone's journey lifted, and fresh enthusiasm spread through their bodies. Setting out from there, everyone went straight into the presence of Krupanath. There, in the company of Jivandas, they all stayed for many days, engaging in bhakti, kirtan (devotional singing), and satsang (holy company). On returning home, they related this Dwarka event to the other devoted household members (nijjan) who had stayed behind. Hearing of this event, everyone was filled with great joy, and with loving devotion, they all became immersed and drenched in the ocean of supreme bliss.

The devotee Dayaldas wrote in the Sadguru-vandana (hymn of homage to the true guru):

_Kuntalpurne marag jata, vipre dharyo ahankar. Kup girat jeev rakhi lidha, aise sarajanhar._ (Meaning: While going on the road to Kuntalpur, a brahmin held pride [about the well-site he had chosen]. Such is the Creator, who saved the lives of those falling into that well.)

While going on the road to Kuntalpur (Koral-Chorda), on the way at Puniyad, a brahmin who had selected the site for a well and had it dug held the pride that "the site I have chosen is good, so no one will come to any harm." But Jivanji Maharaj did not accept the brahmin's word — he called the laborers out, saying the well was about to collapse, and saved them. Jivanji Maharaj was, in this way, like God himself, directly present.

At one time, true guru Jivandasji set out from Shahpura to go to Chorda, the home place of Guru Gopaldas. On the way, a village named Puniyad came. At the outskirts of the village stood a beautiful neem tree, adding to the beauty of the place. Jivandasji stopped under this tree to rest a little and shed the fatigue of the journey. Nearby, some men were at work digging a well. Jivandasji went up to them and began saying: "Brothers, it is not proper to dig any more earth here now. Come out of the pit."

Some sensible men among them, recognizing this as the word of a sant, stopped digging the earth of the well and began to come out. Some others thought, "Why should we listen just because everyone says such things?" and kept on digging. At this moment, some earth from the ridge above fell into the deep pit of the well, burying the laborers who were working there. All the villagers made a great effort and pulled the laborers out, and tended to the injured; Jivandasji gave them his blessing for their safety and well-being. As this extremely distressing and grave event had occurred, all the residents of the village thought: "This is truly some rare and exceptional sant. By not heeding his word, we caused him distress and hurt him; yet through his compassion we were able to obtain safety." They thought further: "If the calamity that was about to befall the village could be averted merely by the sant's brief arrival and stay, then how much good fortune would come to all of us if he were to stay and reside permanently in this very village." Thinking thus, the leading men of the village asked the sant's name and whereabouts, bowed to him with love, and requested him to make a permanent abode in this village.

Seeing the villagers' great insistence and devotion, Jivandasji, yielding to love, promised them all that he would leave Shahpura and come to reside in Puniyad. Hearing just this, everyone was filled with great joy. Knowing that a sant had come to the village, all the villagers gathered together and became ready to give land for the sant's residence. Jivandasji refused to accept the land free of charge, and instead showed his readiness to pay a fair price for it, build a house on the site, and live there.

Whether willingly or reluctantly, so as not to hurt the sant, everyone agreed with him, and all became ready to act according to the sant's wish. Near the neem tree standing at the outskirts of the village, on the far bank of a nearby pond, there lay a large open stretch of land. From this, he chose a small piece of land according to his own means and built his residence there, making Puniyad his own reserved field of work (karma bhoomi). The house and the large plot of land there today were later purchased, and the house built, by Narsinhdasji Maharaj, who came in his lineage.

Thus this ocean of compassion, Jivanji Maharaj, came and settled in Puniyad. But he also gave his blessing to the neem tree, mentioned earlier, under which he had first rested — because of this, its bitterness went away and it became a sweet neem. Many elderly people of Puniyad have tasted the leaves of this neem tree. At present, that tree has perished.

_Bhagat anin kahayke, pooje grah Ganesh. Vyas kyon na tinke sadan par, jam gan kare pravesh._ (Meaning: One who calls himself an exclusive devotee of the Lord, yet worships the planets and Ganesh — Vyas asks, why then would the messengers of Yama [death] not enter that person's house?)

If someone who calls himself an exclusively devoted devotee of God still worships the planets and Ganpati, then, says the devotee Vyas, why would the messengers of Yama not enter that unsteady person's house?

Vyasdasji says in Pad (hymn) 86 that wicked, demonic forces cannot trouble a true devotee.

_Haridasanke nikat na aavat pret, pitar, jamdoot. Aru jogi, bhogi, sannyasi, pandit, mundit, dhoot. Grah, ganes, sures, siva, siv dar kari bhajat bhoot. Sidhi-nidhi, bidhi-nishedh harinamahi, darat rahat kapoot. Sab hi aas-tras taji Vyasahi, bhavat bhakt aakoot. ||86||_ (Meaning: Ghosts, ancestral spirits, and the messengers of death do not come near the devotees of Hari — nor do yogis, hedonists, sannyasis, pandits, shaven ascetics, or rogues. The planets, Ganesh, Indra, Parvati, Shiva, and even ghosts flee in fear before them. Even the eight and nine siddhis [supernatural powers], and every rule of scriptural injunction and prohibition, remain fearful before the Name of Hari — as does the wicked-hearted person. Vyas says: giving up every hope and fear, the devotee wholly absorbed in the Lord is pleasing to him. ||86||)

Ghosts, ancestral spirits, and messengers of death do not come near the devotee of Hari. Further, the planets, Ganpati, Indra, Parvati, Shiva, and evil spirits flee far away out of fear. The eight major and nine minor siddhis, and things like scriptural rules of what to do and not do, remain fearful before him. Even the desire for pleasure and pain, sin and merit, remains fearful and does not arise. Vyasji says: I am pleased by this disposition of giving up the pain of all such hopes and desires.

There was a brahmin named Dave Krishnadas, originally from the village of Idar. His father was Damodar and his mother was Tejbai. Krishnadas was born in the year Samvat 1700. At the age of eleven, his father passed away. In Samvat 1712, a Muslim king conquered Idar and plundered everyone; because of this the pure population did not remain there, and he went to live with his maternal relatives in the village of Hidovar. He became a great astrologer. He studied the scriptures, the Vedas, the Puranas, the Mahabharata, and so on, and also knew Sanskrit and Prakrit. He became a great physician (vaidya). Everyone called him a great pandit (scholar). He held Ganpati as his chosen deity of worship (ishtadev) and meditated on Ganpati a great deal, sharing all his joys and sorrows with Ganpati. In this way he came to have a direct vision (sakshatkar) of Ganpati.

Once a thought arose in his mind that he should ask Ganpati about devotion to God. So he meditated on Ganpati in his mind, and Ganpati appeared before him and said: "Ask, ask — whatever you ask, I shall give. I will give you a kingdom, or adornments, or the knowledge of supernatural powers (riddhi-siddhi), or elephants, horses, many villages, or sons, wealth, and property — whatever wealth you want, I shall give." Then, folding his hands, Krishnadas said: "Every scripture and every Purana has praised devotion to God. Why do you keep it hidden from me? Riddhi-siddhi only leads to hell — why do you offer that to me? Explain to me devotion to Vishnu, by which the soul attains true well-being and all the sufferings of the ocean of worldly existence (bhavsagar) come to an end."

Ganpati then said: "Even Shivji meditates upon this Vishnu; the Vedas and Puranas praise him. The gods and the great sages also meditate upon him. Yet even ones like Brahma cannot attain this devotion to Vishnu. This teaching of devotion was given by the Lord to the Sanatkumaras through his Hansa (swan) incarnation — devotion by which the fear of coming and going [rebirth] in this world is destroyed. But I can give you only riddhi-siddhi; I do not know this unfathomable devotion to Vishnu. So if you keep the company of a sant, your cycle of coming and going will end. In the Kanam region there is a sant who gives such happiness — you will find him." Saying this, Ganpati vanished from sight.

Krishnadas now developed a desire to take a guru, so he walked on foot to the village of Puniyad in Kanam. At the outskirts of the village, he sat down in the shade of the neem tree. There, the devotee Naranadas, coming out of the village, saw him, and after getting acquainted with him, brought him to his own home. Then, while preparing food for a meal, they began to converse. Krishnadas said: "I worship Ganpati as my chosen deity. It is said in the Vedas and Puranas that there is nothing beyond the three gods (Tridev) — Brahma creates the universe, Vishnu sustains it, and Shiva destroys it. This much I know."

Naranadas then said: "The three gods may seem true to you, but my heart does not accept this. When the Supreme Brahman, the Lord, took incarnation, Brahma stole away the calves to test him, but Shri Krishna created other new ones, and so Brahmaji bowed down before Krishna. That is why Shri Krishna alone seems true to me. Moreover, when Krishna took his incarnation, Shivji went to Gokul to have his darshan. And when Narsinh Mehta said, 'Give me whatever is most dear to you,' Krishna showed him the Ras-mandal (the circle of the divine dance). When Parvatiji took the form of Sita, he rejected her. And further, Lakshmiji herself cannot even enter the land of Vraj." When Naranadas had explained all this, Krishnadas asked him to give him kanthi diksha (initiation with the sacred neck-thread). Naranadas then took him to true guru Jivanji Maharaj, and Jivanji Maharaj gave him kanthi diksha; moreover, he took his own personal mala (rosary) off from around his own neck and gave it to him, and showed him the path of devotion.

When he gave his own mala to Krishnadas, the devotees present there wondered why this mala had been given. Jivanji Maharaj then asked Malibai and Jetibai to explain this, and those women said that this Krishnadas had, in a previous birth at the time of the Krishna incarnation, been a companion (sakha) of Jivanji Maharaj, and having recognized the essence of the Vraj-lila (the divine play at Vraj), he had come here — that is why Jivanji Maharaj had offered him his own mala. Jivanji Maharaj further said that this Krishnadasji would liberate many souls. Hearing this, Krishnadasji said he would not be able to bear so great a burden. Jivanji Maharaj then said that if the guru commands, it will not feel like a burden. Thus Krishnadasji received devotion to Vishnu from Jivanji Maharaj and became the guru of the Kanbi people living in Mehsana district.

To show that worship of Ganpati and other minor deities cannot bring about our liberation, Namdevji says:

_Na taris na taris Ram vina, jap leho jeevda tu Ram nam. (tek) Jaldev poojila to kachla hoyla, bhagati na hoyla Ram vina. (1) Chandi poojila to mrugla hoyla, bhagati na hoyla Ram vina. (2) Devi poojila to bhensa hoyla, bhagati na hoyla Ram vina. (3) Harshad poojila to rudhir hoyla, bhagati na hoyla Ram vina. (4) Kshetrapal poojila to kukra hoyla, bhagati na hoyla Ram vina. (5) Ganesha poojila to musa hoyla, bhagati na hoyla Ram vina. (6) Mahadev poojila to vrushabh hoyla, bhagati na hoyla Ram vina. (7) Suraj poojila to ashva hoyla, bhagati na hoyla Ram vina. (8) Sannyasi poojila to Shivlok jayla, bhagati na hoyla Ram vina. (9) Brahman poojila to sargalok jayla, bhagati na hoyla Ram vina. (10) Bhagat poojila to bhagat hoyla, janam janam Namdev nishan bajayla._ (Meaning: You will not be saved, you will not be saved, without Ram — O soul, chant only the name of Ram. [refrain] Worship the water-god, and you become a tortoise or crab — there is no true devotion without Ram (1). Worship Chandi, and you become a deer — no true devotion without Ram (2). Worship the Devi, and you become a buffalo — no true devotion without Ram (3). Worship Harshad Mata, and you become blood — no true devotion without Ram (4). Worship Kshetrapal, and you become a dog — no true devotion without Ram (5). Worship Ganesha, and you become a mouse — no true devotion without Ram (6). Worship Mahadev, and you become a bull — no true devotion without Ram (7). Worship the Sun, and you become a horse — no true devotion without Ram (8). Worship a sannyasi, and you go to Shivlok — no true devotion without Ram (9). Worship a brahmin, and you go to the heavenly realm — no true devotion without Ram (10). Worship a devotee, and you become a devotee — this Namdev proclaims, beating the drum, birth after birth.)

Without devotion to Ram, you will never be saved, never be saved. If you worship the water-god, you will have to become a creature made of clay — a water-dwelling creature like a tortoise or a crab. If you worship Chandi, you will become an animal, a deer; if you worship the Devi, you will become a female buffalo. If you worship Harshad Mata, you will have to become blood. If you worship Kshetrapal, you will become a dog; if you worship Ganpati, you will have to become a mouse. If you worship Mahadev, you will have to become a bull. If you worship the Sun, you will have to become a horse. If you worship a sannyasi, you will go to Shivlok. If you worship a brahmin, you will go to heaven. And if you worship a devotee, you will become a devotee — so declares Namdev, announcing it like a public proclamation.

Das Kabirji has also composed a hymn (shabda/pad) of this same sentiment.

_Gorakhji kya lagaya dhandha, tum phir padega phanda. (tek) Jantar mantar okhad mooli, pavan ghotke sadhya. Guru bin marag kaun batave, phir padega phanda. Ganesh aaradhe musa saraje, Brahma aaradhe rogi. Dhan sanchare bhoring saraje, sunone Gorakh jogi. Devi aaradhe bakra saraje, Bhavani aaradhe thay bhensa. Tirath gayese machhli saraje, samudra me tera janam. Surat aaradhe khet saraje, chandra aaradhe thay hasti. Indra aaradhe raja saraje, phirone navlakh dharti. Jadu sikhe to bhoot ja saraje, moonth sadhe to pade naraka. Julam kare to daitya saraje, ban banme tera pharna. Kahe Kabir suno ho Gorakh, itni baat na boojhi. Anek jug beet gaya, tune satya baat na soojhi._ (Meaning: O Gorakhji, what business have you taken up? You will fall into the snare again! [refrain] You have mastered charms, spells, and medicinal roots and herbs by controlling the breath [pranayama]. But without a guru, who will show you the path? You will fall into the snare again. Worship Ganesh, and you will be born a mouse; worship Brahma, and you will become diseased. Hoard wealth, and you will be born a great serpent — listen, O yogi Gorakh! Worship the Devi, and you will be born a goat; worship Bhavani, and you will become a buffalo. Go on pilgrimage, and you will be born a fish, taking your birth in the ocean. Worship [worldly] perception, and you will be born as a field; worship the moon, and you will become an elephant. Worship Indra, and you will be born a king, wandering over the nine-lakh-fold earth. Learn magic, and you will become a ghost; practice the discipline of casting curses, and you will fall into hell. Commit tyranny, and you will be born a demon, roaming from forest to forest. Kabir says: listen, O Gorakh, you have not understood even this much — many ages have passed, yet you have not grasped the truth.)

Das Kabirji says: "O Gorakhji! What kind of activity, what kind of endeavor, have you set into motion? By doing this you will fall back into the trap of illusion (maya). You have mastered tantric mantras, herbal medicines, and the roots of plants and trees, accomplishing this by controlling the breath through pranayama — but without a guru, who will show you the path of devotion? Without a guru, you will fall back again into the cycle of maya. If you worship Ganesh, God will turn you into a mouse; and if you worship Brahma, you will become diseased on account of sensual indulgence. If you hoard wealth and riches, you will become a curse. So, O yogi, listen to what I say. If you worship the Devi, you will have to become a goat. If you go on pilgrimage, you will have to become a fish, and you will be born in the ocean. If you worship the sun, you will have to become a horse, and if you worship the moon, you will have to become an elephant. If you worship Indra, you will have to become a king, and you will have to wander about over the nine-part earth. If you learn magic, you will have to become a ghost. And if you practice the discipline of casting curses (moonth), you will fall into hell. If you commit tyranny, you will have to become a demon and wander from forest to forest. So Das Kabirji says: O Gorakh, listen! Though many ages have passed while you practiced yoga, you have still not gained even this much wisdom — that devotion alone is the true path to our liberation."

In the Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 7, verse 23, such people are also called of little understanding (alpa-buddhi).

"Whatever form a deity has, along with its ornaments and vehicle, according to that same form and by his own power, does the worshipper's destiny unfold."

But the fruit gained by those of little understanding is perishable. Those who worship the gods attain the gods, but my devotees attain me. Even the gods themselves remain caught in the bondage of maya (illusion).

_Maya ke re vash pare, Brahma Vishnu Mahesh. Narad Sharad Sanak Sanandan Gauriputra Ganesh._ (Meaning: Even Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh fall under the sway of maya — as do Narad, Sharada, Sanak, Sanandan, and Gauri's son Ganesh.)

Therefore, a worshipper of the gods is regarded as being like an animal.

_Atha yo'nyam devatam upaste anyo'sav anyo'ham asmiti na sa veda yatha pashuh._ (Meaning: One who worships another deity, thinking "He is one and I am another," does not know [the truth] — just like an animal.)

Whoever worships other deities does not know who I am — just as an animal does not know.

sections.title_en: Krishnadas Is Shown the Path of Devotion
sections.translation:
_Agalod gaamthi Krishnadas aavya, bhakti mukti paami haide harakhaya ||1||_ (Krishnadas came from the village of Agalod; having attained devotion and liberation, his heart rejoiced.)

Krishnadas's mother's name was Tejbai and his father's name was Damodardas Dave. In Idar, Damodardas Dave was a well-known physician (vaidya) and astrologer. Krishnadas was born in Samvat 1700, on the second day of the bright half of Kartak. In Samvat 1710, Damodardas passed away (attained the heavenly abode). In Samvat 1412, when the Muslims conquered Idar, Krishnadas, together with his mother, lived in Hidovar and pursued his studies there. He used to perform intense meditation (mahadhyan) on Ganpati. When Ganpati told him to ask for a boon, he asked instead for devotion to Shri Hari. Ganpati told him that only a Sadguru can grant the gift of devotion — devotion becomes firm through the company of saints (satsang). Ganpati then brought him, in the Kanam region, to Puniyad, to Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, who was in the form of Sarangpani. At the edge of the village of Puniyad, a conversation took place with Naranadas. His doubts were resolved right there, and when he asked Naranadas for initiation (diksha), Naranadas brought him to Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj. Removing Krishnadas's doubt and confusion, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj gave him initiation, gave him his own rosary (mala), and told him to give up the ritualistic worship of Omkar and to walk the path of [unclear] exclusive devotion (ananya bhakti) of the saints and devotees. Returning home from Puniyad to his native place, he came to Agalod, to the house of his host, the Kadva Kanbi Patel named Dhana. Because he had taken the vow of exclusive devotion from Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, he would not accept cooked food or provisions directly. When this happened, Dhana asked him to...

Then Dhana asked Krishnadas [unclear: to accept him, on the recommendation/token of the Sadguru]. So, taking Mangala and Shitala with him, Dhana came to Puniyad, received kanthi-diksha (thread initiation) from Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, and was made an exclusive Vaishnav, an uda-bhakt. They attained union with Hari (passed away) at their daughter's house in the village of Sabalpur. At the place of their samadhi (final resting shrine) there is a Tulsi enclosure (tulsi kyaro). Their lineage now continues at Sardarpur, Taluka Vijapur, District Mehsana. Even today, as witness to this event, Ganpati is enshrined at the edge of Puniyad. (— From the life-story of Krishnadas.)

Even a deity such as Ganpati cannot grant devotion to Vishnu. Only a saint, a Sadguru, can give this devotion. Therefore Ganpati, who brought about the meeting between Krishnadas and Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, was the giver of Riddhi-Siddhi (worldly power and prosperity). Krishnadas refused the Riddhi-Siddhi that leads to hell. Thus there is no possibility that one who worships Ganpati will attain devotion (bhakti). Moreover, uda-bhakts do not worship any deity or goddess that would lead us to a lower state (adhogati). Worshipping such deities cannot bring about our welfare — this principle is proven true through this episode of Krishnadas.

Jivanji Maharaj's most intimate and grace-favoured devotee (nij jan), the Vaishnav Krishnadasji, having received kanthi-diksha from Jivanji Maharaj, now renounces his original identity — his Brahmin lineage and his former worship of Ganpati and so on — and, taking on exclusive Vaishnav-hood, returns to Agalod by the Guru's command. This highly learned Brahmin, Krishnadasji, who had been a strict ritualist and worshipper of Omkar, has become dyed in the colour of Jivanji Maharaj and has become an exclusive Vaishnav. He wishes to remain continuously in his Guru's presence, but when the Guru's command comes for him to return home, he takes his leave and comes back to Agalod. According to the custom that was traditionally followed, Dhanaji invites Krishnadasji to a Brahmin feast (brahma bhojan), but he respectfully declines, and says:

_Ab mein ananya vrat liyo, kaahuko bartan na jaay chhuyo. To saakut ann liyo na jaai, kaise bhog lagaavu bhai._ (Now I have taken the vow of exclusive devotion — I do not even touch another's vessel. Then how could I accept the grain of a Sakut, a worshipper of Shakti? How, brother, could I offer such a thing to my gracious Lord?)

Krishnadasji says that he has now taken up the vow of exclusive devotion; he does not even touch another person's vessel, so how then could he accept the grain and so on of a Sakut (a worshipper of Shakti)? And how could he offer it to his gracious Lord (Kripanath)? This can no longer be done. Hearing these words, Dhana Patel became extremely grieved and asked the reason. Krishnadasji said, I have accepted Jivandasji as my Sadguru, and so I have now become an uda-bhakt, and I can no longer keep the company of a Sakut. Hearing this, Dhana, deeply grieved, asked to be freed himself from this cycle of the ocean of worldly existence (bhavsagar) and to be granted exclusive Vaishnav-hood. Krishnadasji said that only the Sadguru can do this. So Dhanaji, taking his son and grandson with him, under Krishnadasji's guidance, came along with him to Puniyad, and received the rosary (mala) and mark (tilak) from Jivandasji.

_Mala Jeevandaaski, mili hai diksha sang. Ghana darash dekhata, bahot chadhaayo rang._ (He received the rosary of Jivandas along with the initiation. Seeing this darshan, Dhana was overwhelmed — greatly coloured with devotion.)

In this way, when Dhana Bhagat was given the rosary and kanthi, an extraordinary colour of devotion rose in him, and thus he became an "uda-bhagat." By the command of Jivandasji, Krishnadas began showing the true path to seekers in Agalod and the surrounding villages, and giving them kanthi-diksha. For, [the Guru reasoned,] many others like Dhana Bhagat would come along later, and how many times could they keep coming to and from Puniyad? So, seeing the mettle and learning in Krishnadasji, Jivanji Maharaj told him that from now on he too should give kanthi-diksha on behalf of Namdev and Kabirji, and he said to Dhana Bhagat:

_Tab sadguru bole man laai, suno Dhana Mangala Shitlaai. Tamo mahant Krishnadaskun maano, sab santanko ye darshan cheeno._ (Then the Sadguru spoke wholeheartedly: Listen, Dhana, Mangala, and Shitala! Accept Krishnadasji as your Mahant [spiritual head]; recognize this as the teaching for all the saints.)

O Dhana, Mangala, and Shitala! From today, regard Krishnadasji as the certified head (sanchalak) of the seat (padtharo) of Namdev-Kabirji for our region. I also grant him the authority of a Guru. Consider his word equal to my own word, and conduct yourselves accordingly. Having given this command, he sent them off.

Krishnadasji went there and turned many seekers and thirsty souls into exclusive Vaishnavs, and spread the Uda faith there. Today this region is known as the Kantha area.

Once, families of uda-bhakts lived in villages very close to Shahpura and Puniyad. These families lived in villages along the banks of the Dhadhar river. Jivanji Maharaj would meet them again and again, so that they could get the opportunity to hear his words and to serve him. In the same way, at that time, uda-bhakt families also lived in the village of Thuvavi, near Bhilapur. At present, apart from Bhilapur, bhakt families live only in Beharampur; the rest of the families have migrated elsewhere.

At one time, Jivanji Maharaj came to Bhilapur, to the house of the devotee Bhagwanbhai, and a night-time satsang and bhajan gathering was arranged there. All the devotees from the surrounding villages gathered together, sang hari-kirtan, and took the benefit of the Guru's words. It was the monsoon season, and rain was falling. At that time, the loving devotee women living in Thuvavi prepared sukhdi (a sweet) as prasad and were eager to give it to Jivanji Maharaj to offer to God. But after evening fell, with the rain pouring down, the Dhadhar river, which flows between Bhilapur and Thuvavi, threatened to become an obstacle. If the river's waters rose, it would become difficult to cross to the far bank. These sisters' devotion was strong, and their resolve too was powerful. They resolved, even at the risk of danger, to cross the river. Taking the sukhdi prasad, they arrived at the riverbank.

The Dhadhar river, too, seeing their resolve, seemed eager to become part of their devotion, and made a way for these sisters. Taking this risk, the sisters crossed the river and reached Bhilapur, and offered the prasad to their Guru.

When there is faith in the Guru, no matter what obstacle comes, the task can be accomplished. These sisters' faith was firm, and so they crossed even so difficult a river with ease, and both of them received the darshan of Jivandasji and the benefit of satsang.

On the second day of the bright half of Magsar, Samvat 1737, Jivanji Maharaj was resting at the house of Bhagwandas and Dhanbai in Bhilapur. Then he had a dream: two young men, radiantly beautiful, came to fetch him, holding a red staff in hand. Namdevji, Kabirji, Dhana Bhagat, Seni, Pipa, Rohidas, and other devotees were waiting for him. Then Jivanji Maharaj [promised that he would come] after six months —

— he made a promise that he would come after fulfilling the wishes (manorath) of his devotees, and for the sake of his devotees' wishes, he extended his own life. Great souls (maha purush) such as Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj come into this world for the welfare (kalyan) — through fellowship and holy company (samagam-sant sangat) — of souls like us. Moreover, they are all-powerful, capable souls (sarvashaktiman samarth atma), and so they come into this world of their own free will, and they return of their own free will from this world back to their own abode (dham). On the second day of the bright half of Magsar, Samvat 1737, he had lovingly made a promise of six months for the sake of his devotees. This promise of six months, made on the second of the bright half of Magsar, was completed on the second of the bright half of Jeth; but the festival of Janmashtami was near — two months and twenty-one days away — so he made a further promise, that he would come after celebrating the festival (ochhav) of Janmashtami. Then, knowing that he now had to depart, he began preparing to take leave of this world. He called his own dear ones (nij jan) and told them to prepare grain and other things to make the food offering (bhojan prasad). He also sent invitations to all the children and cowherds (bal-gopal) to be present.

There is a difference between devotees who worship God (Bhagwad bhakti) in general and the devotion of our uda-bhakts who are engaged in devotion to God. Other people besides us perform devotion in order to attain some one or another world — heaven (swarga), Vaikunth, Golok, Chandralok, Suryalok, Janalok, Tapalok, Aksharlok (dham), and so on. But Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has declared all these worlds, including Vaikunth, to be fleeting and impermanent (kshanbhangur). He has further shown that attaining them brings no benefit at all. For the Bhagavad Gita says, _kshine punye martya lokam vishanti_ (when merit is exhausted, those who have gone to that world must come back again to the world of mortals). Therefore he himself had no wish to go to any of these places; rather, he had decided to go to his own abode (Swadham). For all these places are called "loks" (worlds), and we have no right or claim over them — what belongs to the lesser gods cannot be called ours. If there is an Indralok, it belongs to Indra; but if someone like you or me were to go to that world on a visa —

If he had gone abroad, he would have to return to his own native land once his visa expired. But whoever dwells permanently in his own native land, no one can remove him from there. That is why Jivanji Maharaj has gone only to his own eternal abode (Swadham). Moreover, in that abode there is an assembly of great saints such as Sadguru Kabir, and so he asked the messengers who came to fetch him, again and again, whether Kabirji was there — for Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj is not separate from Kabirji, but is himself a part (limb) of Sadguru Kabirji.

Jivanji Maharaj appeared on this earth, by the command of the Supreme Being Kabirji and others, for the welfare of eligible souls. Twice, Jivanji Maharaj postponed death for the sake of the welfare of his devotees. When, in this way, the appointed time promised in a dream came due, the conversation he had with the messengers who came to fetch him was overheard by Panabai, the wife of his son Shyamdas.

Swadham (The Divine Abode)

_ham aaye un deshthi | phir jaano un desh ||_
_eh jugat banai jivana | sab santanke updesh ||_
(I have come from that other Land; know that I go back to that Land. This arrangement, O Jivan[a], is what all the saints teach.)

The individual soul separates (becomes parted) from the Supreme Brahma and comes into this world. Here it experiences pleasure and pain, and then, according to its karma, passes through the 8,400,000 species of life. Or else, according to its karma, it returns to the place it came from and reaches once again the presence of the Supreme Brahma. Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj has shown the Uda Bhakt Ramkabir tradition the vision of this path, and has given the call to walk this simple path. Jivanji Maharaj has given the infinite presence of the Supreme Brahma the name "Undesh" (the Other Land). In this way, for all devotees departing this world, Jivanji Maharaj has shown the vision of this unique and wondrous divine play (leela) of the Supreme Brahma.

On the 8th day of the dark fortnight of Shravan in Vikram Samvat 1737, all the Uda Bhakt exclusive Vaishnavas gathered together in Puniyad. Jivanji Maharaj had invited everyone to come here. Welcoming that invitation, everyone gathered together, and a festival of Hari-kirtan (devotional singing) took place. Describing this occasion in beautiful poetic form, Nana Parekh writes:

_"Ramkabir satya chhe shri Dham Puniyad sakal santno nivas, tahaan Vaishnav Jivandasji birajey chhe, Hari kirtan maha mangal thay chhe, Vaishnav aavi malya chhe, je koi maha param sukh upaje chhe sneh din din adhik vadhe chhe, vrahe vairag vishvas aave chhe. Tamo krupanath chho, aatmane kahadva (uddhar karva) aavya chho."_
(Ramkabir is the truth; the holy abode Puniyad is the dwelling of all the saints. There Vaishnav Jivandasji resides. The great, auspicious Hari-kirtan takes place; the Vaishnavs have come and gathered; wherever this happens, a great supreme joy arises; love grows greater day by day; dispassion (vairagya) and faith come to flourish. You are the Lord of Mercy (Krupanath); you have come to draw out — to redeem — souls.)

_Sakhi:_
_Kabir kede pragate, jagma Jivandas |_
_Dhaja bandhi dharma dadhaviyo, jam kinkar paame traas ||1||_
(1. In Kabir's lineage, Jivandas has appeared in the world; having raised the flag, he has made dharma firm — the servants of Yama, seeing this, are struck with terror.)

_Vaishnavji's doha:_
_Kaanto haath Kabir ke, tahaan sakal dharma toliyo |_
_Jap tap tirath daan, ta mule mitho choliyo ||2||_
(2. In Kabir's hand is the balance-scale on which all dharma is weighed; japa, tapa, pilgrimage, and charity — measured against it, are but a sweet [unclear].)

That dharma is primordial and eternal (sanatan); one may search the three worlds and the twenty-one universes, but no other dharma comes to equal it on the scale. All the saints were sitting together, and discourse and kirtan were going on. When one watch of the last part of the night remained, two Vaishnavs arrived and gave darshan to Vaishnav Jivandasji; no one else could see them — others could hear the conversation but could not see the visitors. One of them was a form of great beauty, holding a red staff in hand, fair of body, in the fullness of youth, without beard or moustache. That Vaishnav spoke to Vaishnav Jivandasji: "I have come to fetch you. There, Kabirji is present, and Rankaji, Namdevji, Seniji, Dhanaji, Pipaji, and Rohidasji are also there."

Vaishnav Jivandasji asked further, "Is Kabirji there?" The Vaishnav replied, "Yes, Kabirji is there." Vaishnav Jivandasji was filled with great joy.

Jivandasji said to those Vaishnavs, "Here, the Vaishnav children have great hope in me; I will come after six months." Those Vaishnavs said to Vaishnav Jivandasji, "Without you, things there are not proceeding well; we are waiting eagerly." Vaishnav Jivandasji said, "Give my greetings to the Vaishnavs, and say Ramkabir to them." After that, those Vaishnavs departed. The Vaishnavs present here, who had heard the conversation, asked, "O Maharaj! With whom did you converse? No one appeared to our eyes."

Vaishnav Jivandasji said: "Some Vaishnavs had come to fetch me. They pleaded a great deal; I have given a promise of six months." When twenty days remained of that promise, he summoned his own Vaishnavs; everyone came and sat together, and unbroken Hari-kirtan went on continuously, without interruption.

Vaishnav Jivandasji said: "Prepare the raw provisions; make khaja, jalebi, and kari-ladu." He appointed some of his own Vaishnavs for daily service. The day of Janmashtami arrived, and everyone came and sat together. Vaishnav Jivandasji spoke:

_Sakhi:_
_"Sadguru sandesa moklya, kyaan bacha sab aav |_
_Naam chintamani Jivana, je bhave so paav ||3||_
_Baal buddhu Jivana, Ram bhaktiki aash |_
_Shoorveer bhaagi chale, daante pakadi dhaash ||4||_
(3. The Sadguru has sent his message: "Come, all my children, wherever you are." The Name is the wish-fulfilling gem, O Jivan[a] — whoever holds it dear attains it.
4. Child and elder alike, O Jivan[a], hold the hope of devotion to Ram; the brave hero presses forward, gripping his resolve firmly, as if held between the teeth.)

"Brothers, if anyone tries to mislead you, do not be misled. The true Lord is the enchanting flute-player [Krishna]; if others — Brahma, the Vedas, and so on — are followed instead, they lead the soul away from the Supreme Brahma." For five days the festival of divine play continued, and all the Vaishnavs came. Four Vaishnavs stayed to render service; their names were: (1) Vaishnav Laldasji (2) Vaishnav Gopaldasji (3) Vaishnav Nadiyada Haridasji (4) Vaishnav Rupa Bhagat.

Here all the devotees came and gathered together. It was understood that this was the last occasion, and everyone wished for a final darshan of Jivanji Maharaj. At this time he called Shyamdasji near him, explained matters to him in detail, inquired about all the arrangements, and said: "Take this body to the garden at Shahpura and perform the cremation rites there. At Shahpura is holy ground, the land of the saints — make a [tulsi] plot there." Then Shyamdasji said:

_Tahaan Ayodhya jahaan Raghupati | Kaahanah tahaan Gokul gaam |_
_Sampuri tahaan Jivana | Jahaan sant sangat Harinaam ||_
(There is Ayodhya, wherever Raghupati [Ram] dwells; there is the village of Gokul, wherever Kanha [Krishna] is. Every place, O Jivan[a], is [as holy as] Sampuri, wherever there is the company of saints and the Name of Hari.)

Wherever Ram dwells, that is Ayodhya; wherever Krishna is, that is the village of Gokul. And wherever, in the company of saints, the Name of Hari is taken, those places are verily equal to the seven holy cities (Saptapuri).

Hearing this sakhi, Jivanji Maharaj was filled with great joy and began to say: "Before coming here, I lived in the presence of Sant Gopaldas; so, knowing this to be the wish of the Merciful Lord, and from the feeling that I would remain always in his presence, I have been insisting on Shahpura. But now, take me to the garden in Puniyad, perform the cremation rites there, and make a tulsi plot there."

Giving this instruction, he said, "I entrust the service to Kahandasji," and placed his own neck-mala upon Kahandasji. But the devotees said that this ought to remain in your own household; so Jivanji Maharaj instead wrapped the mala around Kahandasji's thumb, applied tilak to his thumb, and then, holding Kahandasji's hand, had him apply tilak to Shyamdasji — thereby appointing Shyamdasji as his successor. He then asked for water to be brought so he could bathe. He took his seat beneath the lemon tree behind the house and bathed with the water. Then the sisters Jetibai, Malibai, Baijibai, and Panabai, who had brought sukhadi as prasad, offered it to the Lord, and that prasad was distributed among all the Vaishnavs. At midnight, from Thuvavi, Lalbai came along with Rambai and Tulsidas and others; Vaishnavs came from Bhilapur; and from Shahpura, Mohandas brought kamod-rice prasad, which he partook of, and those present also shared and partook of it.

Finally, he gave his last teaching to all the Vaishnavs, urging them to remain vigilant. And, saying "Ramkabir" to Kandas and to Vaishnav Haridas who had come from Arithha, Jivanji Maharaj departed toward his own eternal abode. Haridas bowed at the feet of Jivanji Maharaj and said "Ramkabir."

Thus Jivandasji departed for Swadham at midnight on the 8th of the dark fortnight of Shravan — Janmashtami day — in Vikram Samvat 1730.

_Jivandas mahima kahi | dhanya dhanya kahe sab koy |_
_Sant kaaj dehi dhari | avar na jaane koy ||_
(Having spoken of Jivandas's glory, everyone said, "Blessed, blessed is he." He took on a body for the sake of the saints — this, no one else knows.)

As they discussed the wondrous greatness of Sadguru Jivandasji Maharaj, everyone praised him and offered blessings. This Sadguru took on a body for the welfare of the saints, but no one else knows this fact.

Krishnadasji Maharaj received devotion to Hari from Jivandas Maharaj and departed; having gained complete knowledge of the tradition of the Uda Bhakt and of exclusive (ananya) devotion, and having received the Uda Bhakt initiation along with the teaching of the dharma of Namdev and Kabir, and having received his own mala as prasad from Jivanji Maharaj, he went to Mehsana district. There, in accordance with Jivanji Maharaj's instruction, he propagated the faith through the divine Name Ramkabir and taught the Vaishnavs of the Uda Bhakt tradition. But the remarkable thing is that neither Jivanji Maharaj nor Krishnadas Maharaj wrote anything with their own hand; rather, Haridas Nadiyada, having heard it from Jivanji Maharaj, wrote the book of Samagam (spiritual discourses), and in some places certain individuals wrote down one or two hymns composed by Jivanji Maharaj. But whatever doubts and questions Krishnadas Maharaj put to Jivanji Maharaj, Shyamdasji has recorded in detail in the Parcharee (hagiographic account) of Krishnadasji. Thus, whatever he had learned from his own father, he has described in very great detail — the complete, exclusive devotion of the Uda Bhakt tradition. Looking at this, it seems to us that if this Parcharee had not been written, we would not have been able to properly know the code of conduct of the Uda Bhakt tradition.

Besides the Parcharee of Krishnadasji, Shyamdas Maharaj wrote other Parcharees and hymn-compositions. Besides these, he also transcribed some sakhis of Jivanji Maharaj and the composition of Sarvang-leela by Govinddas, among others. In one book, on page 103, it is written: "Written by Vaishnav Shyamdas, son of Krishnadasji — whoever reads this, may they say Ramkabir."

The self-composed works of this supreme Vaishnav Shyamdasji Maharaj that we currently possess are as follows:

1. The Parcharee of Krishnadas Maharaj
2. The Parcharee of Jivanji Maharaj
3. Gnan-mahima (The Glory of Knowledge)
4. In the Jaipur manuscript, on pages 11 to 103, Shyamdas composed seven hymns of the Saptapadi Kirtan, describing the episode of the sage Durvasa and King Ambarish.

Besides this, the names of other compositions by Shyamdas Maharaj are also known to us, such as the Parcharee of Gnaniji and the Parcharee of Adhyaruji, among others. But those works, from the places of Sardarpur and Vadnagar, have been lost due to lack of preservation and study. Today we have lost this most precious jewel — a matter of sorrow for the community. But we remain ever indebted to Shyamdasji for the contribution that has survived. We shall always remember him as the second-greatest devotee-poet after Bhakta Haridas Nadiyada. His compositions are steeped in beautiful, sweet devotional feeling and are simple in language; moreover, they are not inferior to any current composition in Gujarati literature.

To this eminent crown-jewel among devotee-poets, we offer millions upon millions of true and reverent salutations.

One day at dusk, an elderly woman named Prembai was sitting on a swing, singing the evening (sandhya) aarti. At that time, an official of the Gaekwad government was passing by; he saw the elderly woman performing the evening aarti and stopped right there. In her courtyard, a child was playing mischievously, while the woman sang the evening aarti with a calm mind. After the aarti was finished, the official remarked, "Sister, you sing so beautifully — if only you would give your child some good upbringing." At this, Prembai said, "Brother, whom are you speaking of? I am a widow, and I have no children."

The official fell into astonishment, and it seemed to him that God himself was truly playing as a child in that sister's home. Deeply moved by her devotion, the official came with the elderly woman to Puniyad. He took the kanthi (sacred neck-thread) initiation from Dwarkadasji Maharaj, became an exclusive (ananya) Vaishnav, and established a seat (gaadi) at Darapura. He propagated the Ramkabir tradition.

Jivanji Maharaj instructed the exclusive (ananya) Vaishnav devotees that, if possible, they should visit Dwarka and Jagannath at least once in their lifetime, and should take along five or ten Vaishnavs with them, since there they could hold a Hari-kirtan festival. Accordingly, Raghavdasji Maharaj, of the fourth generation after Jivanji Maharaj, set out for Jagannath along with a number of exclusive Vaishnavs.

This company of saints came to Jagannath and rested there. There, at the temple of Lord Jagannath, a single rice-prasad is offered without any distinction of caste or community, and everyone partakes of it together. Raghavdasji stated, "We are exclusive Vaishnavs; our Sadguru has instructed us not to accept prasad from anyone other than an exclusive Vaishnav. Therefore we wish to prepare our own separate prasad and offer it to the Lord." Hearing this, the local pandas (temple priests) and pujaris objected, and insisted that everyone must accept the same common prasad. So Raghavdasji stayed there for seven continuous days without taking even a single grain of food, maintaining his request and continuing his effort to explain his position. On the seventh day, all the pujaris and pandas came to Raghavdasji with a proposal: that, following the usual custom, they would offer their prasad, and alongside it the Vaishnavs could also prepare and offer their own prasad — but that whichever prasad the Lord placed a tulsi leaf upon, that prasad alone would be accepted by all. The final decision was left to Lord Jagannath himself. Raghavdasji Maharaj accepted this proposal, and at dawn the two prasads were placed before the Lord. At this time, as Raghavdasji Maharaj placed the prasad before Lord Jagannath, he offered this prayer:

_Aarti shri Jagannath mangala kari | parsat charanaravind aapada hari ||_
_Dhanan dhanan ghant vaage ben bansari | baajat mridang taal naad khanjari ||_
_Dipak jot jagmage shri kanchanapuri | nav baati agartel paavak jari ||_
_Indra daman sindhu gaaje Rohini khadi | Maarkand set Ganga aanand bhari ||_
_Ek naam teen lok chaud bhuvan sancharachari | rom rom rarankaar kaahe su dare ||_
_Garud khambh singhpaur jaatra bhari | hira maanek motipana jotki jhadi ||_
_Ratan sinhaasan aap biraaje betki chhadi | chhapan bhog nit laage hot hari hari ||_
_Sur nar muni dwaare thaade Brahma ved ochari | dhanya dhanya Raagho shri aajki ghadi ||_
(I perform the auspicious aarti of Shri Jagannath; touching his lotus feet removes all misfortune. Conches and bells resound, flutes play; mridang drums, cymbals, and tambourines sound. Lamps blaze with light in the golden city; nine wicks burn with incense-oil as offering fire. The ocean roars like tamed Indra, at the bank named Rohini; the Ganga flows there in blessed joy, as at Markandeya's holy spot. The one Name pervades the three worlds and fourteen realms, all that moves and does not move; in every pore its sound resonates — why then should one fear? At the Garuda pillar, at the Lion Gate, the pilgrimage is fulfilled; diamonds, rubies, and pearls shine with dazzling light. Seated upon the jewel-studded throne, holding the ceremonial staff, fifty-six varieties of food are offered continuously, amid cries of "Hari, Hari." Gods, men, and sages stand at his door; Brahma recites the Vedas. Blessed, blessed, O Raghava, is this present hour!)

This moment stood upon the anvil of trial. It was a difficult time of testing — to protect the community's exclusive Vaishnava devotion and to protect one's own dharma. He made an anguished, heartfelt plea to Lord Jagannath: "You are the King seated upon the jewel-studded throne, but this is my hour of life and death; protecting me lies in your hands." In this difficult moment he made this plea through this hymn. At this hour of testing Raghavdas Maharaj's exclusive Vaishnava devotion, the pandas of Jagannath were astonished, and they bowed at Raghavdasji's feet. The Maharaja of that place at that time had a document written on a copper plate and gave it to Raghavdasji, stating: "From this day forward, I grant permission to any follower of the Uda Bhakt Ramkabir tradition to offer their own separate prasad."

From that time onward, the cooking-pot of the Uda Bhakt Ramkabir tradition is offered separately there. Thus the Lord himself accepted our exclusive Vaishnava devotion.

The workings of time are strange, each moment unlike any other. When Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj founded the Ramkabir tradition, he did not institute any worship of idols or images, nor any form of ritual praise-worship. Yet today, in the sixth generation after Jivanji Maharaj, Narsinhdasji resolved never again to sit upon his own seat, and bowed to it instead. The very seat on which he used to sit daily to hold satsang (holy company) and recite katha-kirtan (discourse and devotional singing), he now bows to again and again, joining both hands, his eyes brimming with tears of love. Streams of tears flow from his eyes. Again and again he falls to his knees in reverence. Bowing with the deepest humility, Narsinhdasji says, "O Maharaj! For the sake of saving the honor of this humble soul, you had to endure so much hardship! You came for my sake! Sitting upon this very seat, you proved me innocent! Now I shall never sit upon this seat again."

This incident took place in Puniyad on Shravan Sud 14 of Vikram Samvat 1872. What had happened was this: Narsinhdas had taken Vasanti and left her at the home of the Thakor of Zulana, where she lived happily with her son. But the very wicked man of Puniyad who had earlier committed misconduct with Vasanti shamelessly demanded her again. Narsinhdasji counselled him firmly and advised him to restrain his lust. This only provoked him further, and he lodged a complaint with the Maharaja of the Baroda state, alleging that this Narsinhdas, posing as a preceptor of the Uda sect, had run away with Vasanti and had killed both her and her son. The Diwan of the Gaekwad government thereupon instructed his Subha (governor) to go to Puniyad in person, investigate, and submit a report.

Troubled by the thought that officials of the Gaekwad government would come to his own home to investigate, that all manner of questions would be asked, and what face he would then show to society, Narsinhdasji left his house before the Subha arrived. He returned in the evening, and the devotees of the village along with the leading Patels came to congratulate him. Narsinhdasji could not understand why, but as he was entering the house, he noticed a streak of light vanishing from above his seat, and beside the seat he found a letter from Shri Vishaji Kashiji, the Subha of the Gaekwad government, declaring him innocent.

He then grasped the full meaning of what had happened: that while he was away, the merciful Lord (Krupanath) himself had come and taken his place, bearing witness and proving him innocent. Overcome, with streams of loving tears in his eyes, he began bowing again and again to that seat.

After Shravan Sud 14, Vikram Samvat 1872, he worshipped this seat daily, bowing to it and offering loving obeisance every day, and kept it placed upon a raised platform. In time, Jagannath

Maharaj gave it the form of a gadi (spiritual seat), and this practice was later followed at other places in the community as well. Thus was Narsinhdas's patience put to the test. Evidence of the events that took place at that time is still preserved today in the Shri Ram Library in Puniyad. Based on this evidence, Pujya Yadunath Maharaj wrote a detailed account of this episode, which has been published by the Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj Memorial Foundation under the title 'Vasanti Charitra - Narsinhdasji's Test of Patience.'

_Main Ayodhyamein jeevana, man mero Gokul manhi |_
_Rishi patni su kol hai, ve birad bisarat naahi ||_
(Though I dwell in Ayodhya, my mind remains in Gokul; the vow given to the sages' wives - that pledge is never forgotten.)

In the Dwapar Yuga, when Lord Shri Krishna used to go into the forest to graze the cows, he was accompanied by companion cowherds of his own age. The Bhagavatam gives their number as sixteen. These sixteen child-companions of Krishna grazed the cows in the forest and performed many kinds of divine plays (leelas). The Puranas tell how, during Rama's life, while in exile in the forest Rama served the sages a great deal, but he did not, in particular, accept any service from the sages themselves or from their wives. Because of this, the sages' wives said to Rama, "Grant us too the good fortune of serving you." Rama then promised them that in the Dwapar Yuga their wish would be fulfilled. And here, they have all come in the form of the gopis and perform their divine play in Gokul. The story of all these gopas and gopis is well known.

Among the sixteen companions in Gokul, one who remained constantly in Krishna's service was, in this present birth, Kabirji; the second was Jivanji Maharaj; the third was Narsinh Mehta. All of them remained ever absorbed in the service of Krishna. Today, at the place called Bansivat in Vrindavan - where the Lord once performed the rasleela (divine dance-play) - there stands, in the form of a marble statue, a depiction of the playful sport (chhakleela) of these sixteen child-companions. The image of Jivanji Maharaj that we see today has been copied from there; beside him Kabirji is seated. These images have been placed there upon a raised platform, and the Tourism Department of the Government of India has given a certificate here declaring this to be the original Bansivat.

So much research has been done on Kabirji's life story that a large volume could be written from it, and many scholars have written about him. The purpose of this piece is not to give his life story but to shed light on the image of him that is commonly current. Studying Kabir's character, one understands that he never falsely praised anyone, nor did he ever bow before falsehood. Kabirji, who grew up in an extremely poor family, had no means of livelihood other than the handloom. Every day he had to run the handloom, weave cloth, and sell it in the market, earning his living from whatever came of it. Kabirji never accepted gifts or money from anyone; he always earned his own living. Thus this extremely poor family remained poor throughout their lives.

Today, the images of Kabirji sold in the market by Kabirpanthis (followers of the Kabir path) and others show him seated on a golden throne, bearded, and clad in white garments. Kabirji never had such opulence in his life, nor did he ever ask his disciples for it. To depict Kabirji amid such luxury and indulgence is an insult to his principles and thought. One who never in his life had the chance to wear such opulent garments should never be depicted wearing them. The way he is shown in the image described above is actually Kabirji seated as one of the sixteen child-companions of the original Bansivat, appearing absorbed in contemplation and simple in bearing. That is his true character. Kabirji never accepted outward show or ostentation, so it is wrong to imagine him falsely as white-bearded or white-robed, seated upon a jewel-studded throne - such a depiction does not do justice to his character. We therefore hold the original Bansivat image to be the authentic one.

The original name of Gnaniji Maharaj, who laid the foundation of the Ramkabir tradition, was Chatursinh. He was a prince of Jaisalmer in Rajasthan. But upon hearing the words "Samevarte savadhan" (be watchful, be alert) at his own wedding altar, he grasped the deeper meaning that one must remain vigilant, and fled from there. Wandering from place to place, he arrived in Gujarat and settled in a village called Mota Sanja on the banks of the Narmada river, near Bharuch. At one point Kabirji came to Gujarat; the very first time Gnaniji set eyes on him, he beheld Rama's presence within Kabir, and the word "Ramkabir" spontaneously slipped from his lips. Gnaniji was an extraordinarily gifted and learned man. At Kabirji's instruction, he built the island of Kabirvad in the Narmada river. Having received Kabirji's blessing, he made his home in the village of Mota Sanja in Jhagadia taluka. He also sent for his wife there and resumed his household life.

He was so learned that he became renowned under the name Gnaniji and spread the "Ramkabir" tradition throughout Gujarat. Beyond Gujarat, the Ramkabir tradition went on to widen the reach of its branches elsewhere as well. Many saints and mahants arose within this tradition. Besides sakhis (devotional couplets) and bhajans (devotional hymns), Gnaniji also composed many new devotional poems on various episodes. In his line of disciples came Dada Sukhji, Gopaldasji Chorandavasi, and after them Jivanji Maharaj; thus, in our line of gurus, he has come to be known as "Gnaniji." Gnaniji Maharaj, of the sacred soil of Mota Sanja, founded the Ramkabir tradition; later, within this tradition, Jivanji Maharaj raised up a distinct sect called the "Uda Bhakt Ramkabir Tradition."

The photograph shown here is of Gnaniji Maharaj's original dwelling place, along with his samadhi (place of final rest) and other sites. It is said that he took jivant samadhi (a living, conscious departure from the body). The well - there is a well near his house; it is said that every morning when Gnaniji came to bathe, the water would rise up on its own from the well, and once he had finished bathing, the water would recede back inside. In addition, there still stands there a sweet neem tree. On one occasion, when lightning struck, this neem tree split into two parts; Gnaniji Maharaj placed a dry wooden plank between the two halves and thereby brought the tree back to life - it stands there to this day, and its leaves are sweet.
