Every single thing that exists in this material world has its own distinct identity. In the very same way, Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj has given us the identity of "Uda." Under this identity of "Uda," what we are to recognize and become acquainted with is as follows.

1) At the center: Jivanji Maharaj is the seer (drashta). He is the one who has set us apart under the name of the Uda Bhakt Ramkabir tradition. He has shown us the entire structure of our society - its customs, its spiritual contemplation and reflection, its kirtan (devotional singing), and so on.

2) The second circle:

(a) Our own identity: Who are we, in terms of our own true self? This identity has been shown to us by Jivanji Maharaj. By giving us the name "Uda," he has made us into unique Vaishnavs (devotees of Vishnu). According to this identity, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj determines our way of thinking. Accordingly, let us look first at:

- The tulsi bed and the plate of prasad (sacred offering): This image shows the very foundation of our way of thinking. Tilak (the sacred forehead mark), tulsi (the holy basil), Ram-nam (repetition of Ram's name), and satsang (holy company) - these four articles of devotion have come to us from the Guru. It further shows that, under this spiritual way of thinking, we are free from superstition, fear, and the like. It has bestowed upon us the good fortune of facing even death without dread. Where does the root of this article of devotion and this way of thinking lie? It lies in:

- Kabirji: Jivanji Maharaj has said in his sakhi (couplet) that Kabirji is the sadguru of all. He gave us all the darshan (vision) of the sadguru, and said, "Whatever I say, I say only what has come to me through the line of our Guru; and the tilak and the tulsi mala (rosary) that everyone wears, I offer these too on his behalf." It is for this very reason that he established the padthara (sacred platform) of Namdev-Kabir. He himself says, "I am but a servant (tahelio) of Kabirji, one who works on his behalf."

(b) The identity of the devotee:

The havan kund (sacrificial fire pit): Under the Kabir way of thinking, Jivanji Maharaj built the structure of our society. Accordingly, he first freed us from free-ranging teachings and from the Brahminical tradition, and gave us an independent way of thinking, which is the mirror of our society. Under this, he laid down fourteen prohibitions: no austerities (tapa), no pilgrimage (tirtha), no vows (vrat), no yoga, no all-night vigils (jagran), no [blind] beliefs, no ritual offerings (arghya), no study of the Vedas, no homa (fire offerings), no yajna (sacrificial rites), no ritual ceremonies, no six schools of philosophy (shat darshan), no six scriptures (shat shastra), no marriage without an auspicious hour (muhurat) - that is to say, there is no need for any kind of outward observance or ostentation. One is only to practice devotion (bhakti), and that too, under the way of thinking of Sadguru Kabirji, to devote oneself only to Ram and Krishna. One must not fall into false belief in other gods and goddesses, nor worship them, nor fall into matters bound up with blind faith. He has shown us the worship of Rarankar (the resonant, unstruck sound), beyond even the worship of Omkar.

(c) The identity of the Sadguru:

Krupanath Ram-Krishna: Since we have been told to devote ourselves only to Ram and Krishna, Jivanji Maharaj has, within this, granted us communal devotion (samuh bhakti). To the beat of the kansi and mridang (cymbals and drum), we sing the compositions (pads) of the unique Vaishnav saints. The women, too, sing tali-bhajans (devotional songs accompanied by clapping). This is our tradition of practicing devotion, in which there is no distinction - all sit together as equals and practice devotion together. The devotees need nothing but a seat, that is, a mat to sit upon. It is for this reason that Jivanji Maharaj arranged, in village after village, the setting up of the padthara of Namdev-Kabir for the practice of devotion there.

Kansi-Mridang: The kansi and mridang (cymbals and drum) are the instruments of our devotion. Beyond this, there is no need for outward show or ostentation, nor any need to incur needless expense. What special instrument, after all, could be needed merely to take the Lord's name?

The Gadi (spiritual seat): From where can this way of thinking be attained? Gopaldas said something beautiful about Jivanji Maharaj - that although you are our guru, you still point us toward the sadguru. That is, Jivanji Maharaj said that whatever way of thinking has come to him, it has come originally from Kabirji; he himself is merely the instrument (nimitta). Moreover, he never regarded anyone through the lens of a guru-disciple relationship; for everyone he used the beautiful term "balgopal" (child of Gopal, i.e. a child of God). But today, the original root of whatever we seek to attain lies here. At this place are kept: 1) Jivanji Maharaj's tulsi mala (rosary), by which the prasad used to be offered to God; 2) the Samagam, in the form of a book, in which whatever teaching he gave has been collected, and which exists here together with the original manuscript; and 3) the asan (seat) - the very seat upon which the Lord gave darshan to Narsinhdasji Maharaj while seated on it, which is also here. Thus these three things are, for us, important and worthy of worship and reverence, which we have accepted as guru prasadi (the Guru's sanctified gift) and to which we pay our respects.

3) The largest, third circle: What remains at the very last is the ultimate essence (antim satva). What, then, is the task that the soul (jivatma) has come into this world to accomplish? Its aim, like that of Arjuna, is to attain the Supreme Being (Parmatma) - to devote oneself to Him. As Parbrahm (the Supreme Absolute), Jivanji Maharaj - following Kabirji - has named Ram and Krishna. But as to what form he truly takes, Jivanji Maharaj explains in the Samagam that the true form of Parbrahm is as follows:

Niranjan (unstained, without a mark of identity): He who has no anjan, that is, no mark of identity; he cannot be given any name - that is to say, he is no one's darling child. He has no son, he has no father; Parbrahm is beyond all such things.

Niralamb (unsupported): He does not dwell dependent on anyone's shelter or support; he has no need of anyone's help or prop.

Nirlep (untouched, unattached): He is set apart from all things.

Nirvikar (unchanging, without blemish): He is without conflict; he is at peace. He has no enemy and no friend; he regards all with an equal eye - he is even-sighted, and bears the title "Bhaktavatsal" (one who loves his devotees).

Nirgun (beyond the three qualities): He is beyond the three gunas - sattva, rajas, and tamas. He should not be regarded as possessing the three gunas, nor should he be regarded as having any fixed form.

Nivikalpa (without alternative or duality): Parbrahm admits of no alternative; he has no equivalent or substitute. Parbrahm is one alone, and it is he who pervades everywhere.

Abhay (fearless): He is fearless; he has no fear of anyone.

Anant (infinite): He is infinite; he remains coiled through the whole moving and unmoving universe.

Achal (immovable, unchanging): Parbrahm remains in the same one form in every land and every time; his form does not change, nor does it alter. He is achal (unmoving) - he cannot be made to waver, that is, he cannot be changed or destroyed. He has no birth and no death.

Achyut (never fallen, imperishable): Parbrahm pervades this entire moving and unmoving world. No place can defile or displace him, for he is the mightiest of all; his position cannot be displaced. That is to say, within this entire moving and unmoving world, it is Parbrahm's own rule that governs, and that Parbrahm dwells throughout the whole world. Jivanji Maharaj has shown us the path of remembering his name and practicing devotion to him.

This wheel of introduction (parichay chakra) provides the complete identity of the Uda Bhakt Ramkabir tradition. Once this is known, nothing further remains to be known.

sections.title_en: The Seat, the Samagam Text, and the Rosary
sections.translation:
We cannot say with certainty in which year Revered Jagannath Maharaj established the gadi (spiritual seat) at Puniyad. However, with the aim of keeping the asan (sacred seat) preserved by Narsinhdas Maharaj in an orderly form, he cut an opening in his own sleeping room and set a door in front of it, making a small chamber. Inside it, on a marble platform, over two mattresses, he placed this asan and made it into a gadi. Further, Revered Shri Jagannath Maharaj placed some handwritten as well as printed books behind the gadi. In addition, some loving devotees from the community also placed certain handwritten manuscripts written by Ramkabir. Over time these booklets were removed and other scriptures were placed there instead. At the very start of the gadi's establishment, the texts titled Samagam (edited by Haridas Nadiad) and Harivansh Mahapuran were placed there from the beginning. At present, the scriptures on the asan (gadi) are, in order, as follows.

1. Harivansh Mahapuran — in the Sanskrit language with Sanskrit commentary, third edition, printed.

2. Samagam — editor: Haridas Nadiad, original edition, handwritten.

3. Uda Dharma Panchratnamala — edition 2, publisher: Revered Yadunath Maharaj.

4. Samagam — devotee Bhagwanbhai Dalabhai's copy made from the original, handwritten.

5. Dasratna Gita — contents: I. Shrimad Bhagavad Gita, II. Vishnor Divya Sahasranam, III. Bhishma Stavaraj, IV. Anusmriti Stotra, V. Gajendra Moksha, VI. Gita Sahasranam Shri Stavaraj Anusmriti, VII. Ram Mantra Patal, VIII. Ramchandra Stavaraj, IX. Ramhriday Stotra, X. Vishnu Panjar Stotra.

East:
1. Ramayan — by Valmiki, printed, publisher: Mumbai Press.
2. Mahabharat Ratnadarpan — short poems etc., Sabha Vanparva.
3. Girdhar's Krishnacharitra — Gokul Lila, Mathura Lila, Dwarka Lila, and so on.
4. Uda Dharma Panchratnamala — edition 3.
5. Bhagavad Gita — handwritten.

West:
1. Shrimad Bhagwat — in the Hindi language.
2. Bhaktamal — printed, Lucknow.
3. Uda Dharma Panchratnamala — edition 1.
4. Sakhi Parayan and Gyan Mahima.
5. Ramcharitmanas — pocket edition, Gita Press.

Haridas Nadiad composed the Samagam text in Shahpur, and it used to be kept at Jivanji Maharaj's original residence there. But the mother of Revered Jagannath Maharaj, Fulba, brought this text from Shahpur to Puniyad. It is said that Fulba, after a ritual bath with her clothes on, carried this sacred text and walked to Puniyad on foot, without wearing any footwear. Before Fulba, many attempts had been made to bring this text to Puniyad, but whenever it was moved from its original place in Shahpura, a fire would break out in it on its own; and when the text was put back in its original place, the fire would go out on its own. Thus the text could not be moved from its original location. But Fulba succeeded in bringing this text to Puniyad. After coming to Puniyad, it has not been taken outside the old and present premises. In Samvat 1939, when Jagannath Maharaj held the Shambhu Mela, this text was brought to Puniyad.

In addition, there is a tulsi (holy basil) rosary; Jivanji Maharaj used to offer prasad to the Lord (Bhagwan) using this rosary. Thus there are three sacred, worship-worthy objects at this place, and it was in this way that the worship of the gadi-asan began at Puniyad. Later, this practice was followed elsewhere in the community too, where gadi-asans were made and worshipped — at Surat (Begampura-Khangadsheri), Hansapura (now Bodeli), Darapura (now Vadi Vayadapol, Vadodara), Falu (Taluka Vijapur), Mumbai, and other places. At all these gadi locations of the community, handwritten books were kept on display for darshan (veneration). But this priceless and venerable literature has now been lost from all these places. Besides the asan-gadi at Puniyad, more than five hundred (500) ancient handwritten works are preserved in the Shri Ram Library.

One of the principal disciples of Kabirji was Padmanabh, who lived in Patan, Gujarat. He was born into the Prajapati caste, but being influenced by Kabirji's teachings, he went to Kashi (Varanasi) and took initiation (diksha) from him. On his Guru's instruction, Padmanabh returned to Patan and settled there. Padmanabh was born in Patan on Thursday, Chaitra Sud 5, Vikram Samvat 1458.

His father's name was Karan, and his mother's name was Lakshmana; they were householders (grihasthi). His wife's name was Patal Devi. Padmanabh was a very influential person. Seeing his stature, Dhanraj Pandya, the minister (pradhan) of the Patan kingdom at that time, was impressed by him and became his disciple. Later, the Guru and disciple together spread the Ramkabir tradition in Patan and kindled the Kabir school of thought. Because of this, the Suba (governor) Saravarkhar gifted Padmanabh 10 vighas of land, and on that land Padmanabh, together with Dhanraj, established a vadi (garden compound) on Sunday, Kartak Sud 14, Samvat 1470. In Padmanabh's lineage, one high-caliber disciple followed another, and they spread the Kabir school of thought and the Ramkabir tradition widely across Saurashtra and North Gujarat. Padmanabhji does not belong to our own Guru lineage, but Gyaniji Maharaj and Padmanabhji were guru-brothers (disciples under the same guru-line), and both worked together with great cooperation to spread Kabirji's teachings in Gujarat. Jivanji Maharaj was influenced by Padmanabh. He recognized that Dhanraj Pandya's compositions were of high caliber, and had these verses (pado) used in our daily, social, and spiritual customs and rites.

At the Patan vadi, Kabirji's shrine (sthan) has been placed on the basis of the Guru lineage; and since we are followers of the very same Ramkabir tradition, Jivanji Maharaj's kyaro (memorial shrine) has been placed alongside Kabirji's kyaro. The well-known Gujarati writer Dr. Kabhikumar Bhadra wrote a very fine article titled "Kabir Shishya Padmanabhji" ("Padmanabhji, Disciple of Kabir") in the ninth issue of Jivanvani, Year 2, Magshar Sud, 2034. It is well worth reading for inquisitive devotees.

||Ramkabir||

||Prem-Bhakti-Prakash|| (Love, Devotion, Light)

_Jaise jaladhar unyo, badhat papaiya pyaas ||_
_Aise harijan aaye Jeevana, prem bhakti prakaash ||1||_
(As the rain-laden clouds swell, the papaiha bird's thirst grows all the more; so has the devotee of Hari come, O Jivan[ji] — the light of loving devotion.)

While engaged in discussion and satsang (holy discourse) with Guru Gopaldas, Jivanji Maharaj seeks to know the true nature (swarup) of Parbrahm (the Supreme Being). Gopaldasji explains the reconciliation (samanvay) of the formed (akar) and the formless (nirakar). Further explaining the nature of Parbrahm, he goes on to say that the truly real is the charming, flute-playing God (Morli Manohar Parmeshwar), whose names are Ram and Krishna. Finally, explaining the nature of Parbrahm in depth to Jivanji Maharaj, he says that the Word itself is God.

Only the Guru can grant the vision (darshan) of Parbrahm, but this darshan does not depend on any form or body — for whatever body or form takes birth is perishable, bound to be destroyed. But Parbrahm should be known only through name, or through words, for that alone is imperishable. Showing the way to reach the true nature of Parbrahm, Jivanji Maharaj explains it thus: just as, on seeing water-laden clouds grown wild with the urge to rain, the chatak bird's thirst to drink the cloud's water grows intense — in the very same way, devotees, through the flow of love-formed devotion (bhakti), can attain the radiant Brahm.

Love is of the nature of a flow (pravah). Just as water remains level and uniform at its surface — never more in one place and less in another, however high or low the ground beneath may be — water preserves equality at its upper surface, so too there can be no distinction among devotees; and only such devotees, free of distinction, can truly practise devotion. This is why love has been likened to the nature of water, and devotion (bhakti) to the nature of a bird — and it is only through the means of devotion that Parbrahm, who shines as radiantly as crores of suns, is to be attained. Thus it is only through the Guru's words — that is, through his Word — that He is to be known. This is why Jivanji Maharaj says: the Word itself is God.

Harisharan Jagmohanbhai writes about Shahpura —

_Sadguru vase tya(n) vase ek gam,_
_prem bhaktinu(n) Shahpura dham. ||_
(Wherever the Sadguru resides, that alone is a true village — Shahpura is the abode of love and devotion.)

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, the founder of Uda Dharma, is spoken of thus —

_Gurjar gira pavan kari, dhan Jeevan avatar._
_Apang pret kaink uddharya, krupanath kirtar. ||_
(He sanctified the Gujarati tongue — blessed is Jivan's incarnation. He redeemed many crippled and wretched souls — the compassionate Lord and Creator.)

Along with Mota Gopaldas of the saintly devotee family of Malwa, Khediya, Gopaldas of Chandoriya, Santdas, and Ramdas and Kalyandas of Devshahi, [Jivanji Maharaj] arrived at the festival (ochhav) at Samiyala. At this festival, Nana Gopaldas came from Dhanyavi, bringing Haribhai along with him. When they arrived, they beheld a vision of the state of separation (viraha) within loving devotion. Nana Gopaldasji reminded them of the remembrance of Namdev and Kabir. Prostrating in full reverence (sashtang pranam), Haribhai expressed his wish to take refuge in the Sadguru. Seeing the loving devotion in Haribhai's heart, he said:

_Nadiya jari koila bhai, samundar lagi aagi._
_Machhi taravar chadhi gayi, uth Kabira jaagi. ||_
(The river has burned down to charcoal, and a fire has broken out in the ocean; the fish has climbed up a tree — awaken, O Kabir, wake up!)

The water of sensual craving in the river of the senses has burned away. The "fire in the ocean" means: so that one is not scorched by worldly existence — O mind, remain in the shelter of the saint, the greatest deliverer. O great soul dwelling within this body, awaken now; give up the sleep that is delusion.

Sadguru Jivanji and the saintly families arrived together with Nana Gopal and Haribhai. All of them resolved to live their lives relying on Sadguru Jivanji alone, and to practise single-minded (ananya) devotion — leaving behind the path of ritual works: austerities (tap), pilgrimage (tirath), charity (dan), vows (vrat), ritual offerings (ardhya), scriptural study (adhyayan), fire-sacrifice (hom), ancestor rites (kanagat), household duties (kutumb), planet-pacifying rites (grahashanti), and the fire-witnessed rites of the wedding ceremony — and to remain uda (detached, beyond these). The sunrise of a new life came about in the newly settled village where Sadguru Jivanji, possessed of the full glory of the sixteen attributes (sol kala), resides, and where satsang with saints takes place day and night. This beautiful, delightful place is presently on the bank of the sacred river Dhadhar, about 20 km from Vadodara. It is heard from the elders there that this was the site of the samadhi-shrine (kyaro) of Mota Gopaldas, a saint-companion (satsangi) of Sadguru Jivanji. On the Sharad Purnima festival night of Ashwin month, Samvat 2038, on the initiative of Swami Jagdishchandra, the shrine was re-established, and the gathering (mijlas) of saints present was sanctified by the occasion.

At present, there is a beautiful garden-retreat named Sant Kutir on the bank of the Dhadhar, belonging to the family of devotee Buddhisagar Bhaijibhai, where invited saints are hosted and served.

It was at Shahpura that Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj held satsang (samagam), and it was from there that he established the Uda Dharma.

Harishran Jagmohanbhai writes about Puniyad:

_Mathura chhodi Shyam aaviya, haanre ene vaas kidho Puniyad dhaamma_ (Leaving Mathura, Shyam [Krishna] came and made his home in the divine abode of Puniyad.)

Shri Dham Puniyad is the place where all the saints abide in the abode of happiness, and where Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj is seated. O Lord of Grace, you have come to lift souls out of the ocean of worldly existence (bhavsagar).

Puniyad is located in Vadodara district, 2 km from Bamangam on National Highway 8 out of Por. Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj came from Shahpura and settled in Puniyad, and an account of this is known through oral tradition. As Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj was travelling with his company of saints, singing the praises of Hari, they arrived at Puniyad, where a well was being dug. Jivanji Maharaj saw this and fell into thought; he told the well-diggers to come out at once, for through his foresight he had seen that the well was about to collapse. By the power of his word, no sooner had the labourers climbed out than the well caved in with a crash.

As this news spread through the village, the village elders and leaders came, and they were filled with reverence for the saints. They made this request to Jivanji Maharaj: "See how you have saved us from being buried in the well - so stay here and save us from the well of worldly existence (bhavkoop) too. Holy company (satsang) is the root of all good fortune - that is our heartfelt wish," they said. "Maharaj, we have heard that the dry peepal tree of Dhanora turned green, and we were coming to have your darshan (sacred sight). We have also learned, O Maharaj, that it is true you gave new life to Harmabai, who was disabled from birth, and removed her disability. Harmabai has resolved in mind, deed, and word to wed herself to you, and you graciously accepted, saying that at present you hold the state of a sadhu (renunciate) and must go on pilgrimage, but that in future you would fulfil her wish - this promise you gave. If this is true, then knowing our wish, accept what is in our hearts. It is our wish that you, together with Harmaba and the saints, come and settle in our village."

Sadguru Jivandas said, "As the merciful Lord wills. When we return from pilgrimage we will try to fulfil your wish. There must be some unfinished bond (lenden) between us and this land." Signs from beyond (agam) were felt that in time to come, so that the devotional longing of the saints might be fulfilled, this sacred land would become an abode of devotion (bhaktidham). Saying "Ramkabir" to all, they then set out from there on pilgrimage.

Whatever the feelings in Harmaba's heart, and whatever reverence the villagers held for Sadguru Jivanji, it is recorded in the genealogist's (vahivancha) register that in Samvat 1730 Jivanji settled in Puniyad. Puna means "again" and yaad means "remembrance" - such may be the meaning of the name Puniyad: just as, on the peak of Kaleshwar (Kailash), the kunj bird never forgets to care for its young, so too, as if a remembrance came to him of caring for his own children (baalgopal, his devotees), he settled in Puniyad, and toward the end declared:

_Tahaan Ayodhya jahaan Raghupati, Kahanad tahaan Gokul gaam, Saptapuri tahaan Jeevana, jahaan santsangat Harinaam._ (Wherever Raghupati [Ram] is, there is Ayodhya; wherever Kahan [Krishna] is, there is the village of Gokul; wherever Jeevana [Jivanji] is, there is one of the seven sacred cities [Saptapuri] - wherever the company of saints chants the name of Hari.)

Hearing such words from his own devotees, he agreed to keep the garden (vaadi) of Puniyad. Until now, eleven generations of Jivanji Maharaj's lineage have held this seat (gadi). In Puniyad, the abode of loving devotion, worship of the seat (gadi puja) is performed in his own temple. On the seat, the relic of Jivanji Maharaj's presence (samagam), Jivanji Maharaj's own prayer beads (mala), and the quilt (godadi) that Jivanji Maharaj used when he appeared in the form of Narsinhdas at the time of Narsinhdas's calamity and cured the Suba's leprosy, are all worshipped.

This is the original seat (mool gadi) of the Uda devotees, established through Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj.

Harishran Jagmohanbhai writes about Dhanora: Harma Ba's Deliverance.

_Dhanora gaame sarovar paal, sooko peepal leelo thaay, Ratansingh mukhi-nu naam, apang Harmaabaanaa thaay kaam, Sooku sarovar jal bharyu, apangpanu to sahaje talyu._ (In the village of Dhanora, by the lake's bank, the dry peepal tree turned green; through the name of Ratansinh the headman (mukhi), the deed was done for the disabled Harmaba; the dry lake filled with water, and her disability was easily removed.)

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, together with his company of saints, was going to the abode of his own Sadguru Gopalji on the occasion of the Sharad Nisha (autumn full-moon night) festival. It was afternoon, and the heat of the Otara-Chitra season was blazing. The saints were drenched in sweat. The devotee-saints Santdas, Gopaldas, Devdas, and Ramdas walked along, singing kirtan (hymns) of Hari and the praises of Ram. Before reaching Choranda, everyone silently wished in their hearts to rest for a short while. But who would say so aloud? Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, knowing everyone's mind, said, "Santdas, if it is the wish of the saintly devotees, let us settle here on the bank of this lake." Gopalji of Chanderiya thought: since this thought has come to the Sadguru's mind, surely the fortune of this land is about to awaken. As the Sadguru wishes! But while spreading a seat for the Sadguru, it was noticed that the peepal tree was dry and gave no shade.

If they had sat in the shade, the mind would have found ease. Santdas said, "One who has the shade of Sadguru Jivanji - what further need has he of any other shade?" Devidas said, "We are truly most fortunate to have received the good fortune of living in the Sadguru's shade." Rupa Bhagat said - _Taruvar sarvar sant jan, chautha varse maih, Parmarath ke kaarane, chaaro dhariya deh_ (Trees, lakes, saints, and, fourth, the rain-cloud - these four have taken bodily form for the sake of others' welfare). Nana Gopal said, "Your sakhi (couplet) is true, but here the opposite seems to be the case." Santdas said, "How does it seem opposite?" Nana Gopal said, "A tree should be green, but this peepal is utterly dry; if it were green and leafy it would give good shade, and if the lake were full of water, people and animals could quench their thirst. Yet here, even though the monsoon has passed, the peepal stays dry and the lake is empty. Now, explain that!" A doubt lingered in Devidas's mind, so he said to Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, "O Bapji, how could this be? Someone will surely say, what kind of company of saints is this, sitting under a tree with no shade, settling by a lake with no water!"

As this conversation was going on, four men arrived carrying axes and said, "O sadhus and saints, we must cut down this peepal. Ratansinh the mukhi (headman) has sent us for it. By evening the mukhi will ask us about the work, so let us do it - please move your camp from here." Sadguru Jivandasji Maharaj said, "Brothers, in the Gita the Lord says, 'Among trees, I am the peepal tree' - therefore the peepal is sacred and must not be cut." The leader of the labourers said, "Maharaj, that would be right if the peepal were green. But here the peepal is dry." Just then the eyes of Santdas and Devidas moved over the tree, and they saw green shoots sprouting on the upper branches. They said, "If the peepal is green, then surely it must not be cut, brother." The leader of the labourers said, "Yes, a green peepal should not be cut, but this one has stayed dry through the whole monsoon." Santdas said, "Brother, just look up for a moment." Hearing this, everyone looked up at the branches and saw the shoots that had sprouted. The poor labourers fell into confusion, not knowing what answer to give now, for they were bound by their own word to the saints that a green peepal must not be cut.

The foreman (mukadam) said, "The whole village knows the lake's peepal is dry - you are being lazy in your work. So let me go and tell the mukhi that the peepal is green and that the Maharaj of this company of saints refuses to let it be cut. Let the mukhi come and do as he wishes - our task is done." He said to Jivanji Maharaj, "Bapji, please wait a while - I must go and tell the mukhi why the peepal has not been cut." Jivanji Maharaj said, "As the merciful Lord wills."

Reaching Ratansinh's house, the labourers' foreman began, "Bapu, we labourers went to the outskirts (bhagol) to cut down the dry peepal." The mukhi said, "Yes - have you cut it and stacked the logs properly so they don't scatter?" The foreman said, "No, Bapu." The mukhi said, "Then why have you come here?" The foreman said, "Bapu, when we went to cut it, a company of saints had settled there to rest. When we asked them to move away, their mahant (leader) said that according to dharma a peepal must not be cut." The mukhi said, "Yes, according to dharma a green peepal is not cut - but this one was dry, so you should have said it may be cut." "Bapu, we said just that: if it were green it should not be cut, but since it is dry, Mukhi Bapu has ordered it cut. Then what was the problem, you ask? Bapu, while we were saying this, one of the men in their company said the upper branch showed green shoots, and when we all looked, we truly saw green shoots on the upper branch. Then the mahant said, 'Now, being green, the peepal must not be cut, according to dharma.' We said, wait, let us go and tell Mukhi Bapu - they agreed to do as told." The mukhi said, "Can such a thing be? The whole village knows the peepal has dried up." The foreman said, "Bapu, see it with your own eyes and tell us, and we will do as you say." The mukhi said, "This just doesn't sink into my head. Go, tell two or four of the village leaders that they are to come with the mukhi to the outskirts."

The foreman went off, and the mukhi, putting on his coat (dagalo) and tying a turban (moryu) on his head, turned toward the house and said, "Listen, I am going to the outskirts for a while - I just cannot understand how a dry peepal could turn green." His wife said, "What did you say - the lake's peepal at the outskirts has turned green? That cannot be, what are you saying?" In the house their daughter Harma was listening to this. Harma had been disabled from birth; the mukhi had tried much medicine and treatment, as well as charms and threads (dora dhaga), but nothing had helped. Harma said, "Where have Father and Mother gone, what were they saying?" Her mother told her that a company of saints was seated under the dry peepal, and that the peepal had turned green. "Oh Mother! Please take me for their darshan - may my suffering be removed through the saints." Her mother said, "Child, when your father returns I will speak to him. If it is God's will, good things will happen."

Meanwhile the mukhi sent word to the other leaders to come with him to the outskirts. They said, "Now why should we go there?" The foreman explained that the peepal on the lake's bank had turned green, with shoots sprouting on its branch. They said, "What, can such a thing be? Come, we are coming." This news passed from ear to ear through the village of Dhanora, and the villagers gathered at the outskirts to see this wonder. They saw the saints singing the praises of Hari, and shoots visible on the topmost branch of the peepal.

People began saying among themselves, "Believe it or not, these are true saints." Someone said, "No, no - this Bapji is a worker of miracles. We should ask him why water does not stay in our lake - if the lake held water, cattle and livestock would all have the comfort of it. This is like the Ganga arriving at our very doorstep - why go elsewhere to wash our hands?" Someone said, "There is a great sorrow right in Mukhi Baba's own household - Harma is disabled, we should ask for a remedy so her disability may go." Another said, "Don't be so eager - if Mukhi Baba wants to ask, let him; what is it to us?" A third said, "Stop your cleverness, listen to what Mukhi Bapa has to say." Putting the mukhi in front, the crowd of villagers went to the outskirts; a great flood of people, young and old, had surged there. The mukhi and the leaders signalled the crowd to stand back, and they themselves reached the bank of the lake where the company of saints was seated.

Seeing Jivanji, they said, "Jai, jai, Bapji." Jivanji said, "Tell me, why have you come?" The mukhi said, "This peepal was dry." Jivanji said, "Yes, the peepal was dry." The mukhi said, "Bapji, now green shoots have sprouted on top." Jivanji said, "Yes, green shoots have sprouted on top." The mukhi said, "Bapji, how did this happen?" Jivanji said, "By the grace of the saints the peepal has turned green. It had dried up, and water does not stay in this lake either - is that not so?" The mukhi said, "Bapji, we were about to ask why water does not stay in the lake." Jivanji said, "Because of the bones of an ungrateful person (kritaghni), this peepal had dried up and the lake does not hold water." The mukhi said, "Bapji, the peepal has indeed turned green - but if you would do something so that water remains in this lake, the suffering of the people and animals of the village would be removed." Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj said, "Santdas, go into the lake, remember the saints, and lift up one clod of earth - go, by the grace of the saints, water will appear in the lake."

_Kritaghni ke haadsu peepal sooko en, Kunwaari ko doshan lago, kahi samjhaave chen._ (Because of an ungrateful one's bones this peepal had dried up; a maiden's fault had attached to it [unclear] - so he explained, setting their minds at ease.)

Taking the Sadguru's command upon his head, Santdas went, saying, "Wah Guru, your glory is boundless - you made the peepal green, now let us see the grace of the merciful Lord." Coming to the middle of the lake, he looked toward the Sadguru; the Sadguru's eyes were smiling. It occurred to Santdas that the Sadguru's divine play (leela) is boundless. Remembering the Sadguru, he lifted the clod of earth - and behold, a spring burst forth like a small stream! "Wah Guru, wah Sadguru!" Standing there he called out, "Say, victory to Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj!" - declaring it was as if Mother Yamuna herself had appeared. Everyone's eyes saw the spring of water; the saints of the company called out, "Victory to Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj! Victory to Baba Namdev Kabir!" The whole gathering took up this cry of victory, and the Sadguru's triumph resounded there.

Ratansinh the mukhi and the village folk, young and old, seeing this grace, felt themselves blessed and fulfilled. The mukhi said, "Bapji, please come into the village." Jivanji Maharaj said, "We must reach our Guru's abode, so we are in haste." Ratansinh's wife sent word to the mukhi to speak about their Harma. The mukhi remembered his daughter's suffering, told Jivanji Maharaj about Harma, and sent two people to bring her there. Joy filled Harma's heart - the peepal had turned green, the lake had filled with water. "If even lifeless things received new life through Jivanji's sacred footsteps, then I, who am a living, conscious being - my disability will surely, surely go." Those who had come seated Harma on a cot and carried her along.

Thoughts moved in Harma's mind: her body's disability would be removed - not by a physician's medicine - and her body would be freed from lying always in one place; her frame would move about freely. The wise say that to remove the disability of the mind, the darshan of the Sadguru and holy company (satsang) are necessary. "My fortune will awaken, my life will be set right" - such a wheel of thought kept turning, and then she saw the gathered crowd and the company of saints seated, singing the praises of Hari. Harmaba said, "Wah! In the company of saints everyone sings Hari's name; in this world the mind runs about in the chase of 'mine and yours,' but for a moment here it comes to rest in the remembrance and kirtan of Hari. Your darshan is purifying." The people made way for the cot carried like a palanquin. As Harma's eyes fell upon the company of saints, memories of a previous birth began to surface from her unconscious mind. It seemed to her that she had had this darshan before, though her memory could not fully support it - she could not quite recall it. It came to her like the memory of Kubja, who was with the child-cowherds (baalgopal) when Krishna went to Mathura at the time of the slaying of Kansa.

The eyes of Santdas, Gopaldas, and Devdas turned toward Sadguru Jivanji - how would the nectar-stream of compassion flow from this ocean of compassion? Seeing Harma's condition, they said inwardly, "Your suffering will go, and through the Sadguru's darshan happiness will come; now the glory of the gracious Ramji will resound throughout your life." Sadguru Jivandas said, "Santdas, bring water from the lake." Santdas went to fetch it. Sadguru Jivandas then told the story of Shabari: every day, before the sages went for their morning bath, Shabari would clear away thorns and pebbles from the path leading from Sage Matang's ashram to Pampa lake, keeping it free of thorns. This Shabari was a Bhil (tribal) princess who, distressed by the violence [animal slaughter] that would take place at her wedding, left her family and lived in Sage Matang's ashram. Because of this, the sages, using the entry of an 'untouchable' girl into the ashram as a pretext, kept Sage Matang apart from all of them, claiming that his body had made the water of Pampa lake impure; but Sage Matang declared the remedy - that it would be purified by the touch of Shabari's feet.

_Adhik badhaavat aapse, jan mahima Raghuveer, Sabari pad raj pasarte, shuddh thayo salila neer._ (Raghuveer [Ram] raises the glory of his devotee even higher than his own; when the dust of Shabari's feet spread there, the water became pure.)

Santdas came and handed the water-pot (kamandal) to Sadguru Jivan. Calling out "Victory to Namdev Kabir," he sprinkled the water from the kamandal on Harma and gave her some to drink, and by this Harma's disability was removed. Gopaldas called out, "Victory to Sadguru Jivanji!" and the crowd gave a joyous response. (It occurred to Ratansinh the mukhi to give Harma into Jivanji's service, and he consulted the other village elders about this.)

Feeling her disability lifted from her body, Harma stood up and, prostrating full-length (sashtang dandvat) before Sadguru Jivanji, said, "I am the maidservant of your feet - grant me your service birth after birth. O Sadguru, remove the hardship of all my lives to come." Harma said, "I have already wedded myself to you in mind, deed, and word - fulfil the longing of all my lives," and she spoke this sakhi (couplet):

_Harmaabaai harakhiyaan Jeevan darshan paay, Sharir saanso metiyo, bhayo gyaan prakaash. Gyaan prakaashi guru milaa, so kyon bisari jaay, Jab Govind krupa karai, tab guru miliya aay._ (Harmabai rejoiced upon receiving the darshan of Jivan; the anguish of the body was erased, and the light of knowledge dawned. Having found a guru who illumines knowledge, how could he ever be forgotten? Only when Govind [God] bestows his grace does one come to find the guru.)

Hearing this sakhi, Jivanji was pleased and said, "This woman is full of devotion. The merciful Lord will fulfil your longing." Harma said, "Lord, I have wedded myself to you in mind and word - accept me. Know me as the maidservant of your feet and grant me service at your feet."

Jivanji said, "We are a sadhu (renunciate) and cannot accept you. Besides, we are going on pilgrimage to Jagannath and Badrinath." Harmaba said - _Tumku chhaand avar kahaan jaau, nishdin tumaari sang rahaau_ (Leaving you, where else could I go? Day and night I would remain with you).

It occurred to Ratansinh the mukhi that this Harma had received new life through Jivanji's grace: "If this is her wish, we should consult the elders and consider it. Among us Rajputs there is a custom of regarding a daughter as unlucky and putting her to death by drowning in milk (a form of female infanticide), yet even though she was disabled from birth, such a thought never once arose in my mind regarding her. On the contrary, seeing her, I always felt she was a gift of God (Paramatma) - perhaps God gave her to me to be served, since being disabled she could not be joined in marriage to anyone in society. So why should I not gladly serve her, being pleased with God's will? My heart tells me this Harma is a trust (amaanat) placed by God - why should this divine trust not be entrusted to this saint, who is the very form of God!" The village leaders also thought, "Blessed is this - Ratansinh's daughter was disabled from birth, yet he never did anything to hurt Harma's heart. Today his heart is set on entrusting her to this saint - why should we refuse? His yes is our yes as well."

After deliberating, they all began to insist and plead with Jivanji to accept Harma. Jivanji looked within (antardarshan), and the future Uda community became visible to him. He said, "We will accept her when we return from pilgrimage." It occurred to Santdas, Gopaldas, Devdas, and Ramdas: rather than wandering about in the company of saints like this, if their family and community had one settled place, they could enjoy the benefit of the Sadguru's company day and night. "Wah Guru, wah Sadguru, your divine play is boundless."

sections.title_en: Religious practices of the Uda faith
sections.translation:
Religious practices of the Uda faith

The Uda sect is a community of followers established by Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj (1649–1737). A saying current among the people, taken as the sure mark of an Uda devotee, is "Uda is different from all" (Uda sabse juda). The conduct of the Uda faith differs from that of followers of Hinduism in many social customs and religious rites. It opposes scriptures such as the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Puranas on doctrinal grounds. Its followers do not perform Vedic rituals. This shows itself at the occasions of birth, marriage, and death, where Uda devotees are distinct. The rites of birth are performed without the presence of a priest who would otherwise conduct such rituals. After a child's birth, initiation with the sacred neck-thread (kanthi diksha) is given by a devotee at the guru's seat or a partharu shrine, at one and a quarter months of age or even before. At that time a gathering of men and women is present. A hymn of the Parbrahma-vani (the utterances of the Supreme Being) is sung. A tilak of gopi-chandan clay is applied and the mark of a Vaishnav devotee is given. Tying the tulsi-wood neck-thread, refuge in Shri Hari is bestowed. Sweet prasad (sukhadi) is distributed.

At a wedding, the filling of the gotraj (clan-deity vessel), the installation and worship of the family goddess (kuldevi), and the installation of Ganesh are not done. Instead, the guru is ceremonially received and installed. When the guru arrives for this occasion, he is welcomed at the edge of the village with a procession and brought to the wedding pavilion while dhol-mangal (auspicious songs) are sung. When the turmeric paste (pithi) is applied, the couple first bow to the guru in reverence, and instead of kumkum, saffron is sprinkled while the wedding-invitation hymn (kankotri) is sung. A hymn in praise of the glory of Braj is recited. As the applying of turmeric paste begins, a hymn of the Parbrahma-vani is sung. Bawdy wedding songs (fatana) are not sung in the wedding pavilion; instead, hymns composed by saint-poets of the bhakti tradition on the occasion of the marriage of Ram and Krishna are sung. In the wedding procession, instead of a band, cymbals (kansi) and mridang drums accompany the singing of dhol-mangal, while the women sing the hymn of Raghunathji's little horse (ghodli), a hymn describing the wedding procession of Ramchandraji. In the wedding pavilion, the hymn of Sitaji's sohaila (bridal joy-song) is sung. There is no structure representing the traditional wedding canopy (chori); instead, the devotees of the congregation recite and respond to the saint's sohaga hymn (bridal blessing-song). The customs of the antarpat (screen held between bride and groom), the feeding of kansar (sweet wheat dish), and the pressing of the toe (vinchhi dabvani) are kept. The pole-star (Dhruva) is not shown to the couple as in the Hindu rite; instead, at the verse describing the vision of the Supreme Being who granted Dhruva his unshakable position, the bride and groom rise. There is no dowry or bride-price of trousseau-giving. Bawdy songs are not sung in the wedding pavilion; rather, at the time of the marriage rite, the whole assembled congregation listens with single-minded attention to the saint's sohaga hymn sung by the officiant (gor). At this time no other noise of any kind is made, and if any occurs, it is stopped.

When the wedding party (jaan) comes to dine, the women of the party arrive singing the dhol song of Kanaiyaji's aarti. When the bride and groom rise after being married, hymns of devotional feeling are likewise recited.

Death rites — in this respect this sect stands apart even more from the rest of Hindu society. At the final moment of a dying soul, instead of wailing, the hymn of the lodhi-karaj (funeral rite) is recited to them. The body of the deceased is bathed, dressed in new clothes, marked with tilak and given the tulsi neck-mark, seated in a cross-legged posture with the two palms cupped together, and a coconut placed in them. However, keeping a coconut in the hands is not proper; it is proper instead to keep tulsi leaves in the hand. All who come on this occasion offer flowers and bow, saying "Ramkabir." But offering flowers is not necessary — it is enough and proper simply to bow saying "Ramkabir." The men and women present recite devotional bhajans and read scripture (parayan). Women do not sing dirge-like laments (marsiya); but the fact that some women nowadays do sing such songs is entirely improper.

The men perform kirtan with cymbals and mridang drums. For the funeral procession, the body is placed on a bier (sandhasan, a palanquin) decorated with flowers. The men, singing kirtan with cymbals and mridang, arrange the body on the pyre, and the guruji or a devotee of the partharu shrine places tulsi leaves in its mouth. When the fire is lit from the side, the men present recite the kadva hymn (a verse for the occasion). After the hymn is finished, they go to the house of the deceased and perform Hari-kirtan, then take sukhadi prasad and a meal offering before dispersing. Death is called "taking refuge in Hari" (Harisharan). At the house of the deceased, scripture-reading (parayan) and Hari-kirtan are performed nightly for a set period. No rites of sutak (ritual pollution), kaan (mourning period), the twelfth-day or thirteenth-day rites, or shravani are performed.

sections.title_translit: Sadguru Jivandasji Maharajni Punya Sthalio Vishe Sankshipt Parichay
sections.title_en: A brief introduction to the sacred places of Sadguru Jivandasji Maharaj
sections.translation:
Ramkabir

A brief introduction to the sacred places of Sadguru Jivandasji Maharaj

The places on earth where holy souls have wandered become joyous through the blessed presence of these great beings. The air is fragrant with the resonance of the holy one's words. An atmosphere polluted by worldly attachment and aversion becomes fragrant instead with love, goodwill, knowledge, and devotion. The experience of this fragrance goes on stirring every particle for a long time afterward. A visit (darshan) to these places is purifying. It awakens in the visitor a sense of wonder: "My Beloved dwelt right here." It shakes one's own unconsciousness awake and inspires the awakened consciousness to walk the path of the divine.

Divine souls keep coming into the world for the welfare of people. Their arrival happens when the smoke of attachment and aversion thickens, when people abandon the way of even-sightedness and, acting out of self-interest, do things they should not do, building up this world while forgetting the world to come.

These sacred places are like lamps that give true guidance to travellers wandering in darkness.

_Dhan dhan re Jamuna tat, dhan Vrajno re vaas. Param bhagya aa bhumina, vahalo ramiya chhe raas._ (Blessed, blessed is the bank of the Yamuna, blessed is the abode of Vraj — supremely fortunate is this land, for the Beloved played the raas dance here.)

Narsinh Mehta praises such a land in this way.

Let us now become acquainted with the sacred places of the Uda faith, and let us feel fulfilled through the experience of their darshan.

Vrindavan

_Taako hai Vrindavan vaasa, jaako hai Jagjivan naama._ (His abode is in Vrindavan — he whose name is Jagjivan.) — from Gyan Mahima

The abode of this Supreme Being, the Paramatma, is in Vrindavan… whose name is Jagjivan.

In the supreme abode of Vrindavan, at the old Bansivat (the Banyan of the flute), Jivandasji Maharaj was present with Lord Krishna in the chhakalila (divine play). There are images of the acharyas of the bhakti tradition there. Among them is an image of Jivandas alongside Kabirji. At the site of the old Bansivat of Vrindavan there are two trees in the courtyard of the Bansivat. One of these trees is the dadhi-lata (curd-vine); if its leaves are dipped in milk, the milk turns into curd. In front of the platform of that tree, in an enclosure, are small images of the sixteen acharyas of the bhakti tradition:

(1) Jivanji Maharaj. When I went there in Samvat 2060, the Sikh visitors thought this image resembled Guru Nanak, and so they had five or six images of their own placed in that enclosure; but when I went there again, these images had been removed. (2) Kabirji. (3) Lalji (belongs to the Vallabhacharya family lineage) — the Punjabi people hold him in particular regard, and his following is greater toward Haryana. (4) Vitthalji (belongs to the Banke Bihari, Haridasji tradition). (5) Harivanshji (fifth, in the Radhavallabhi tradition). (6) Charandasji (Shuk tradition). (7) Manmohanji (of the Vyas family, was a disciple of Harirama Vyas at the court of the king of Orchha). (8) Madhu Pandit (Gaudiya tradition). (9) Shri Bhatji (Nimbarka tradition). (10) Mangal Bihariji (Sant Gyaneshwari tradition). (11) Vallabhji (Vallabhacharya). (12) Govinddas (Nimbarka tradition). (13) Bihari Sharan Devacharya (Nimbarka tradition — given special prominence in Vrindavan). (14) Vitthal Vipul Devacharyaji (Shuk tradition — he had no arm at all, so his image appears to have a broken arm; for this reason, in the temple of Banke Bihariji that stands in Vrindavan today, the bell is not rung, because Vitthal Vipul Devacharya had no arm — and even today no bell is rung in that temple). (15) The arm of Surdasji's image was broken when a monkey got into it (he belonged within the Vallabha tradition). (16) There is no ninth image in between — that one, of Narsinh Mehta, broke in Samvat 2030 or 2032.

_Mathura maahlo desh, Kathiyavaade kutamb vase. Aayo Gurjar khand, santo tane melavade._ ||1|| Doho (My country was Mathura, my family dwelt in Kathiawad. I have come to the Gujarat region for the gathering of the saints.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: in an earlier age, in the Krishna avatar, my country, my native land, was Mathura, and my family was in Dwarka in Kathiawad. But in this avatar I have come to the Kanam region of Gurjarkhand (Gujarat) for the darshan of saints.

In Samvat 1687, when a famine occurred, on the tenth day of the bright half of Aso...

Jivanji Maharaj went to meet Guru Gopaldasji. From there he went to Vrindavan and other places. It is written on page 412 of the genealogist's (vahivancha) ledger that Jivanji Maharaj held a feast (bhandaro) for the six schools of philosophy (shat-darshan) in Vrindavan, at the village of Puniyad, and also held a feast at the Galta seat in the village of Jaipur, and had a cow-shelter (goshala) built for his own bard (barot), giving woollen cloth (banat) worth 125 rupees in Samvat 1735. Thus Jivanji Maharaj went to Vrindavan twice.

Patan

_Patan padyo avatro, je Gokulno Kahaan. Sukhsagar sada Jivana, je diyo Sudama daan._ ||22|| Naamrup (He who was Kahaan [Krishna] of Gokul has taken avatar in Patan — he, Jivana, is forever an ocean of joy, who gave the gift [of devotion] to Sudama.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that the same Lord who was Bhagwan Krishna in Gokul has taken avatar in Patan as Bhagwan Padmanabh. He is forever the giver of the greatest joy. The same wealth of happiness that he gave to Sudama, he granted as the wealth of devotion to the one who was born as Sudama in the form of Adhyaruji.

_Krishna Kabiro avatarya, bhagat het Bharvaad. E jugal jodi bhaj Jivana, je Padmanabh avatar._ ||21|| Naamrup (Krishna and Kabir took avatar out of love for their devotees — Krishna as a Bharvaad [herdsman] and Kabir [Gopal] as a lovely maiden. Worship, O Jivana, that paired couple [of guru and disciple] who, at the time of the avatar of Padmanabh, had taken birth again as guru and disciple.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that for the welfare of devotees, Krishna took avatar as a Bharvaad (cowherd) and Kabir (Gopal) as a maiden; worship that paired bond of guru and disciple, who had taken avatar as guru and disciple at the time of the Padmanabh avatar.

In Vrindavan, during the childhood sport (baal-lila), when the companion boys of Vraj crowned Krishna king in play, Shiva went there and gave his blessing. On that occasion the Lord asked Radhaji for a necklace to give as a gift to Shiva, but Shiva would not accept a necklace made of pearls obtained through violence to a living creature. So Radhaji obtained a pearl from the waters of the Yamuna, other pearls were made from it, and the necklace was given to Shiva from these. At that time Kalahansa, the daughter of Bhoja Gurjar, stole three pearls from among those pearls. For this she was cursed to be born in the womb of a tree. That Kalahansa was the tamarind tree that grew in Patan. To redeem her, Jivanji Maharaj came to Patan indirectly for this purpose; therefore, in the Patan-vaadi (garden), next to Kabirji's tulsi planter, stands the tulsi planter of Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, in this same Patan garden. In this way Jivanji Maharaj brought about Kalahansa's redemption.

Adhyaruji Maharaj, having taken initiation from Bhagwan Padmanabh, composed twenty-eight kirtans. Jivanji brought us the devotion of these kirtans and gave it to us; therefore it is said:

_Patan aambo moriyo, zhintyo Zalawaad. Fal laagya chhe Malve, vedyo chhe Gujarat._ (The mango tree blossomed in Patan, was tended in Zalawad; its fruit grew in Malwa, and Gujarat had the good fortune to harvest it.)

The mango tree of Krishna-bhakti — the mango tree in the form of Padmanabh — appeared in Patan; the care of its young orchard (vadoliyu) took place in Kathiawad, in Dwarka-Sudamapuri, that is, Porbandar. Its fruit grew in Malwa in the form of devotees like Mira, and in Gujarat came the good fortune of harvesting that fruit.

The mango tree of Patan was in the form of Padmanabh; its devotion, in the form of the orchard of the twenty-eight kirtans, was tended by Sudama in the form of Adhyaru of Kathiawad.

The devotion of those kirtans was spread by Jivanji in Malwa, and in Gujarat the community of devotees gathered and preserved it.

Kashi

_[unclear — source text corrupted]_ ||55||
_[unclear — source text corrupted]_ ||56||
(In Kashi you appeared in the guise of Kabir, and in Patan you were Shri Padmanabh; you are the one desired in the hearts of all saints.)

In Kashi, your (Jivanji-Krishna's) form was present as a shadow-form under the guise of Kabir, and in Patan you were Shri Padmanabh — you, the same Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, have appeared as the one dear to the minds of all saints. Thus all the saints have attained you, who are dear to the minds of all of them.

Jivanji Maharaj manifested in Kashi as Sadguru Kabir, and Jivanji Maharaj has affirmed Kabirji as Sadguru. In Patan, Kabirji was also the guru of Bhagwan Padmanabh. Thus the Lord manifested at one and the same time in two forms — as Kabir and as Padmanabh. The Lord's divine play (lila) is wondrous. At the churning of the ocean, the Lord took on three avatars simultaneously: in the form of Vishnu he wedded Lakshmi; in the form of Kurma (the tortoise) he held up the [unclear] mountain; in the form of Mohini he gave the nectar to the gods to drink. The importance of Kashi for Sadguru Kabirji is as the battlefield where he confronted the followers of the path of ritual works (karma-margis). It is the land of the Sadguru's manifestation.

In Ahmedabad, a clay tulsi-planter for Padmanabhji was built by Madhavrav, a descendant of [unclear] Bhagwan, on the bank of [unclear] lake. This planter was built because Madhavrav is a descendant of the Padmanabh lineage.

Jaisalmer

_[unclear — source text corrupted]_ ||123|| — Pravodh

Jivandasji Maharaj says that when the yogi Gorakhnath manifested as [unclear] in the region of Gujarat, the devotee Kabir showed him grace, gave him his blessing, granted him devotion to God, and thereby delivered him.

Gorakhnath went to Kabir to display the power of his eighty-four siddhis (occult powers), and, sitting atop his trident, began calling Kabir to come and converse with him. Then Kabir took one end of a ball of thread, kept it on the ground, threw the ball into the sky, and sat down upon its upper end, saying, "Come and sit facing me, then we shall talk." In this way Gorakh's pride was broken. He therefore went to Kabir's refuge and asked for devotion. Kabir said, "You have spent this incarnation chasing after siddhis (occult powers); therefore I shall give you devotion only in another incarnation." So this Gorakh took birth in Jaisalmer in a royal household, and his name was Chaturasingh.

Although Chaturasingh reached a marriageable age, he refused to marry. So, by persuading and coaxing him, they set about marrying him to a girl named Ganga, daughter of the king of Jodhpur; but he fled from the wedding canopy (chori) and, going to Jaipur, took initiation from Krishnadas Payahari, and performed austerities for fourteen years at Shulpaneshwar. Searching for him, four soldiers came bringing Gangaba (Ganga) along, and began entreating him to return. But Krishnadas Payahari had given this Chaturasingh the name "Gyani" (the wise one), and this Gyaniji gave the soldiers such teaching that all four of them became fakirs. One of these soldiers stayed at Bavaghor, where his grave is; the grave of another soldier is near Fatehpura in Vadodara. (That grave was destroyed in the communal riots of 2005 CE; it has since been rebuilt.) Thus Gyaniji set up a household with Gangaba; their samadhi (tomb-shrine) and descendants are alive today near Mota Sanja, Jhagadia. In this way, Jaisalmer, being the birthplace of Gyaniji Maharaj, is a sacred site as the birthplace of our guru.

It is written in the file of papers of Nazar's research — in the paper it is written — that the spring bearing Jivanji Maharaj's name, the living spring of water, is at Gyaniji's shrine (at Mota Sanja).

In Galta, in Rajasthan, is the gadi (spiritual seat) of the guru of the king of Jaisalmer. On that gadi came Khojiji, who was the guru of Gyaniji — he was Gyaniji's raj-guru (royal preceptor).

Once, while Khojiji was sitting to relieve himself, he saw a banyan seed being carried away and began to laugh, thinking: from this very seed a banyan tree could grow so vast that even great elephants could not pull it down, and yet here this seed is being swept away in the urine. Seeing Khojiji laughing, Gyaniji laughed too. Then Khojiji said: "Tell me the reason I laughed — whoever gives the true answer shall be guru to both you and me."

_[unclear — verse illegible in the source]_ (a couplet followed here in the source text, but it is too badly garbled to transliterate or translate reliably.)

Khojiji's mind became absorbed in contemplating the creative power hidden within a tiny banyan seed. But when he later met Sadguru Kabir, the doubt in his mind was resolved. Kabirji explained this mystery to Gyaniji at Kabirvad, in the manner described above. Therefore, as the seat of Khojiji — the raj-guru of Gyaniji — Galta too, being connected to the seat of our guru's lineage, is a holy place (punya sthali).

As disciples of Khojiji, there is the ashram of Narayan Maharaj situated in Jaipur. One branch of it exists in Dakor, known as the temple of the Jaipur people. The people at the Jaipur ashram regard Khojiji as their guru, and in Jaipur they have built a yajna-shala (hall for sacrificial rites), on whose walls Khojiji's sakhis (devotional couplets) are also inscribed; among these, the sakhis relating to ritual observances (karmakand) are spurious. I have heard that the Jaipur people have had Khojiji's sakhis printed, but I have not been able to obtain a copy. In Puniyad, in handwritten manuscript registers no. 5, 9, 25, 31, 85, 101, 106, 105/1, 14, 66, 143, and 218, there are in all about 45 scattered sakhis of Khojiji, and from the yajna-shala in Jaipur too I have copied down about 9 sakhis.

Kabirvad

At Kabirvad, Gyaniji met Kabirji. There Kabirji gave Gyaniji spiritual teaching (upadesh). When Kabirji placed his hand on Gyaniji's head, Gyaniji beheld the form of Ram; and when he opened his eyes, he saw Kabirji standing there. So Gyaniji asked: "O Baba, are you Kabir, or are you Ram?" Kabirji replied: _"Sheeshe mein jo cheez hoti hai, vohi dikhti hai"_ (whatever thing is truly within the mirror — that alone is what one sees).

Thus Gyaniji beheld Kabirji under the combined name Ram-Kabir, and this is how he gave us the name Ram-Kabir.

This village lies next to Zaghadiya. There is the gadi (spiritual seat) of Gyaniji Maharaj there, and his samadhi (memorial shrine) with its tulsi-kyaro (a raised bed for the tulsi plant). Gyaniji resided at this place in order to carry on a householder's family life together with Gangaba.

In their courtyard, lightning once struck a neem tree; Gyaniji wedged a wooden beam into the hollow it left, and that beam still survives today. Today, Gyaniji's descendants are living at this place.

sections.title_en: Shrimali and Koshmali (villages in Surat district)
sections.translation:
Shrimali, Koshmali

In Surat district, next to Orna, there is a village named Shrimali. There, in a temple, are the images of three great souls: Gyaniji, Madhavdasji, and Bhandasji — the images of all three together. Some time ago, since these images had grown old, new images were installed in their place.

Thus, among these images, our own Gyaniji Maharaj too sits enshrined in that temple. Therefore this Shrimali is a holy place (punya sthali) for us.

Palasvada

Santdas, a disciple of Jivanji Maharaj, established a gadi (spiritual seat) in this village. Since there proved to be no heir to it, an heir from Gyaniji Maharaj's own family, from Mota Sanja, now occupies this gadi. Gyaniji Maharaj's gadi has thus been established there, and near the temple there are seven tulsi-kyaras (raised tulsi-plant beds); one of these is likely Santdasji's. Jagdishchandra Jugaldas Maharaj, the last to occupy this gadi, used to say that among these tulsi-kyaras there is also likely one belonging to Raghunathdasji, who was born within Gyaniji Maharaj's lineage. Thus this place holds the memory both of Gyaniji Maharaj and of Santdasji, the disciple of Jivanji Maharaj, and moreover has these tulsi-kyaras. This is how tulsi-kyaras are found within our own tradition — as at Patan, Mota Sanja, Palasvad, Puniyad, Sabalpur, Sardarpur, Bodeli, Hansapura, Amadara, Tandalja, and elsewhere. For this reason, this

Palasvad is, for us, a closely-connected and important holy place.

At Patra, in the satsang gathering held at the home of devotee Lakshmanbhai Raghunathbhai, a reckoning of Jivanji Maharaj's gadis is set down on page 64 [of that record].

On page 1577 of that same gathering's record _[unclear]_, is written the account concerning Jivan['s authority] (the passage here is too damaged to render with confidence). This is followed by the sakhi of Visram Bija, of the lineage of Rankavanka:

_[unclear — the couplet itself is too badly garbled in the source to transliterate or translate reliably.]_

The truth of this saying is borne out by this very gathering — that many people have had parcha (a manifest sign) of Jivandasji.

(1) Malva; (2) _[unclear]_, son of a devotee of Pransvadi-Dhaman; (3) _[unclear]_ — this is indeed the gadi at Surat itself; (4) Sardarpur — from among these _[the rest of this sentence is too garbled to render reliably]_.

Their names: first, the Vaishnav of Malva, Gopaldas Santdas, of Chanderiya village — the gadi in Malva continues through him. Further, Santdasji came to Gujarat to join Jivandasji. He took up residence in the village of Paransvada and carried forward the tradition (nad) there — that is the second gadi.

Then, when Vaishnavji [Jivandasji] came to reside at Mangleshwar, the spirit of Bhoja Gujar had entered the body of Rambai, wife of Keshavdas Zadeshariya; he delivered her from it. Through this, devotion arose in Keshavdas Soni, and he made people of the villages of Surat pargana into Vaishnavs, carrying the tradition forward as a gadi in Surat.

In the village of Puniyad, Vaishnavji used to bring about Hari-parcha (manifest signs of the Divine) at satsang gatherings; in that connection, Krishnadasji, a worshipper of Ganesh, came to him, and Vaishnavji, in his grace, gave him the mala (rosary) and tilak; his gadi continues in the village of Vijapur, in Sardarpur pargana.

When Vaishnavji departed for his heavenly abode (sadham), at the gathering held on that occasion the Vaishnavs assembled together. Among them was the Vaishnav Kanhandasji, humble and wholly devoted. Vaishnavji, upon seeing him, showed very great grace and placed his own neck-mala upon Kanhandasji, entrusting him with the dharma of the tradition; this was accepted by all the Vaishnavs present, who then paid homage to Kanhandasji. Then the Vaishnavs of that assembly, finding Samdasji to be exceedingly discerning, and recognising him as a revered, manifest form born of Vaishnavji's own body, made repeated entreaty to Vaishnavji, saying: "The service (tehel) of this seat has been entrusted to Kanhandasji, but should Samdasji remain in your household, then, by the will of the Vaishnavs present, the dharma of the household-tradition belongs to him." Hearing this, Vaishnavji, through Kanhandasji, graciously entrusted the service to Samdasji as well; and the gadi of Samdasji's family continues in the village of Puniyad.

Samdasji's son, Dwarkadasji, received the mala and tilak from Vaishnavji in his presence, along with the Naha Parekh. Later, when they met again at a satsang gathering, it was affirmed that this is the eternal (sanatan) dharma of the tradition. But because Dwarkadasji began to carry on the practice of dharma while harbouring a hidden self-interest, Parakhji's mind was wounded, and he asked for a word of the guru's grace; Dwarkadasji granted it. He then went and settled in the village of Darapara, and fulfilled the words of the true guru, Bhakti-Satguru Jivandasji; many devotees came there to meet him, and to them, with grace, he revealed the Vaishnav dharma — that is another gadi.

6. Darapara, 7. Hansapura — these [two gadis] continue to this day.

In their lineage is Ratanji Bhanaji; in that household was Samdas Ratanji, who became the leading figure (narsaiyo) of their dharma. Further, upon Samdasji's gadi there came to sit the head (swami) of the Bund lineage. He carried himself with an attitude of self-importance, on account of which the Vaishnavs suffered distress. Then, at the village of Sahapar, there was an old, established temple of the Vaishnavs; recognising this, it was made into a place of rest (visram). That gadi was carried on by entrusting its service to Mohandas Swami, son of Vitthaldas Swami — but it is not accompanied by parcha (manifest divine proof); it appears to carry on merely the customary rites pertaining to the body/lineage.

In this way, seven gadis have come to be known up to this day, and they have been described and set down here in writing. Further, should any Vaishnav come to learn more, let this seventh and final gadi be expanded upon accordingly.

In the family of Parakhji, holder of the sixth gadi, is Ratanji Bhanji. He had four sons: (1) Kanhandas, (2) Keshavdas, (3) Samdas, and (4) Dialdas — the last born of a different mother; his own sons numbered three: the eldest, Laldas Mohota; the second, Harjivandas; the third, Jagjivandas. On account of Jagjivandas, Laldas Mohota performed an act of renunciation (khovatpanu) — regarding which there is this sakhi:

_[unclear — the couplet is too badly garbled in the source to transliterate or translate reliably.]_

Thuvavi

In Thuvavi lived devotees who loved Jivanji. When their womenfolk came to Bhilapur to meet Jivanji, the Dhadhar river gave them passage across. Such powerful devotees dwelt there.

In Thuvavi there is the gadi (spiritual seat) of Gyaniji's descendants, and their heirs still live there. It therefore calls to mind our guru Gyaniji, and also the ardent devotees of Jivanji. So Thuvavi too is a holy place (punya sthali).

Zadeshwar

In Zadeshwar lived the descendants of Gyaniji; they may still be there today. At Mangleshwar, Jivanji had delivered the wife of Keshavdas, Rambai, from the spirit of Bhoja Gujar that had entered her body — this Keshavdas was from this very Zadeshwar, and so Keshavdas is known by the name Keshavdas Zadeshwariya. This Keshavdas was a goldsmith (soni) by caste.

Devotee Narsinhbhai Ramji, of the Naria neighbourhood (khadki) of Vadodara, was employed at Vadsal. While he was there singing the aarti (devotional hymn), a goldsmith living nearby, overhearing him, began to say: "This is our aarti, to Padmanabh." Narsinhbhai replied: "No, this is our aarti." As this pulling back and forth continued between them, the goldsmith said: "We are Uda Sonis (goldsmiths of the Uda order)." Saying this, he gave him a handwritten manuscript. Narsinhbhai had shown this manuscript to me, but today it is no longer with his heir Vitthalbhai — which is a matter of regret.

This episode thus recalls an event from the lifetime of Jivanji. So this Zadeshwar too is a holy place.

Note: Keshavdas Soni may have become an Uda [renunciate], but the heirs of Krishnadas of Sardarpur did not give up their brahmin status and remained brahmins, and so the mahants of Sardarpur are brahmins. In the same way, it seems the heirs of Keshavdas did not give up their status as goldsmiths, and so remained goldsmiths. But it has come to be known that the last among them was, in this way, a goldsmith known as Uda Soni.

sections.title_en: Shuklatirth (a pilgrimage site on the Narmada)
sections.translation:
Shuklatirth

Dada Sukhji, also known as Jasvantji, was a disciple of Gyaniji Maharaj. His disciple, Gopaldas of Choranda, was in turn the guru of Jivanji.

As their place of residence, this Shuklatirth deserves to be reckoned a historic site, and in this way it is a holy place (punya sthali). No memorial of this great soul remains there, but it is a holy place as the abode of Dada Sukhji.

Guru Gopaldasji, the guru of Jivanji, lived at this place. Nothing has remained after him that would serve as a memorial, so this Chorenda is regarded as a place of merit (punya sthali) simply because it was Guru Gopaldasji's residence.

The writing on pages 95 to 97 of handwritten manuscript no. 28 was copied by the revered Yadunath into pages 340–345 of handwritten manuscript no. 111. It was printed in Jivanvani, Year 1, Issue 2, on the full-moon day of Falgun, Samvat 2032, pages 1–2, and reads as follows. It mentions Chorenda and records an episode from the life of Jivanji.

Ramkabir: _Jivanji Maharaj Dhanore padharya te Chanderiyethi Chorande padharya._ (Jivanji Maharaj arrived at Dhanora, having come to Chorenda from Chanderiya.)

Jivandasji arrived at Dhanora together with Gopaldasji, Santdasji, and Rupa Bhagat. Devdasji and Gopaldasji had arrived at Dhanora, coming by way of Deva Sahi from Chanderiya to Chorenda. On the occasion of the Sharad-nisha festival (the autumn full-moon night celebration), they came, on the way, to a village named Dhanora, where Jivandasji and the other Vaishnavs all sat beneath a peepal tree by the lake, and hari-kirtan (devotional singing) was taking place. Now this peepal tree was dry, withered away. The village Patels (headmen) sent a man to cut it down, but Jivandasji said, "The peepal tree is in fact green — it must not be cut. Moreover, the peepal tree is spoken of in the Gita too, that it is not to be cut." This is the word of the Gita, chapter 10:

_Ashvattha sarvavrikshanam devarshinam cha Naradah, Gandharvanam Chitrarathah siddhanam Kapilo munih. ||25||_ (Among trees I am the peepal; among the divine sages, Narada; among the Gandharvas, Chitratha; among the perfected beings, the sage Kapila — Bhagavad Gita 10.25.)

Note: Trees speak, and they plead too; the example of the peepal tree fits this account well. (Kalyan, Year 33, Issue 9, page 1201.)

_Hari daal mat todiye, laage sukha baan, das Maluka yon kahe, apni so 'jiya jaan'._ (Do not cut a green branch — it feels as if struck by a dry arrow; so says servant Maluka: know it as you would know your own [pain].) (Jagdish's manuscript no. 258; Shamal Haribhai's no. 1, part 1, page 141.)

Then that man went back and reported that the peepal had indeed turned green. Hearing this, all the villagers came and had darshan of the saints. As they did so their minds grew clear, and they asked, "This peepal was dry — how did it turn green?" Jivandasji said, "This peepal dried up on account of the bones of an ungrateful person, and that is also why water does not stay in the lake."

_Kritaghni ke haadsu peepal suko jaay, kunvarika ku doshan lagyo, kahi samjhavi chinh._ (Because of the bones of an ungrateful one the peepal withers; blame fell upon a maiden — so it is told and explained.) (Najarnani's no. 8, page 32.)

Note: See Amarcharitra, part 5, pages 245–247. Registration no. 251/15, "Janabai, the Image of Devotion."

_So jivan lilo kiyo, satguru tane pasaay._ (Thus Jivan[dasji] made it green, by the grace of the true guru.)

Then it became known that he was some great and holy soul. Knowing this, they came with a request and said, "In our family there is a girl who has been disabled in body since birth." They brought her and placed her at his feet in surrender. He then said to Santdasji, "Go, fill water from the lake." Santdasji took the kamandal (water pot) and went, but no water came, so he returned and told the Maharaj there was no water. Jivandasji said, "Brothers, in this world the peepal has dried up on account of the bones of an ungrateful man, and there is also no water in the lake — but by the power of the saints, water will come." He then sent Santdas again, saying, "Go — there is water in the lake now."

_Adhik badhavat aapte, jan mahima Raghuvir, savari pad raj prasatan, sudh bhayo salita nir. ||1||_ (The glory of the Lord's devotee grows ever greater, like [that of] Raghuvir [Lord Ram]; through the touch of the dust of his feet [as with Shabari], the water of the river became pure. (1)) (Najar's large notebook no. 9, page 46; Venkateshwar Press, Bhaktavala, page 27.)

In this way water appeared. Santdasji brought the water and gave it to the Maharaj, who took it and sprinkled it on the girl's body and had her drink it; her disability left her body, she became radiant, and knowledge (gyan) dawned within her.

The words of Harmabai: _Harmabai harakhiyan Jivan darshan paay, sarid sanso mitiyo, bhayo gyan prakash._ (Harmabai rejoiced on receiving the darshan of Jivan[dasji]; all doubt and distress were dispelled, and the light of knowledge dawned.)

The words of Harmabai: _Gyan prakashi guru miliya, so kem visaryo jaay, jo Govind kripa kare, guru malege aay._ (The guru who kindled the light of knowledge — how could he ever be forgotten? If Govind [the Lord] shows grace, the guru will come and be met again.)

Reckon these as her sakhis of joy. They rejoiced, saying that this girl was some blessed, divine being. Recognizing this, Jivandasji placed his hand upon her head. Hearing of this happening, Ratansinghji said, "I offer this girl to you; please accept her." Hearing this, Jivandasji replied, "We have set out to wander through the land, and ours is the life of a sadhu (mendicant), so this is not fitting for us." Then, pleading earnestly, Harmabai said:

_Tumku chhod avar kyan jaau, nisdin tumari sang rahavun._ (Leaving you, where else could I go? Day and night I would remain in your company.)

Hearing these words of Harmabai, he accepted her — just as, of old, Lord Jagannath Swami gave Padmavati to the devotee Jaidevji, so too did Jivandasji, by Hari's will, accept Harmabai. He himself stayed there for one month, performed hari-kirtan, and gave everyone the teaching of knowledge (gyan). He then told Harmabai, "We shall go visit Jagannathji, Naimisharanya, Kashi, Ayodhya, Mathura, and Badrikashram; when we return we shall look after you." Saying this, he set out for Chorenda.

This account was copied out of devotion from the notebook of the Vaishnav Dana Bhagat of Malwa and Savji Bhagat, by Bhagat Kashiram, a resident of Bhoj village, and I include it here through the tradition of the saints. (Handwritten manuscript no. 25, page 97.) The Malwa notebook was copied out in the month of Magha, Samvat 1836. See handwritten manuscript no. 111, pages 346–347.

At this place, Jivandasji Maharaj first set eyes on and met Guru Gopaldasji. Gopaldasji was returning from someone's memorial rite (karaj) when he met Jivanji. This Keslu-ba is the village today known as Kesru, near Bharuch. When a meeting with one's future guru takes place even before he formally becomes one's guru, that meeting place is considered worthy of remembrance. Thus Keslu-ba is a place of merit (punya sthali).

He had gone to Malwa together with Guru Gopaldas in Samvat 1867. There the two became separated, and Gopaldasji passed away in Ujjain. There, on the bank of the river Shipra, stands the Gopal Mandir, which houses the image of Morli Manohar (the flute-charmer, Krishna). While teaching Jivanji, Gopaldasji had said that the true Morli Manohar was the cowherd of Gokul, who carries one beyond the Vedas of Brahma [i.e., surpasses even scriptural knowledge through pure devotion]. Because this temple in Ujjain belongs to Gopaldasji, who spoke these words, and because it is also the place where Gopaldasji gave up his body, Ujjain is a place of merit (punya sthali). Moreover, when Jivandasji returned from the Himalayas, he came to Ujjain. He must have remembered his guru, and, thinking also of his beloved devotees, he came here. Around Ujjain, in places such as Chanderiya and Khediya, his devotees lived; one of them, a woman named Jyotibai, had also come to Ujjain to shop. She spotted Jivanji there, and, overjoyed [almost beside herself], went and brought the other devotees to him. Thus this Ujjain is a place of merit (punya sthali) that recalls the meeting of guru and disciple, and disciple and guru.

_Gaam Sokhde saadh sabhi rahe, taki baat aay sabe kahe._ (In the village of Sokhda dwell all manner of holy men [sadhus]; everyone who comes tells their stories.)

In the village of Sokhda a number of sadhus used to live; everyone who came would tell their tales. In Sokhda there lived Jagaji, a disciple of Guru Gopaldasji (the guru of Jivanji Maharaj). His seat (hermitage) is in the forest. It is known today by the name of the "Valley Saint" (Veliya). If one wants to see what a real forest looks like, this place is like a magnificent forest.
