Nowadays, because of development, what was once wilderness has been turned into something pleasant and garden-like, but when I saw it before this development happened, in 1997, it looked like a fearsome forest. The followers of Jagaji are the native people of Sokhda. They have built a grand marble temple to Jagaji in Sokhda. Jagaji's followers use two hymns from Adhyaruji's compositions — the aarti and the vani. These followers of Jagaji state that his appearance (praagatya) was in [Samvat] 1117, but this is a mistake: Padmanabhji's appearance was in 1457 and Jivanji's appearance was in 1660, so Jagaji's appearance must have been around 1600. In a handwritten manuscript obtained from Kunvarpura village there are sakhis (couplets) of Jagaji, so it is likely that this Jagaji had some connection with the community of devotees (bhakt samaj). We shall therefore recognize this place of Sokhda as the seat of Jivanji's guru-brother (a fellow disciple of the same guru). Ritualism (karmakand) had a strong influence in Jagaji's tradition, so when Jivanji's devotees heard of the fame of Jagaji's saint, they went to meet him. Although Jivanji had forbidden it, they went anyway. But on hearing discussions that felt watery and unsatisfying, they began to regret it, and, realizing that Jivanji Maharaj had been right to forbid their going there, they were glad. Even though this village of Sokhda is the village of Jagaji's disciples, the Mahant Hariprasad of the Swaminarayan sect has had a grand ashram built there. Because of this, the people of the village have been drawn toward the Swaminarayan sect.

In Borbar there lived Anantdasji, a guru-brother (fellow disciple) of Jivanji Maharaj; he too was a disciple of Gopaldasji. Today his descendants live on in Borbar and carry out worship at the Ranchhodji temple. Because they were addressed as "Swami," when it comes to marrying their sons and daughters into Patel families, it brings a stain (stigma) upon the lineage — so today they do not like being called "Swami." Their daughters have been married into Patel families in Kandari. Thus we shall honor this seat of Jivanji's guru-brother as a place of merit (punya sthali).

One of Gopaldasji's four disciples, Pandyaji, lived in Kandari. His tulsi-kyaro (raised tulsi-plant shrine) stands along the road leading to Kandari's railway station. This tulsi-kyaro had fallen into disrepair, and Premjivanbhai has had it repaired. The local people regard this tulsi-kyaro with reverence and consider it miraculous. Pandyaji's temple stands today in Kandari as the temple of Chaturbhuj. Revered Bhagvandas, in a time of hardship, had made his home in Kandari. Since Kahandasji, too, lived in Kandari, we shall, for these several reasons, embrace this Kandari as a sacred place of merit (punya sthali).

Shri Jivanji Maharaj was born into the Amin family of Karamsad. This is known from the writing in the genealogist's (vahivancha) register — register page 412, Vagor Bhatt Keshavdas Bhagvandas, Jaipur register, page 412.

Shri Jivanji Maharaj belonged to the Leva Patidar Amin family of the village Karamsad. The family renounced its house, mansion, and estate (jagir) and took up the path of teaching. He was born in the village Karamsad, in the settled family, in the year Samvat 1649.

From this account we shall regard Karamsad, as the birthplace of Jivanji Maharaj, as a sacred place of merit (punya sthali).

The genealogist's register records that Shri Jivanji Maharaj manifested (pragat) in the village Goriyad, at eleven years of age, in Samvat 1660, on Shravan Sud 8.

The samagam (satsang record) states: In Samvat 1660, on the eighth day (ashtami) of the bright half of Shravan, in the greater region of Gujarat, within the Kanhanav circle (mandal), lies the village called Goriyad — also known as Ghayaj — where the Vaishnav Jivandasji came, for the welfare of the soul. There the dharma of Namdev and Kabirji became manifest, and love arose to sing its glory (leela), from the age of eleven onward.

There is no surviving memorial to him in Goriyad itself, but devotees lived in the neighbouring villages of Darapura, Bhoj, and Samiyala, and presumably in Goriyad as well. Today, the devotee Ishwarbhai (Nanabhai) Bhagvanbhai and his family, living in Shiyabaug in Vadodara, are known by the title "Goriyada." Thus Goriyad, as the place where our faith first arose, is a sacred place of merit.

Once the dharma that had manifested in Goriyad kindled the love to sing its glory, Jivanji Maharaj moved on from there to Shahpura, to live in the presence of Sant Gopaldas, and spent nearly his entire life there — living in Puniyad only for the last seven years. In this Shahpura he established the Uda tradition (dharma), and his samagam (satsang record) too was kept there in worship; in Samvat 1931 the revered Fulba brought it to Puniyad. Thus this Shahpura, as the field of Jivanji's life's work (karmabhoomi), is a sacred and holy place.

In Bhilapur, at the home of Bhagvandas-Dhanbai, Jivanji Maharaj lay down to rest on Magsar Sud 2 of Samvat 1737. There he had a dream (svapnantar) in which two messengers (duta) came to summon him; Jivanji Maharaj asked them for a delay of six months. At the spot where Jivanji Maharaj had lain to rest, there stood a dense thicket of trees. Today, at that site...

...the owner of the site, Rambhai, built his own house there in its memory. In it he has kept his household shrine of daily worship at that very spot. Thus this is a historic site, and so it is a place of sacred merit.

Aritha

When Bhagat Haribhai of Aritha came to Shahpura to meet Jivanji Maharaj, Jivanji Maharaj was sitting under a mahuda tree in his own field, holding satsang (holy company). There, in the height of summer, a field of val-papdi (a bean crop) stood green — how could that be? Jivanji Maharaj said that it had turned green for the sake of the saints. This same Haribhai had a field in Aritha which had likewise turned green. In memory of this, this field in Aritha is known as the val-papdi field, a sacred ground. The devotees there have built a temple to Shivji in that field. This urge to raise such a temple is a consequence of the polluted climate of the present age. As Kabirji has said:

_Shaligramku shila par patku, Brahmaka katu shir |_
_Shivjiko sukhri lagadu, Vishnuku pahuchau shunya ||_
(I would dash the shaligram stone against a rock and cut off Brahma's head; I would smear Shivji with something to leave him writhing as though with an itch, and send the three-natured Vishnu off into the formless void.)

Kabirji is saying that he would smear Shivji with something so as to leave him restless with an itch — as if rubbed with something maddening — that he would cut off Brahma's head, and that he would send the three-natured Vishnu away into the formless void: such is Kabir's saying. So the raising of a Shiva temple in the field that carries Jivanji's memory is a result of the influence of this age; but this village, with its field of val-papdi, remains a sacred place of merit.

The samagam record states that in Samvat 1709, on Vaishakh Sud 5, Haribhai came from Aritha to Shahpura, and Vaishnav Jivanjidas himself went to the field, along with all the Vaishnavs. They went to the field and saw a great abundance of growth (rasayan) there. Then Haribhai said, "Vaishnavji, this is Vaishakh — high summer — where has this lush growth come from?" In reply it was said that this is the word of Bhagat Bardaoli —

_Dharati ambar aade dei ane ravi rashi pani pavan ||_
_Sant jaan e to rachi nahintar karan kavan ||1||_
(The earth, the canopy of sky, the sun, the water, and the wind — know that it is the saint who has fashioned these; otherwise, what other cause could there be?)

This is the word of Parashuram:

_Gaau santan ke karane | Hari varsavat meh |_
_Take pichhe Parashuram | Duniya paale deh ||1||_
(For the sake of the cow and the saints, Hari sends down the rain; and because of that, Parashuram sustains the bodies of the world.)

_Gau santan bhukhe mare | Duniya lapalap khay |_
_Ta karan the Parashuram | Suka pad pad jay ||2||_
(When the cow and the saints go hungry while the world eats greedily, it is for that reason that Parashuram lets the land turn dry and barren.)

From the wording of this samagam it is said that Jivanji made the growth green in the field at Shahpura; but if we also say that he made the val-papdi field green at Aritha, confusion arises. The explanation for this, from the handwritten manuscript (hasta likhit granth) no. 98, page 29, is as follows.

As an illustration of how the growth was made green at Shahpura: it is like a person who irrigates with water from a well to make a garden, in which other grasses and the like also grow. Using this illustration, in a mystic (samadhi) idiom, to explain its true purpose, it is written that:

"The one who owns the well is the Lord of Grace (Kripanath); the saplings are the saints; the wild grass and undergrowth are the world — this growth was made for the sake of the saints." This manuscript no. 98 records, regarding the growth God made for the saints, the following account:

Question Two

Ram Kabir, Question Two — the village of watermelons. In Shahpura, Vaishnav Jivandasji resides. In Samvat 1709, on Vaishakh Sud 5, Vaishnav Haribhai came from the village Aritha. He came to the field. There the Vaishnav brought and set out the growth (rasayan). "Bucha, Maharaj — how did this growth come about, in the month of Chaitra?" When the Vaishnav asked this, Vaishnavji said: there is a well; from it a garden has been made; there are many saplings in it, and within it countless wild grasses and undergrowth are nourished. This is only an illustration — the principle to be understood is that the growth was made for the sake of the saints.

Thus, regarding Jivanji at Shahpura, the above is what is written in the handwritten manuscript no. 98, pages 29 to 31. On reflection, it appears that when Haribhai came from Aritha to Shahpura, it must have been in the heat of summer, in a month such as Vaishakh, and watermelons were being offered to the devotees to eat; these watermelons must have been grown by him in his own field named Vadiya, that...

...field is currently recorded as Survey No. 201, and is in the possession of the devotee Gunvantbhai, alias Jashbhai Vitthalbhai, of Vadodara. From this it can be inferred that the abundant summer growth (rasayan) Haribhai saw in this field included watermelons as well, and that Jivanji Maharaj welcomed the saints and devotees with watermelon.

There is also another traditional story (dant-katha), that Jivanji Maharaj made a field of val-papdi green in Aritha; that field lies at the edge of the village. The question arises whether Jivanji Maharaj showed Haribhai the abundant growth at Shahpura, or at Aritha — but if we consider this with reason, it may be said that Haribhai, seeing how Jivanji Maharaj carried on the work of farming at Shahpura, was himself inspired to farm in the same way; so the val-papdi and other greens that he grew in his own field came, out of gratitude to Jivanji Maharaj, to be spoken of as "the field Jivanji Maharaj made green." One thing, however, is certain: that Jivanji Maharaj did carry on farming. Jivanji Maharaj never once asked a devotee for a gift. Haridas of Nadiad writes: Jivan placed his own hand upon his own head — he never stretched out his hand toward another.

Tandalja

Jivanji Maharaj had five sons; one of them, Govinddas, was the fourth son, whose wife was Krishnabai. This Govinddas was known as Daji Kaka. His tulsi-kyaro (raised platform for the sacred tulsi plant) stands at the edge of Tandalja. He left no son as heir, but this site of the tulsi-kyaro at Tandalja is a sacred place of merit.

Govinddas is also called Bapuji. Just as, in Aritha, a temple to Shiva was built in the val-papdi field, so too, under the influence of this age, the devotees at Tandalja have built a temple to the Mother [goddess] — which is regrettable. There are many places of worship in Tandalja; at one of these, ascetics (bavas) used to live as well.

sections.title_en: Mangleshwar (a village/temple-site name, lit. "the auspicious Lord")
sections.translation: On Jeth Sud 2 of Samvat 1716, Jivanji Maharaj came to Mangleshwar. There, Rambai, the wife of Keshavdas Jhadeshwariya the goldsmith (soni), was possessed by the ghost (pret) of Bhoja Gurjar. Jivanji Maharaj liberated (delivered) that spirit, and made Keshavdas an Uda devotee. Thus this place is where Bhoja Gurjar was liberated, and it is also the place where Keshavdas Jhadeshwariya Soni received initiation (diksha) — so it is a sacred place of merit. The chief reason for Jivanji Maharaj's manifestation (pragatya) was for the liberation of Bhoja Gurjar; along with him, Jivanji Maharaj also liberated many devotees such as ourselves.

Jivanji Maharaj's third son was Harakhji, who is known by the name Bava Kaka. His wife's name was Vahalbai.

This Bava Kaka's tulsi-kyaro (a raised platform planted with sacred tulsi/basil, marking a devotee's memorial) is in Nana Amadara, and so it is a punya sthali (a place of religious merit). That place was given by the grandfather of Muljibhai of the Amin family.

Malwa

In Samvat 1687 he went to Malwa together with Guru Gopaldas. There, at places such as Khediya and Chanderiya, Jivanji gave discourse and made devotees; among them the very first devotee was Naranadas Khatri of Bareli. This Naranadas met Krishnadas Maharaj at Puniyad. At present Jivanji's devotees are still living in Ratlam, and so these places located in the Malwa region are counted as punya sthali (places of religious merit): (1) Bareli, the village of Naranadas Khatri; (2) Chanderiya, the village of Nana Gopaldas; (3) Khediya, the village of Mota Gopaldas.

In Chanderiya, Santdas became a devotee. He began preaching in Palasvad, and so the gadi (spiritual seat) at Palasvad is known by the name of this Santdasji. Around Samvat 2020, Revered Yadunath Maharaj conducted a count of the devotees of Surat; in it, in Jagdish Notebook No. 177, page 60, under village Chanderiya's Hanumanji temple, village No. 75, the name of devotee Parbhubhai Rambhai is recorded. Thus the people of this Chanderiya reached all the way to Surat. Therefore we shall honor these three villages of Malwa as punya sthali.

Devotees used to live in six or seven villages around Ratlam. All of them had a pantiyalo parathāro [unclear] at the home of Dhasi Ram, who lived in Ratlam. Festivals such as Ram Navami and Janmashtami used to be held in this Ratlam. At present there is one devotee, Chogalal, in Javara, but he has become a disciple of the Kabir temple at Shiyabag, Vadodara — yet he used to come to Puniyad. Today in Ratlam, devotees have again begun coming — including the family of a devotee from Doshigam and others — and on Ram Navami and Janmashtami a number of about 25 to 30 people regularly attend.

Kukash

Jivanji's fifth son was Akshaykumar; his wife's name was Manbai. There is not much information about this son, but the Maharaj of Sardarpur, Rambhai, said that a son of Jivanji once lived here in Kukash — he himself had gone there once — but the temple of Nayakaka in Kukash belongs to followers of Pirana (a separate sect), and their tomb is there, so that temple does not concern us. Still, this son's site must be somewhere in Kukash, though it no longer exists today; even so, as the site of one of Jivanji's sons, this is counted as a punya sthali (a place of religious merit).

Surat

Jivanji Maharaj's eldest son is known by the name Vasantdas, Vaishnavdas, or Naranadas. His wife's name was Mathurabai. This Naranadasji ran the gadi (spiritual seat) of Surat. After him, an acharya (spiritual head) is appointed from among the devotees of Surat. When I inquired, I learned a little: that there used to be a tulsi-kyaro (a sacred tulsi-plant platform) behind the temple at Surat, though today no one has information about it. But the line of acharyas of the Surat gadi has continued on from Naranadas. Thus Surat is a punya sthali (a place of religious merit), and today there is a grand temple there.

Mumbai - 33

In Mumbai, so that devotees of Surat district could conveniently stop over on their way to America, the devotees built a Ramkabir temple in Vile Parle. At that place the Surat community has arranged facilities for travelers, and I too have made use of it. When I came to this temple in the year 1990, on my way to America, I stayed there overnight and then went on to America. A temple of Kabirji has been built at this place. Thus this Mumbai too is a punya sthali (a place of religious merit).

America - Carson

In America, at Carson in California, the devotees of Surat have built a grand temple. Because a dispute arose over this temple, some brothers from Surat built a second hall-temple in Los Angeles. Thus there are two temples in America, and these are our punya sthali (places of religious merit).

Pachiyapura

At present only about one devotee from Surat lives there; earlier, devotees used to live there. This is mentioned in an article by a doctor of that place, published in an issue of Janakalyan (a magazine), somewhere in its Year 4 to Year 6, which wrote that in this village there was the house of a Kabir-panthi (follower of the Kabir path) devotee. At their home there was a mud grain-bin (kothi); it never needed to be refilled with fresh grain — rather, grain was taken out daily from its lower compartment to run a sadavrat (a continuous free food distribution). That house and grain-bin were destroyed when a flood came in a certain year. So at present there is nothing there except perhaps a single devotee. Thus this can be said to be our punya sthali (a place of religious merit). In Udadharma, Edition 1, and in Bhajan Sagar, three devotees from this village are counted.

Idar, Hindovar, Davad

Krishnadas Maharaj's ancestors came from some village in Gujarat and settled in Idar. When Muslim rule was established there, Krishnadas went to live with his maternal relatives in Hindaver. When he met Naranadas at Puniyad, he told him that he was a resident of Davad; so it is said he used to live in Davad. Thus Idar, Hindovar, and Davad are punya sthali (places of religious merit) associated with the name of Krishnadas.

Agalod

Having taken diksha (initiation) from Jivanji Maharaj, Krishnadas went to Agalod. There he stayed at the home of the devotee Dhana Mangala Shitala, and Krishnadas made his own home there. Today at that place there is only a ruined, abandoned plot resembling an old tulsi-kyaro. From there his descendants came and settled in Sardarpur; therefore Agalod is a punya sthali (a place of religious merit).

Today, the descendants of Krishnadas Maharaj have established the gadi (the guru's seat of succession) at Sardarpur. It stands as the guru-gadi for the devotees of Kantha district. Thus this Sardarpur is a sacred site. A few tulsi-kyaros (tulsi-plant memorial platforms marking a departed saint's resting place) of the gadi's descendants are also there, though they now lie neglected and deserted.

Krishnadas Maharaj lived in Aglod, but he passed away at Sabalpur, at his daughter's home; hence today there is a tulsi-kyaro of Krishnadas Maharaj at Sabalpur. In recent times, his relatives, residents of Ahmedabad, have had this garden grandly renovated and have appointed a caretaker there. Next to it stands a school building. Thus this Sabalpur is a sacred site.

The tulsi-kyaro of the family members of the descendants of Navi Jithardi is in the field of Bhagat Vitthal Bhagwan of Kasampur. That field came to him from Khushal Swami. Khushal Swami's son, Bhagwan Swami, was the last in that line; he passed away around Samvat 2060. At present there is no one at Kasampur. Bhagwan Swami had only a daughter; he passed away at her home in Ganpatpura. Thus this Kasampur is a sacred site. It was to the village of Or that devotees had invited Jivanji; this Or is the very same place as Kasampur.

_Rasik jan Jivan bhaye, kini bhakti prakash. Nahana nikat bolaayke, rakhya charan nivash. ||1||_ (Jivan[das] became a devoted seeker and made the light of bhakti [devotion] shine forth; calling Nahana near him, he gave him a home at his feet.)

_Gaam hamara Darapara, Sai hamara Ram. Sadguru Jivandasji, Parakh dhariya naam. ||2||_ (Our village is Darapara, our Lord [Sai] is Ram; our true guru is Jivandasji — I took on the name Parekh [as his disciple].)

The papers recording the time when Jivanji Maharaj departed to the eternal abode were burned in the original satsang (holy company/gathering). So Nana Parekh supplied the missing account, and in it he mentions his native place, Darapara. It was in this village that he began his own independent preaching. He had received initiation into Uda Dharma (the tradition's ascetic vow) from Dwarkadas, the grandson of Jivanji Maharaj. His tulsi-kyaros (tulsi-plant memorial platforms marking a departed saint's resting place) are at Darapura, ranging from Jivanji down to Nana Parekh. Thus this place is a sacred site.

After Nana Parekh, since no one remained behind at Darapara, the gadi (the guru's seat of succession) was brought from Darapura to Vadodara; Bhagwan Swami brought it from Darapara to Hathipol. From Hathipol, Bhagnadas Swami brought it, in Samvat 1954, to Vayadapol, at the fair (mela) of Ranchhod Haribhai. When the site of Gordhan Pitambar became available for installing the gadi, Bhagat Ishwarbhai Zaverbhai had a new building constructed on the Gordhan Pitambar site and installed the gadi there on Shravan Vad-8 of Samvat 1982; it continues there to this day. Thus this Vadodara is a sacred site.

In the lineage of Jivanji Maharaj, Vitthaldasji, the brother of Vasantdas, established a second gadi (seat of succession) at Hansapura. Thus, in the garden (vadi) at Hansapura, are the tulsi-kyaros (tulsi-plant memorial platforms marking a departed saint's resting place) of the swamis of Hansapura, beginning from Jivanji. Later the gadi was taken from Hansapura to Bodeli, but the site where the gadi once stood remains at Hansapura even today. Thus this place is a sacred site.

The gadi (seat of succession) was taken from Hansapura to Bodeli. There, that gadi continues to this day, but no member of the swami's family now sits upon it as swami; it is run by trustees. The tulsi-kyaros (tulsi-plant memorial platforms marking a departed saint's resting place) of the swamis who occupied the gadi are at Bodeli, but no tulsi-kyaro has been built for the last swami, Bapalal. Thus this Bodeli is a sacred site.

The revered Jagannath Maharaj built a temple at Falu in Samvat 1956. That temple has since been shifted to New Falu (Nava Falu). Jamnaba, wife of Jagannath, who had come from Puniyad, used to tend to that gadi (seat of succession). After she passed away there, Gangaba, Jagannath's second wife, stayed on for some time to tend to it. After Jagannath's own passing, she returned to Puniyad; thereafter a priest (pujari) was appointed. Today the gadi continues with the cooperation of the village; it is a sacred site.

Jugaldas, a cobbler (mochi) by caste, a native of Bordi Falia in Shiyabag, Vadodara, tried to accept Uda Dharma (the tradition's ascetic vow), but his community would not accept him back. So he took initiation from Mahant Vallabhdasji of the Kabir temple at Shiyabag and became a sadhu, yet he continued to observe Uda Dharma. He composed a hymn summarizing 28 kirtans (devotional hymns). On hearing news that his guru had passed away, he too passed away immediately after. Thus guru and disciple departed to the eternal abode on the very same day. The samadhis (memorial tombs) of both of them were at Manjalpur, his and his guru's, placed side by side. But on Maha Sud-5 of Vikram Samvat 2065, when I went to record the inscription on his samadhi, the entire building was being newly rebuilt, and it had been demolished; however, I had already noted down the inscription there beforehand, and it reads as follows:

'Satyanam, Shri Sadhu Jugaldasji, [disciple of] Guru Shri Vallabhdasji Saheb, departed to the true realm (Satya Lok) on Wednesday, Kartak Sud 15, Samvat 1974.'

In the same way, an inscription was also found on Vallabhdasji's samadhi. His guru's name was Shri Sadhu Guru Bijakdasji.

Dudhrej

_Suni shatpragnaswami yash varmirtan, rutharej gaye sumuhit man ||_ ([unclear] — the source line is garbled)

It is stated therein that Jivanji Maharaj came to Dudhrej together with about five hundred renunciant sants (ascetic saints). At that time a miracle is also mentioned as having occurred there. All the sants and devotees [text continues on the next page]

...to prepare food, they checked for milk but did not find enough. So, on Chhathabava's instruction, they filled water from the Dugdhsar (Milk Lake) there and brought it, and in those vessels the water turned into milk. From it a milk pudding (dudhpak) was prepared.

Kantikumar Bhatt has given information about this on pages 23-27 of the book of Jivanji and Jivanji's devotees. Thus this Dudhrej is filled with the memory of Jivanji, and therefore it is a punya sthali (a sacred, blessed place).

Patdi Bajanu

While going to Dwarka, at the halting place of Patdi Bajanu, a jambu (jamun) tree had dried up. It was said that by the time they returned after going to Dwarka it would turn green again — and it did turn green. Thus this place is now known as Jambudiyo Ovaro (the Jamun-tree landing/ghat). Therefore this place of Patdi Bajanu, with its Jambudiyo Ovaro, is a punya sthali. The Patravala devotee Kanubhai Jivaji has gone and visited this place.

Thus we shall call these places, which remind us of Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, by the name punya sthali (sacred sites).

Ganpatpura

When Jivanji Maharaj was going from Puniyad to Orgam (Kasampur), on the way, the children of other devotees who were also travelling with him became thirsty. They made a request to Jivanji Maharaj, so at one place he lifted the lever of a well (a dhenkli, a counterweighted water-lifting device) and drew out water, and gave everyone to drink. This place is located near Ganpatpura, where there is a pond (talavda). Therefore this Ganpatpura too is a punya sthali (sacred place).

We do not hold pilgrimage (tirth yatra) itself sacred, but we shall call the memorial, sacred places of our Sadguru by the name punya sthali. Just as holy souls are addressed by the title punya shlok (of blessed repute), so too we shall call such places by the name punya sthali.

Dwarka

The garden estate (vadi) of Thakor Gangaram, who was a servant of Shyamdasji — his temple, on entering the fort (kot), is on the left-hand side. In the yard there is a well (kui); between that well and the room, Jivandasji Maharaj used to cook daily. Having stayed there nine days and having seen the divine play (leela) of Dwarka, he came to Dhanor. At that time all the Vaishnavs gathered together. Jivandasji Maharaj told them of the leela of Dwarka, saying that it is the abode of the Lord (Prabhu's dham). Therefore one should go there — but Vaishnavs should go together in groups of five or ten, so that the joy of katha (discourse) and kirtan (devotional singing) in company may be had. He said, with his own sacred mouth (shrimukh), that at the place where he, the Vaishnav Jivandasji, used to cook, it would be good if a proper (pucca) tulsi platform were built.

In the yard of Gangaram's temple there was a well; between that temple and the well, at the place where Jivandasji used to cook, Jivanji told them to build a proper (pucca) tulsi platform. If, on searching, Gangaram's temple (house) cannot be found, then one should simply remember Jivanji Maharaj instead.

Jagannathpuri

_Purushottampur pahunche jab hi, ati manmod thayo hain tabahi ||_

_Nitya prati darshanaku uthi jaave, prem sahit, magan gun gaave ||8||_

(When he reached Purushottampur [Jagannath Puri], there was then great joy of mind. Every day he would rise to go for darshan [sacred viewing], and with love, absorbed in devotion, would sing His praises.)

After some days Jivandasji stayed in the temple hall (mohol) of Jagannathji. One time, night fell within the hall of Shri Jagannathji. Then the Vaishnav Jivandasji remained behind, hidden by a pillar. No one was normally permitted to stay there at night. The attendants (sevaks) bolted and locked the doors and went to their own homes. At midnight, inside the hall, a rhythmic dance-sound (theikar) suddenly began. Countless instruments played; countless dance-rhythms sounded and countless songs were heard, but nothing could be seen. Then Lord Shri Jagannath rose and sat up, and Jivandas bowed his head and paid obeisance (pranam). The Lord asked, "Tell me, from where have you come here?" — saying this, the two embraced each other around the neck. The Lord asked further, "For what reason have you come and manifested yourself here?" Then Shri Jivandasji said, "I received a direct command, and so I have manifested myself to give happiness to the sants. I received the command of the Purna Brahm Paramatma [the complete, Supreme Being], and so I have come here from my own abode (swadham)." Jagannath said, "O sant, listen — the tale of the Lord's own divine play (leela) is endless. I am but one portion (ansh) of Him, and day and night I do nothing but sing His praises." Jivanji said, "I wish to partake of that play of the Lord. As for you, you know how to test how much love I have for you." Seeing such devotion (bhaavna) in Jivandas, the Lord then set the divine play (khel) in motion. Instruments began to play, and the hue of loving devotion (prem bhakti) deepened. In the morning, seeing Jivanji Maharaj in the temple, everyone felt reverence for him, saying that Jivandasji was blessed to have become fortunate enough to stay in the temple. Thus both this Dwarka and Jagannathji [Puri] are punya sthali (sacred places).

Bareli

Naranadas Khatri lived in Bareli. His doubt (sanshay) of 32 years was removed by Jivanji Maharaj. To get this doubt removed, Naranadas used to run a sadavrat (a free food-distribution charity), and would tell his doubt to every sadhu and sant who came there, but no one was able to resolve it. But when Jivanji Maharaj went there, he removed this doubt. And thus Naranadas Khatri, the very first disciple of Jivanji Maharaj, became an udabhakt (an awakened, foremost devotee). Therefore this Bareli can be counted as one punya sthali (sacred site) in memory of Jivanji Maharaj.

Zulana

When Radhavdas Maharaj had gone on pilgrimage, he made a night halt near Zulana. Then, at night, robbers attempted to loot the group (sangh), but seeing the Lord protecting them, they were not able to carry out the robbery. Having heard the praise of the protecting Lord, the Thakor of that place, Gumansinh, made Radhavdasji his guru. Thus, after Naranadas of Bareli, Gumansinh of Zulana became an udabhakt (awakened devotee). In Vikram Samvat 2024, when [the author] went to Zulana, the Thakor of that place, Vishveshwarsharansinh Das, met me. He was [unclear — number illegible in source] years old. From him I obtained four handwritten manuscripts (granths). In one of those manuscripts the kirtans of Adhyaru were written; it is written therein that it was written for the reading of the young Thakor Gumansinhji of Zulana. Furthermore, a manuscript of Gumansinh was also obtained from Kuvarpura. Thus this Zulana too is a punya sthan (sacred place) of another devotee of Malva.

Bhakt Pipaji
Gangrod Fort, Jhalawar, Rajasthan

Among the eminent disciples of Ramanand, Pipaji holds a foremost place. He was the king of Gangrod Fort, but, becoming a disciple of Ramanand, he became devoted to Ram (Ram bhakti) — a worshipper of Ram (Ram upasak). At the time of Jivanji Maharaj's departure to his own abode (swadham gaman), among the holy men (sant purush) who came to take him, he too was present. In this way, the importance and standing of Pipaji is very significant for Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj. Even today in Rajasthan, the Pipa lineage tradition (Pipa vanshi sampraday) continues.

Dhana Bhagat
[unclear village name], Dist. Kota, [unclear — state name garbled in source, likely Rajasthan]

In Puniyad, on the day of Jeshtha Sud 2, Vikram Samvat 1737, the sants who came to take Jivanji Maharaj to his own abode (swadham) included Dhana Bhagat, Pipaji, Senaji, and other prominent devotees. Dhana Bhagat's lifetime would have been earlier than that of Jivanji Maharaj — he would have been a contemporary of Kabirji. Dhanaji was a great landholder (jagirdar) of 800 vigha of land, but, becoming coloured in the hue of Kabirji, he became a propagator of Kabir's thought. The entire produce of wheat from the 800 vigha of land used to be consumed in the storehouse (bhandara, i.e. given away in charitable feeding). Guru Nanak Sahib too was greatly influenced by Dhana Bhagat, and a collection of his verses (pado) is included in the Guru Granth Sahib, which is venerated by followers of the Sikh faith.

Sherkhi

[unclear]

Sherkhi village, 10 km from Vadodara, is the karmabhoomi (place of spiritual work) of Ravidas, disciple of both [Sant Shashtaprajnadasji and Bhan Saheb]. Bhan Saheb was himself the disciple of Sant Shashtaprajnadasji, the fourth-generation saint in the lineage of Nilkanthdas.

Kamijada

Bhan Saheb's living samadhi (shrine) is located here. People of the Lohana Thakkar community come here regularly, and Bhan Saheb is regarded as the kul guru (family guru) of the Thakkar community. Today there are more than 165 temples of Bhan Saheb across Gujarat.
